title: PSI-1 Version 1 Round Robin - Thermophysical Property Measurement(ELF-2 Round Robin) Investigation
objective: The key scientific objectives are: (a) Conducting baseline space ESL containerless property measurement experiments for two paired classes of levitation-based thermophysical properties:Density/Thermal Expansion, Viscosity/Surface Tension. (b) Selecting materials compatible with both electrostatic levitation (ESL) and electromagnetic levitation (EML) to allow comparison between space facilities. (c) Using modeling to evaluate theories used to predict the influence of gravity on propertymeasurement experiments. (d) Actively encouraging collaboration with existing science teams using other facilities through organizing a Round Robin test consortium
approach: The experimental approach involved inserting a sample carousel of 20 individual samples into the JAXA ISS-ELF facility, conditioning the test atmosphere, and conducting individual melt cycles on each sample. The heating lasers were used to precondition the sample when the sample is heated to a desired pre-bake temperature. Following the preconditioning period, the sample was charged by the electrodes and released to achieve stable positioning. The lasers were then used to thermally cycle the sample. The cycle starts by application of the highest laser heating power (activated by a control current setting in the ELF software measured in amps) until the sample is fully molten and achieved the maximum liquid superheat temperature. The heater power was then turned down to maintain the desired isothermal hold. Surface excitation was conducted using varying volage from the electrodes at this temperature. Surface tension and viscosity was measured using the droplet oscillation behavior. The laser power was then turned off to allow the molten sample to cool down. Density and cp/ε evaluations are conducted during the free cooling without any influence from the laser. Once recalescence occurred, the sample was then allowed to become fully solid at room temperature which marks the completion of a thermal cycle. Overall, processing a single melt cycle can take up to 10 - 15 minutes excluding the pre-bake. Following the cycle completion, the sample is retrieved back into the cartridge to end the test on this sample. Using the described experimental approach several thermophysical properties were measured on a variety of metallic melts as described below: 1. Density –One high-speed video camera was used to monitor the sample size as a function of time during the free cooling phase. Sample edge was detected using a custom algorithm for the density measurement. The volume of the sample was calculated using a known calibration of pixels/mm3, which was subsequently correlated with temperature allowing calculation of density and thermal expansion coefficient (from the slope of the density curve). Tracking of sample mass loss was accomplished post-mission using Langmuir’s equation of evaporation. 2. Surface tension – After melting, the heating laser is set to a reduced value such that the sample is held at constant temperature. A sinusoidal modulation of the positioning voltage was applied to both electrodes to excite surface oscillations without changing sample position. The resulting sample deformation was measured by the high-speed linear array. A frequeny sweep was conducted to identify natural frequency. Two method was applied to identify the natural frequency from the sweep: (1) Maximum amplitude method where maximum deformation is observed at the natural frequency and (2) Excitation crossover method where the natural frequency was observed at the linear intersections of the damped and free oscillations. Natural frequencies identified using both methods were used to evaluate the surface tension. 3. Viscosity – In conjunction to surface tension, viscosity was measured from the damped oscillations at the identified natural frequency. The characteristic exponential time decay from a sinusoidal fit was used to evaluate the viscosity. 4. Specific heat capacity and emissivity – The ratio of these two quantities was evaluated from the cooling curve as monitored by the IR pyrometer after correction for conductive mass losses to the gas environment. 5. Evaporation – Integration of the time-temperature profile allows calculation of evaporation assuming a known relationship using Langmuir’s equation for loss as a function of temperature. Pre- and post- measurement of sample mass anchors these predictions. Dynamic mass is crucial for tracking for density, surface tension and viscosity measurement.
hypothesis: The experimental hypothesis was that in microgravity environment in the absence of stirring, high quality thermophysical property would be measured compared to the ground-based levitation facility. This was successfully observed for gold samples.
research_impacts: This research aids in dissemination of an baseline archived dataset allowing researchers to validate models accounting for gravity-induced systematic error in property measurement used for industrial welding, casting and additive manufacturing operations . Industry will be better able to correlate ground and space results to expand the quantity and quality of available information without the requirement for access to space. Advance the understanding of how to best allocate the scant resources available for space-based materials property measurement using levitation. In the future this could lead to development of a model where fidelity and cost can be readily calculated for a given material classification and serve as the basis for prioritization of specific ground and space thermophysical property investigations.
hardware: JAXA ISS-ELF TEMPUS Parabolic Flight EML NASA MSFC Electrostatic Levitator (ESL)

title: PSI-10 Version 1 Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments / Flame Design(ACME/Flame Design) Investigation
objective: The primary objectives of this flight experiment are: A. Obtain soot-inception limits of quasi-steady normal and inverse spherical diffusion flames as functions of flow rate, Zst, amount of inert (N2 or CO2), and pressure for C2H4 and CH4 flames. Identify the corresponding temperatures in hot regions. Obtain similar limits and temperatures for inverse and normal coflow flames. B. Obtain detailed measurements in quasi-steady normal and inverse spherical diffusion flames for C2H4 and CH4. Determine the effects of flow rate, Zst, amount of N2, and pressure on flame temperature, size, color, and soot volume fraction. Evaluate the possible existence of steady flames. C. Obtain extinction limits as functions of Zst, amount of N2, and pressure for normal and inverse spherical C2H4 and CH4 flames. Identify the corresponding temperatures in hot regions. Identify the presence of radiative or kinetic extinction. Evaluate whether pseudo-flammability limits can be obtained for these flames.
approach: Perform spherical diffusion flame tests in drop towers and aboard the International Space Station. Consider a broad range of reactant dilutions, flow rates and pressures for normal and inverse convection directions. Observe the flames with a broad suite of cameras, radiometers, photomultiplier tubes, and thermocouples.
hypothesis: 1. Soot formation requires a region where local C/O ratio and T exceed their critical values, and where strain rate is sufficiently low. 2. Microgravity spherical diffusion flames extinguish when the peak temperature first decreases below 1130 K. 3. Steady-state spherical diffusion flames are possible.
research_impacts: This project has the potential for improving efficiency and reducing pollutant emissions in terrestrial combustors. For example, it is contributing to novel designs of future coal power plants.
hardware: Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments (ACME) Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR) Reconfiguration of Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR)

title: PSI-100 Version 4 Spacecraft Fire Experiment-III(SAFFIRE-III) Investigation
objective: The objectives of this investigation were to: (1) determine how rapidly a large scale fire grows in low-gravity and (2) investigate the low-g flammability limits compared to those obtained in NASA’s normal gravity material flammability screening test.
approach: The Saffire-III experiments were performed on the Orbital Science’s Cygnus resupply vehicle after it deberthed from the ISS. As a follow on to the Saffire 1 investigation, the Saffire III investigation also used SIBAL as the sample material. However, the experiments were conducted at a flow velocity of 30 cm/s compared to 20 cm/s during Saffire I. The flow was either concurrent or opposed. Once the sample was ignited flame images were captured using two cameras. In addition, thermocouples provided flow, flame, and plume temperatures, two radiometers recorded flame radiation, solid state sensors were used to measure pressure, CO2 and O2 mole faction, and two anemometer tracked flow velocity. All data was compressed, and subsequently downlinked. Details related to samples and experimental parameters are provided in the Experimental Details file in the Science document folder.
hypothesis: This investigation hypothesizes that due to large differences between fire behavior in normal and reduced gravity, the use of terrestrial fires and fire standards to design spacecraft fire safety systems presents an inherent risk to the vehicle because of the significant level of uncertainty. While this approach has been successful thus far, the uncertainty and risk will increase as exploration missions venture further from earth with considerably longer transit times for a safe return. There is a significant lack of microgravity data available for spacecraft designers on which to base their fire safety designs and procedures. To address this knowledge gap, this investigation proposed to conduct large-scale fire safety experiments in an expendable spacecraft without risk to a crew.
research_impacts: The Saffire-I experiment provides a new way to study a realistic fire on an exploration vehicle, which has not been possible in the past because the risks are too high. Instruments on an unmanned cargo vessel measure oxygen, carbon dioxide, heat, pressure and flame growth, and two video cameras provide views of the flame. Results determine microgravity flammability limits for several spacecraft materials, help to validate NASA’s material selection criteria, and how microgravity and limited oxygen affect flame size. The investigation is crucial for the safety of current and future space missions. Studying fire in small, sealed environments such as the Cygnus cargo supply vehicle benefits fire safety and prevention efforts on Earth, including inside mines, airplanes, or submarines.

title: PSI-101 Version 4 Smoke Aerosol Measurement Experiment-Reflight(SAME-R) Investigation
objective: Similar to the original SAME investigation, the primary objective of the SAME-R investigation was to quantify the sizes that the liquid smoke particulate achieves in low gravity and to relate the droplet size distribution to the smoke generation and smoke transport conditions in the experiment. One of the problems encountered during the SAME investigation was that after the thermal precipitators were returned to the ground, it was found that all the TEM grids were severely contaminated with some unidentified foreign particles, making these grids unusable although some of them showed shapes of certain types of smoke particles. Based on that experience the SAME-R investigation employed several modification covering new materials, extended operating conditions, and diagnostic equipments.
approach: SAME-R utilized the SAME hardware used on-orbit. Based on the experience gained from SAME, SAME-R included the following modifications: 1) a new test material, Pyrell®, an intumescent fire-retardant foam by Foamex, was introduced to replace DBP samples, 2) test conditions were broadened including higher heating temperatures and no-flow during sample heating time, and 3) a new instrument, M-pass, developed in-house GRC, was used to replace one of the two Commercial Diagnostic Enclosures that includes a DustTrak and an ionization detector used in SAME. SAME-R flight tests were conducted from July 16, to September 9, 2010, successfully completing 66 test points. After SAME-R flight tests, three major post–flight ground tests were performed to improve data reduction process and to validate the lognormal distribution assumption, the key to the moment method employed by SAME and SAME-R.
hypothesis: The three hypotheses that motivated the original SAME investigation is also applicable for the reflight SAME-R investigation: In a μg environment, with the absence of the strong buoyancy-induced flows, smoke particle growth from a pyrolyzing/smoldering source, as a result of nucleation, condensation, and coagulation, will lead to larger particles compared to those produced in 1g. The formation of the larger particles is favored by the expected higher vapor concentration and smoke residence times near the source due to the reduced velocities and mixing at μg conditions. In particular, it is hypothesized that liquid aerosol smokes produced in microgravity will exhibit substantially larger droplet sizes than under the same conditions in normal gravity (with a corresponding decrease in the particle number density for the same mass of smoke). The change in the size distribution and number density will, in turn, affect the response of the smoke detectors and possibly result in some detectors not producing an alarm when exposed to this smoke.
research_impacts: Along with the results from the original SAME investigation, the results from SAME-R can lead to technology for an advanced fire detector for future spacecraft that will be used for long duration missions. SAME will provide quantitative data on the sensitivity of these detectors to reduced gravity smokes that will allow evaluation of the adequacy of these existing technologies using relevant data. The current Fire Prevention, Detection, and Suppression (FPDS) program plan allows for the re-evaluation of future sensor technology, to allow new technology and capability to be utilized. The results from SAME are needed to provide the reduced gravity baseline data against which future detection technology developments can be evaluated. The smoke detectors developed from the results of SAME can also be useful in other extreme environments on Earth, such as submarines or underwater laboratories. Accurate detection of smoke in these environments can save lives.
hardware: Comparitive Soot Diagnostic Hardware; Refer to final report

title: PSI-103 Version 3 Shear History Extensional Rheology Experiment - II(SHERE-II) Investigation
objective: SHERE-II investigation involves a non-Newtonian fluid that will undergo preshearing (rotation) for a specified period of time, followed by stretching. This combination of shearing and extensional deformations is common in many earth-based polymer processing and manufacturing operations such as extrusion, blow-molding and fiber spinning. However, in order to accurately predict the flow behaviour of polymeric fluids under such deformation histories, an accurate knowledge of the extensional viscosity of a polymer system and its variation with strain rate is critical and will be measured during this experiment. The fundamental understanding and measurement of these complex fluids is important for containerless processing, a key operation for fabrication of parts, such as adhesives or fillers, using elastomeric materials on future exploration missions.
approach: SHERE-II is designed to investigate the effects of a pre-shear history on the transient extensional viscosity in a uniaxial stretching flow for a model filled viscoelastic suspension (consisting of inert rigid non-Brownian spheres dispersed in a dilute polymer solution).This experiment will generate additional scientific data for dilute viscoelastic polymer solutions in a broad subclass of transient uniaxial extensional flows.Understanding extensional rheology is key in understanding how to process thermoplastic elastomers (flexible elastic polymeric materials), which are very resilient and can be made very thin, and hence, lightweight.Understanding the rheological properties of highly viscoelastic suspensions may be of paramount importance for lunar in-situ resource utilization and for the future construction of a permanent lunar base.SHERE can provide data for engineering design tools that are part of computer-assisted manufacturing (CAM) systems to ensure that the rheological properties of polymeric parts have not been impacted in a variable gravity environment
research_impacts: Understanding the extensional rheology of a complex fluid such as a liquid polymer is key for containerless processing because the absence of the bounding walls of a container or vessel removes the shearing component of the deformation which typically dominates earth-based processing operations. The resulting flow is thus shear-free or extensional in character. Containerless processing is a central component in the development of in-situ fabrication technology, such as a means of producing new parts on demand or replacing existing parts or tools. This represents a critical element in the evolution of an autonomous exploration capability. In-situ fabricated parts, which may include both new and recycled materials, will be composed of plastics, filled polymers, metals, ceramics and composites. SHERE plays a role in SHERE plays a role in this area by measuring, in microgravity conditions, a material property that has a direct connection to in-situ manufacturing and fabrication of polymeric parts. In-situ manufacturing operations can occur in microgravity or reduced gravity levels (e.g. on the Moon or Mars) and may include for example, the extrusion and processing of thermoplastic elastomer films, which are very resilient and can be made thin and lightweight. These elastomeric materials may form the basis of adhesives and fillers utilized in a wide variety of repair applications, especially under a reduced gravity environment, such as the repair of space suits or other similar materials. Understanding and exploiting the ability to fabricate new parts in-situ from a limited number of precursor components is critical in future space missions where weight plays a critical role in the overall cost of a mission. Additionally, in-situ repair provides a means of maintaining systems during transport and during future exploration missions. A fundamental understanding and measurement of the extensional rheology of complex fluids also allows Earth-based manufacturing processes to be controlled and improved. Ground-based work using variants of the Filament Stretching Rheometer includes studies of spinnability, and the investigations of cohesive and adhesive instabilities which manifests themselves in adhesion and tackiness of materials. It has lead to the development of a Resin-spinning technology that allows the formation of ultra-fine elastic threads analogous to spider-silks. Control of the fluid shear history and extensional rheology of test fluid is essential to optimizing the ultimate web properties. Extensional rheology is of critical importance in optimization of polymer processing operations that involve complex flows, i.e. flows that contain both shearing (rotation) and elongation (stretching) components. Suspensions of particles in viscoelastic liquids are used in many terrestrial processing operations: polymer melts with fillers, ceramic pastes, biomedical materials, food, cosmetics or detergents. The final properties of the suspensions are greatly determined by the shape, concentration and size of the filler. In particular, the fillers can range from nanoscopic to microscopic characteristic dimensions, and this leads to very different types of flow behaviors, filler/matrix interactions and dynamics.

title: PSI-105 Version 4 Shear History Extensional Rheology Experiment(SHERE; SHERE-R) Investigation
objective: The objective of this investigation was to study the effect of pre-shear on the transient evolution of the microstructure and viscoelastic tensile stresses for monodisperse dilute polymer solutions. The SHERE flight experiment aimed to investigate and quantify, for the first time, the transient extensional stress growth characteristics of a dilute polymer solution after a defined pre-shear history. Following the initial SHERE campaign a re-flight of the investigation was carried out as SHERE-R with additional experimental runs.
approach: The test fluid used for this investigation was a dilute solution (0.025 wt.%) of a narrow polydispersity high molecular weight polystyrene (Mw equals 2.25×106 g/mol, PDI ≈ 1.02) dissolved in oligomeric styrene oil. The FM core consists of two endplates and an inner shroud, which is slid back to deploy the fluid column between the two endplates. A steady shear rate between 0 and 50 s-1 is then imposed on the fluid sample by rotating one endplate from 0 to 500 rpm for a predetermined time (5 to 60 s) while holding the other endplate stationary. As soon as the rotation ceased, an elongational deformation was imposed by axially translating one of the endplates in an exponential manner in order to generate constant strain rates ranging from 0.1 to 5.0 s-1. The tensile force and filament shape were monitored during the stretching flow. The position of the moving plate is recorded to verify the imposed displacement profile. By backlighting the test fluid with an electroluminescent panel and viewing the fluid column from above with a video camera, one half of the (symmetric) fluid column shape was recorded for subsequent image analysis in order to determine the evolution in the filament profile during stretching and subsequent relaxation. The fluid and air temperatures were digitally recorded using thermistors for later post-processing and temperature correction. After cessation of the extensional flow, the experiment monitored the subsequent evolution of the midpoint radius (via a laser micrometer), the filament shape, and the tensile force in the column.
hypothesis: Constitutive equations for viscoelastic fluids such as dilute polymer solutions generally predict large changes in the extensional rheology of the material as the elongation rate is increased. This investigation attempts to test the validity of this hypothesis by performing experiment with dilute non-Newtonian polymer solutions in extensional flows.

title: PSI-106 Version 3 Structure and Liftoff In Combustion Experiment(SLICE) Investigation
objective: Objective: The objective of this investigation is to better understand the structure and stability of laminar diffusion flames in microgravity. Specific objectives of this investigation were: 1. To investigate the structure of laminar diffusion flames in microgravity to understand the stabilizing mechanisms at the flames base. 2. Determine the liftoff velocity limits for different fuels and burner diameters. 3. Evaluate the impact of fuel dilution with nitrogen on soot formation and flame stability. 4. Quantify the effects of microgravity on flame length and radiative heat loss compared to normal gravity conditions. 5. Validate numerical models for flame dynamics, soot production, and thermal radiation in non-premixed flames.
approach: The SLICE apparatus consisted of a fan-driven flow duct, exchangeable burner tubes, and integrated sensors to measure flow rates and temperature. This setup used several fuels such as methane, ethylene, and nitrogen-diluted mixtures. Flames were then manually ignited and observed under controlled coflow air conditions. A high resolution camera captured still images while sensor data was overlaid on these images. Calibration tests for airflow velocity, soot measurement, and the fans were conducted to ensure the accuracy of the results. More than 4,000 high-resolution images were captured across 13 testing experiments. Data was then analyzed to correlate flame structure with stability with flow dynamics and fuel properties.
hypothesis: The hypothesis is that the structure and stability of laminar diffusion flames in microgravity are significantly influenced by burner diameter, coflow velocity, and fuel composition and are fundamentally different than flames observed on Earth.
research_impacts: 1. Improved numerical models for flame behavior lead to more efficient combustion technologies on Earth. 2. Understanding soot formation aids in designing combustion systems with minimum emissions. 3. Insights into flame stability and behavior to enhance fire safety. 4. Findings will inform the development of cleaner, more efficient engines and industrial burners.

title: PSI-107 Version 4 Smoke Point In Co-flow Experiment(SPICE) Investigation
objective: The objective of SPICE is to better understand the complex process of combustion by observing flames in a microgravity environment aboard the International Space Station (ISS) and analogous ground experiments. Specific objectives were: (1) Identify the laminar smoke-point properties of non-buoyant jet diffusion flames under various co-flow conditions in microgravity. (2) Determine the effects of burner diameter and co-flow velocity on the luminous flame lengths and smoke points. (3) Quantify the sooting propensity of different fuels, such as ethylene, propane, and propylene mixtures. (4) Validate the correlation between luminous flame shape and residence time under microgravity conditions. (5) Investigate the impact of air and fuel flow rate variations on smoke point phenomena in space.
approach: The experimental setup in the microgravity science glovebox consisted of an apparatus with a flow duct with integrated nozzles, cameras, and fuel delivery systems. Fuels tested included methane, ethylene, propane, propylene, and propylene mixtures. Each flame was ignited in a controlled co-flow air environment, with burner diameters of 0.41 mm, 0.76 mm, and 1.6 mm and co-flow velocities ranging from 5.4 cm/s to 65 cm/s. Fuel flow rates were adjusted to identify the smoke point, marked by the flame's transition to emitting soot. Data such as flame lengths were recorded using still and video cameras. Measurements included flame height, radiative heat losses, and co-flow air velocity distributions. In total 526 flames were studied.
hypothesis: The research hypothesizes that by minimizing gravity-driven transport phenomena scientists can study the laminar smoke-point properties of non-buoyant jet diffusion flames. Flame properties are expected to differ significantly from those observed under normal gravity.
research_impacts: (1) Will improve our understanding of soot formation mechanisms and help design safer spacecraft environments. (2) Will contribute to refining our computational models for predicting flame behaviors under non-buoyant conditions. (3) Will enhance our knowledge of soot generation (4) Could possibly provide insights to better fuel formulations and combustion processes.

title: PSI-108 Version 4 Surface Tension Driven Convection Experiment-1(STDCE-1) Investigation
objective: The main objectives of STDCE-1 are to investigate: -The extent and nature of thermocapillary flows in transient periods as well as under steady conditions. -Temperature distributions along the free surface and in the bulk fluid. -The effect of the heating mode and the heating level on the flows. -The effect of the liquid free surface on the flows -The onset conditions and nature of oscillatory flows
approach: The STDCE program employed a comprehensive and multifaceted approach to investigate the complexities of thermocapillary flow. This strategy encompassed a combination of theoretical analysis, numerical modeling, ground-based experiments, and ultimately, microgravity experiments aboard the Space Shuttle. Theoretical Analysis Dimensionless Parameters: Researchers derived and identified the key dimensionless parameters governing thermocapillary flow, including the Marangoni number (Ma), Prandtl number (Pr), aspect ratio (Ar), and the novel surface deformation parameter (S). These parameters facilitated the understanding of the relative importance of different forces and physical mechanisms at play and provided a framework for data analysis and comparison. Scaling Laws: By analyzing the governing equations and boundary conditions, scientists established scaling laws that characterized the behavior of key flow features, such as boundary layer thicknesses and velocity scales. This theoretical groundwork offered valuable insights into the expected flow characteristics under different conditions. Numerical Modeling Computational Fluid Dynamics (CFD): Sophisticated CFD models were developed to simulate thermocapillary flow behavior under various conditions. These models accounted for factors such as heat transfer, fluid properties, surface tension effects, and free surface deformation. The numerical simulations provided detailed predictions of flow patterns, velocity distributions, and temperature profiles, serving as a basis for comparison with experimental data and for exploring a wider range of parameters than feasible experimentally. Ground-Based Experiments Reduced-Gravity Simulations: Researchers conducted experiments in drop towers and other reduced-gravity facilities to observe thermocapillary flows under conditions with minimized buoyancy effects. These experiments served as a stepping stone towards the microgravity experiments and provided preliminary data for model validation and refinement. Test Fluid and Hardware Development: Extensive ground-based testing was undertaken to optimize the experimental setup, including the selection of the test fluid (silicone oil), the design of the test cell, and the development of flow visualization and temperature measurement techniques. Microgravity Experiments Space Shuttle Missions: The culmination of the research effort involved conducting the STDCE experiments aboard the Space Shuttle, taking advantage of the extended microgravity environment to study thermocapillary flows over a broader range of parameters and conditions than possible on Earth. This included meticulous execution of the test matrix, encompassing various heating modes, power levels, and free surface shapes, while collecting detailed flow visualization and temperature data. Data Analysis and Model Validation Comparison of Results: The experimental data from both ground-based and microgravity experiments were rigorously analyzed and compared with the predictions from numerical models. This iterative process allowed for the assessment of model accuracy, the identification of areas for improvement, and ultimately, a deeper understanding of the fundamental physics driving thermocapillary flow.
research_impacts: While the STDCE program was primarily driven by the need to understand and predict thermocapillary flow behavior in microgravity environments, its findings and technological advancements have yielded valuable insights and applications for Earth-based processes as well. Enhanced Understanding of Thermocapillary Flows Fundamental Physics: STDCE significantly advanced the understanding of the fundamental physics governing thermocapillary flows, including the interplay between surface tension gradients, heat transfer, and fluid motion. This knowledge provides a solid foundation for tackling complex fluid flow problems in various terrestrial applications. Numerical Model Refinement: The experimental data from STDCE served as a critical benchmark for validating and refining numerical models used to predict thermocapillary flow behavior. These improved models now offer more accurate and reliable predictions for a wider range of applications, both in space and on Earth. Technological Advancements Non-Intrusive Measurement Techniques: The development and refinement of non-intrusive measurement techniques, such as infrared imaging and particle image velocimetry, for the STDCE have expanded the toolkit for studying fluid flows in various settings. These techniques are now widely employed in research and industrial applications on Earth, including the study of combustion processes, crystal growth, and microfluidics. Flow Visualization and Analysis: The advanced flow visualization and analysis methods developed for STDCE have facilitated the study of complex flow patterns and structures in various terrestrial applications. These tools enable researchers and engineers to gain deeper insights into flow dynamics and optimize processes for improved efficiency and performance. Earth-Based Applications Materials Processing: The insights gained from STDCE have direct relevance to materials processing techniques on Earth, particularly those involving free surfaces and high-temperature gradients, such as welding, crystal growth, and the fabrication of thin films and coatings. Understanding and controlling thermocapillary flows in these processes can lead to improved product quality and reduced defect formation. Microfluidics: The knowledge gained from STDCE is applicable to the burgeoning field of microfluidics, where surface tension forces play a dominant role in manipulating and controlling fluids at the microscale. This has implications for the development of microfluidic devices for applications such as drug delivery, medical diagnostics, and chemical analysis. Overall, the STDCE program, while initially motivated by the challenges of microgravity research, has generated valuable knowledge and technological advancements with far-reaching implications for various Earth-based applications. The enhanced understanding of thermocapillary flow and the development of advanced measurement and analysis techniques have contributed to the advancement of materials processing, microfluidics, and numerous other fields, demonstrating the profound impact of fundamental scientific research on both space exploration and terrestrial technology.

title: PSI-109 Version 4 Surface Tension Driven Convection Experiment-2(STDCE-2) Investigation
objective: The main objectives of the present work are to investigate: 1. The onset conditions and nature of oscillatory flows. 2. The effect of the heating mode and the static free surface shape on the oscillations. 3. The shape and motion of the free surface during oscillations. 4. The coupling among the free surface deformation, the surface temperature distribution, and the velocity field.
approach: The STDCE-2 investigation employed a systematic approach to explain the role of free surface deformation in oscillatory thermocapillary flows under microgravity conditions. This approach comprised: Controlled Variation of Key Parameters: -Container Size: Utilizing three chamber diameters (1.2 cm, 2.0 cm, 3.0 cm) allowed researchers to examine the influence of scale on the onset of oscillations and assess potential inertial effects. -Heating Mode: Employing both submerged heater (CT mode) and CO2 laser (CF mode) systems enabled the comparison of flow behavior under constant temperature difference and constant heat flux boundary conditions, respectively. -Free Surface Shape: Tests were conducted with flat, concave, and convex free surfaces to explore the interplay between surface curvature and flow dynamics. Advanced Diagnostic Techniques: -Flow Visualization: The use of tracer particles enabled the visualization and qualitative characterization of flow patterns, including the three-dimensional, time-dependent structures observed during oscillations. -Infrared Imaging: An infrared scanner captured the temperature distribution across the oil's free surface, providing insights into the thermal gradients driving the thermocapillary flow and their evolution during oscillations. -Optical Deformation Measurement: A Ronchi system was employed to measure the free surface deformation and motions, allowing researchers to quantify the dynamic changes in surface shape and correlate them with observed flow behavior and temperature variations. Interactive Operation: The experiment was conducted interactively, allowing the researchers on the ground to communicate with the astronauts onboard the Spacelab, observe the downlinked video images in real-time, and adjust test parameters based on the observed phenomena. This flexibility facilitated the exploration of unexpected results and the fine-tuning of the experimental conditions to optimize data collection. The STDCE-2 investigation gathered comprehensive data aimed at complex dynamics of oscillatory thermocapillary flows and verifying the hypothesized role of free surface deformation in their onset.
hypothesis: The onset of oscillatory thermocapillary flow, particularly in microgravity environments, is significantly influenced by free surface deformation, which acts in conjunction with the Marangoni number (Ma). • Buoyancy masks the true oscillation mechanism in Earth- based experiments: The experimental data on oscillatory thermocapillary flows taken in normal gravity environments are often confusing or contradictory due to the presence of buoyancy. This suggests that buoyancy may obscure the role of free surface deformation in the oscillation process. • Marangoni number alone is insufficient to predict oscillations in microgravity: The unexpected stability observed in the prior STDCE microgravity experiments, even at Marangoni numbers exceeding the critical threshold observed in ground-based tests, indicates that Ma is not the sole determinant of oscillatory onset in the absence of buoyancy. • Free surface deformation is a key factor: The interaction between thermocapillary forces and free surface deformation plays a key role in the oscillation mechanism.

title: PSI-110 Version 6 An International Space Station Experiment into Fundamental Regolith Processes in Microgravity(Strata-1) Investigation
objective: The primary objective of the Strata-1 investigation was to study the mixing and segregation dynamics of regolith on small bodies by exposing a suite of regolith simulants to the microgravity environment aboard the International Space Station (ISS) for a period of one year. In response to variable gravity levels and ambient vibrational environment the Strata-1 experiment aimed to investigate the behavior of regolith simulants specifically chosen to represent models of regolith covering a range of complexity and tailored to inform and improve computational studies.
approach: The Strata-1 experiment consisted of four evacuated tubes partially filled with regolith simulants.The simulants, namely, glass beads, glass shards, meteorite, and carbonaceous chondrite, were chosen to represent models of regolith covering a range of complexity and tailored to inform and improve computational studies. The four tubes are regularly imaged while moving in response to the ambient vibrational environment using dedicated cameras. The imagery is then downlinked to the Strata-1 science team about every two months. Analyses performed on the imagery includes evaluating the extent of the segregation of Strata-1 samples and comparing the observations to computational models. After Strata-1's return to Earth, x-ray tomography and optical microscopy will be used to study the post-flight simulant distribution. There two simulation methods that have been proposed for this research are the Soft-sphere Discrete Element Method (SSDEM) and the Contact Dynamics Method (CD).
hypothesis: By utilizing the prolonged microgravity and vibrational conditions of ISS as analogues to those on small Solar System bodies, the Strata-1 investigation aims to answer fundamental questions about how regolith evolves on planetary bodies and what roles particle density, shape, and composition play in the evolution of regolith dynamics.
research_impacts: Strata-1 supports the space exploration program by enabling new interpretation of a wide range of NASA missions including but not limited to Stardust, Deep Impact; EPOXI, Near Earth Asteroid Rendezvous (NEAR), OSIRISREx and Hayabusa-1 and -2. The new Strata information on regolith behavior and mechanics directly assists planning for the Asteroid Redirect Mission ARM), the OSIRIS-REx mission, In-Situ Resource Utilization (ISRU) efforts on small bodies, and upcoming NASA missions to comets and asteroids. The Strata-1 study advances our fundamental understanding of the mechanical behavior of loose material. Results may find utility in any application that involves the mixing of dry materials, such as pharmaceutical tablet manufacture, the study of dune migration and dynamics, and similar fields.

title: PSI-111 Version 7 SUBSA Brazing of Aluminum Alloys IN Space(BRAINS) Investigation
objective: The primary scientific goal of the proposed terrestrial and planned microgravity molten metal capillary flow experiments is to better understand the physics of the flow of molten metals over the topographically modified surfaces (e.g., filling in the holes, flow over sharp edges and/or flow over surfaces having variable curvatures). By performing capillary flow tests both on Earth and in a microgravity environment, the effects of microgravity on the kinetics of the larger masses of melt flow, and ultimate equilibrium shape of the meniscus will be closely examined. The objective of the microgravity experiments is to provide benchmark data against which theoretical models and computer simulations can be tested. The BRAINS project’s primary pragmatic/engineering obective is that a capillary flow of braze under microgravity conditions would enable a repair or bonding of larger and/or more irregular mating surfaces defects, compared to the terrestrial conditions. This would be important for future development of advanced brazing techniques with applications to both damage repair and construction in space.
approach: Before being assembled into the ampoule, the samples were always ultrasonically cleaned in the sequence of (i) soapy water, (ii) water, (iii) 190 proof ethanol, and then dried in air or a compressed air. A double nitrogen purge was done before sealing the ampoule. Three configurations of the Al alloy filler and corresponding substrates were considered as relevant for the intended study: (i) HOLE, (ii) PIN and (iii) Hollow Pin. Solidification Using a Baffle in Sealed Ampoules” (SUBSA) furnace, which was designed for operation in the ISS’s Microgravity Science Glovebox (MSG) was used for this investigation. All samples were placed in the isothermal region of the furnace instrumented with thermocouples. The furnace was heated to the dwell temperature (600 - 605 °C ± 2K) at a rate of 5 K/minute (optimal 10K/minute). A dwell time was maintained for completion of capillary flow and establishing of the equilibrium meniscus shape. Subsequent cooling of the samples was performed at the maximum cooling rate allowed by the facility. Capillary topography identification and microstructure evaluation was performed on all samples.
hypothesis: A series of space (ISS) and terrestrial experiments, integrated with modeling and analysis are expected to answer the following practical and fundamental questions: (1) How can the absence of gravity and dominance of capillary forces be take advantage of in transporting the molten braze? (2) Which brazing alloy and the brazing technique will enable strong and efficient bonding of selected proxies of structural elements and facilitate a repair. That is, can brazing be done in space and/or on board of space vehicles by using flux-less braze? Specifically: A comparison between flux and flux-less brazing under space and terrestrial conditions can answer underlying scientific questions related to molten metal flow kinetics, specifically wetting and spreading of liquid clad/filler over topographically modified surfaces.
research_impacts: A brazing process may be used to mitigate the consequences of high velocity micro meteoroids’ and/or space debris’ impacts, and possible catastrophic penetration of aluminum man-made objects in space. Second, construction in space would necessitate joining complex assemblies, e.g., habitat systems, with brazing being one meaningful manufacturing option of permanent bonding. Validation fundamental models including phase field models will allow prediction of terrestrial brazing quality.
hardware: Solidification Using a Baffle in Sealed Ampoules (SUBSA) furnace

title: PSI-112 Version 6 Solidification Using a Baffle in Sealed Ampoules - Effect of Convection on the Columnar-to-Equiaxed Transition in Alloy Solidification(SUBSA - CETSOL) Investigation
objective: The objective of the proposed investigation is to better understand the columnar-to-equiaxed grain structure transition (CET) in solidification of metal alloys. By performing solidification experiments both on earth and in a microgravity environment, the effects of gravity-driven melt convection and sedimentation/floatation of unattached dendrite fragments and equiaxed crystals on the CET will be examined. The origin of equiaxed grains in non-refined alloys is of particular interest in the proposed experiments. The benchmark data from these experiments can be used to test theoretical models and computer simulations.
approach: Experiments were conducted in the Solidification Using a Baffle in Sealed Ampoules (SUBSA) furnace to investigate the CET for stationary samples without an imposed temperature gradient. Most experiments with aluminum-copper (Al-Cu) alloys, namely, Al-4wt%Cu, Al-10wt%Cu and Al-18wt%Cu alloys. The reason is that Al-Cu alloys are better suited for the duplicate ground-based experiments. If solidified upward (low temperature at the bottom, high at the top), thermosolutal natural convection of the melt will generally be minimized. The sedimentation or floatation of dendrite fragments and small equiaxed grains can be controlled by the solute concentration. For smaller solute concentrations, the solid is heavier than the melt and will sediment, while for higher solute concentrations the solid is lighter and will float. Hence, dendrite fragments and equiaxed grains in the Al-18wt%Cu alloy will float upwards ahead of the columnar front, and a CET can be expected. On the other hand, for the Al-4wt%Cu alloy, the fragments will sediment and remain between the primary columnar trunks, and a CET may not occur. For Al-10wt%Cu alloys, the solid is approximately neutrally buoyant in the melt. An additional experiment with an unrefined Al-7wt%Si alloy was also conducted. No grain refiner was used. In all proposed CET experiments, the samples were first fully melted and then solidified by decreasing the temperature of the SUBSA furnace at a controlled rate. The samples were not moved, and no temperature gradient were explicitly imposed. Corresponding flight and terrestrial experiments were conducted. Samples were analyzed by measuring the grain structure and any macrosegregation.
hypothesis: The primary hypothesis of this investigation is that fragmentation of columnar dendrites can lead to a CET in non-grain-refined alloys. The secondary dendrite arms that detach from the primary columnar trunks are a potent source of new (equiaxed) grains. However, for a CET to occur the growth of the primary columnar trunks must be blocked by equiaxed grains. This can only be accomplished if the secondary dendrite fragments are transported to the columnar front, rather than remain between the primary columnar trunks. Due to natural convection of the melt and sedimentation or floatation of the fragments, such transport can be expected to readily occur in the gravitational field of earth. In the absence of gravity, it is not clear if fragmentation alone, without fragment transport, is sufficient to cause a CET.
research_impacts: The CET refers to the transition between the elongated grains in the outer portions of a casting and the more rounded grains in the center. Understanding this transition is fundamental to determining what type of grain structure forms in castings of most metal alloys (steel, aluminum, copper, etc.). Often, a fully equiaxed structure is preferred, but the fully columnar structures of many turbine blades are an important exception. In addition to its high practical significance, the CET represents a “holy grail” in the area of modeling and simulation of casting. This is because in order to realistically predict the CET, almost every physical phenomenon at every length scale must be taken into account simultaneously. This investigation will not only provide an improved understanding of the CET, but also models and computer simulations of the grain structure formation in metal castings that can be used by industry to better industry to better understand and optimize their casting processes.
hardware: Solidification Using a Baffle in Sealed Ampoules (SUBSA) furnace Solidification Using a Baffle in Sealed Ampoules (SUBSA) furnance - AIAA

title: PSI-113 Version 4 Solidification Using a Baffle in Sealed Ampoules(SUBSA) Investigation
objective: There are both technology demonstration objectives and scientific objectives. The technology demonstration objectives are to test the performance of an automatically moving baffle in microgravity and to determine the behavior and possible advantages of liquid encapsulation in microgravity conditions.The science objectives are to visualize the melt/encapsulant behavior in microgravity and to grow doped InSb without dewetting. The key goal of SUBSA was to clarify the origin of the melt convection in space and to reduce the magnitude to the point that it does not interfere with the transport phenomena.
approach: In the space environment, accelerations produce circular motions that affect the solidification of crystal growth/semiconductor materials flight experiments, resulting in a material that is less useful.The objectives of SUBSA are:Test the performance of an automatically moving baffle (used to minimize melt motion).Visualization of the melting process to identify what causes the melt motion.Production of several crystals with reproducible properties.To determine the behavior and possible advantages of liquid encapsulation in microgravity conditions.
hypothesis: A baffle placed inside a melt reduces the effective size of the melt and leads to a decrease in the amount of convection. The combined effect of microgravity (reduction of gravitational acceleration by a factor of 10^6 ) and a small zone melt (reduction of the size and temperature differential by a factor of 10^3 ) will generate the effective conditions of “nano-gravity” (the Rayleigh number will be reduced by a factor of 10^9 ).
research_impacts: The SUBSA furnace, with its capability to control and visualize melting and solidification of semiconductor crystals has increased our understanding of semiconductor crystal growth phenomena. The transparent furnace coupled with the video downlink and real-time commanding capability provided a powerful tool for scientists to watch the motion of the crystal-melt interface as semiconductor crystals were formed. The design of the SUBSA ampoule which includes a baffle and a system that prevents de-wetting resulted in crystals whose properties have not been disrupted by micro-accelerations at the Station, making it possible for future researchers to produce the high-quality semiconductor crystals that are in demand on Earth.

title: PSI-114 Version 5 Tiegelfreies Elektromagnetisches Prozessieren Unter Schwerelosigkeit; Electromagnetic Processing(TEMPUS) Investigation
objective: The TEMPUS (Tiegelfreies ElektroMagnetisches Prozessieren Unter Schwerelosgkeit) facility is a research instrument designed to perform electromagnetic levitation studies in reduced gravity. TEMPUS was a joint undertaking between DARA, the German space agency, and the Microgravity Science and Applications Division of NASA. Specific objectives for the different investigations carried out by US Principal Investigators using this facility is categorized by different classes: Class A: Studies of undercooling phenomena and the kinetics of nucleation (Prof. M. Flemings, MIT, Prof. R. Bayuzick, Vanderbilt Univ), Class B: Measurement of specific heat in liquid metals using an AC calorimetry technique (Prof W. Johnson, CALTECH), Class C: Measurement of viscosity and surface tension of undercooled metals (Prof. J. Szkeley, Prof. M. Flemings, MIT), Class D: Measurement of thermal expansion in undercooled materials (Prof W. Johnson, CALTECH). In addition to the US Principal Investigators, available data from European investigations performed on TEMPUS and captured here include Viscosity and Surface Tension of Undercooled Metallic Melts (Dr. Egry, DLR, Germany), Thermophysical Properties of Undercooled Metallic Melts (Dr. Egry, DLR, Germany), Thermal Expansion of Glass forming Metallic Alloys in the Undercooled State (Dr. Samwer, Georg-August-Universitat Gottingen, Germany), and Thermodynamics and Glass Formation Undercooled Liquid Alloys (Dr. Wunderlich and Dr. Fecht, University of Ulm, Germany).
approach: Metallic samples of 7 or 8 mm diameter are positioned in the TEMPUS coils by electromagnetic forces and melted by induced currents. A ''squeezing'' force is then applied to a stably positioned liquid sample to induce oscillations. The rate of decay of the amplitude of these oscillations can be observed in order to measure the viscosity at different temperatures, while the frequency of the oscillation modes is used to deduce the surface tension at these temperatures. Measurements are planned on reactive, refractory melts (Zr), high-viscosity eutectics (ZrNi, PdSi), and industrial alloys (Fe-Cr-Ni) in addition to standard materials for comparison (Au, Ni). In addition, mathematical modeling designed to give a detailed understanding of what can be expected from prevailing conditions in the flight experiments was also developed.
hypothesis: Levitation, positioning and processing of materials which are not in direct contact with container surfaces, provides a unique opportunity to study a number of phenomena. In particular, the lack of contact with container walls reduces the possibility for heterogeneous nucleation in studies of the processing of molten materials. The study of the properties and solidification of undercooled materials is facilitated by containerless processing.
research_impacts: The accurate determination of the thermophysical properties of liquid materials is important for fundamental and practical reasons, including verification of atomistic models of the liquid state, nucleation studies of phase transition, and modeling of materials processing operations. In addition, these studies often focus on advanced materials such as metallic glass forming materials. Metallic glasses are an industrially important new class of materials. They are ductile, isotropic and corrosion resistant and are used in magnetic storage media films.

title: PSI-115 Version 3 Utilization of the Smoke Aerosol Measurement Experiment Data for Advanced Modeling and Simulation of Smoke Generation in Micro-Gravity Investigation
objective: The objective of this investigation was to use numerical simulation to explore the influence of gravity on pyrolysis smoke growth from a fundamental perspective. The intention of this effort is to quantify the differences between microgravity and Earth gravity smoke, and to identify the fluid dynamic mechanisms that cause the differences.
approach: The formation and growth of dibutyl-phthalate (DBP) particles in Earth gravity and microgravity environments was simulated. Direct numerical simulation via a Navier-Stokes nodal approach was utlilized. The smoke originates from pyrolysis vapor expelled from a heated sample in a geometry similar to that considered in the SAME experiments. This study considered two cross-flow velocities of sufficiently low speed that buoyancy cannot be neglected in the presence of gravity. Simulations are presented to assess the dependence of particle size distributions on thermophoresis, particle settling, and flow geometry. The final report for this investigation introduces the simulation and modeling methodology, followed by a description of the flow geometry and the parameter space under consideration.The differences in the wake geometry attributable to buoyancy for the lower of two flow speeds was examined. Instantaneous scalar fields were used to describe particle accumulation and growth in the buoyant and non-buoyant wakes that form downstream of the hot vapor source.
hypothesis: Without buoyancy, mixing and heat transfer are reduced, the time-temperature history of the combustion vapors (or particle precursors) and particle trajectories are significantly altered, changing the composition of the smoke. The chemical composition of the burning material also affects the characteristics of the smoke generated.
research_impacts: Models and tools that characterize particles generated as smoke can be used to ascertain how temperature, gravity, and material properties affect the smoke produced. This would directly lead to better smoke detection devices and prevent fires that can lead to loss of materiel and loss of life.

title: PSI-117 Version 2 Effect of External Thermo-Convective Perturbation on Cool Flame Dynamics: A Multidimensional Multi-Physics CFD Analysis Investigation
objective: The objective of this ground investigation was to use flight data obtained from PSI through NASA’s Flame Extinguishment Experiment (FLEX) to quantify how externally imposed thermal and convective perturbations regulated the dynamics and ultimate fate of already established droplet cool flames, and to explain run-to-run variability by isolating the roles of deliberate heating and unintentional drift-induced convection. Focusing on both small and large droplets, the work mapped stability windows for ignition, sustained oscillation, transitions to hot ignition and warm-flame behavior, and extinction under microgravity. By leveraging and extending the FLEX data in the PSI, this study produced reusable models and sensitivity analyses that coupled low-temperature chemistry with transport and radiative effects.
approach: OpenFOAM was used to develop a 3-D CFD model of n-alkane droplet cool flames in microgravity, coupling variable-density Navier–Stokes flow with low-temperature combustion chemistry, coupled heat and mass transfer, and radiation. Model fidelity was established against ISS FLEX measurements, after which controlled simulations examined three forcing modes (i) convection alone to mimic droplet drift, (ii) imposed heat flux, and (iii) combined convection plus heating applied to both large (1–4 mm) and sub-millimeter (~0.5 mm) droplets. To accelerate progress, the study began with simplified chemistry and transitioned to reduced mechanisms for parameter sweeps over forcing amplitude and frequency, ambient composition (including ozone-assisted cases), and pressure. From each case, predictive observables were extracted (ignition delay, oscillation frequency and amplitude, stand-off and extinction diameters), and were used to construct stability maps that delineated conditions for cool-flame onset, persistence, and quenching. These maps were reconciled with FLEX observations and were used to guide next-generation test matrices for both large- and small-droplet experiments.
hypothesis: External thermo-convective perturbations (imposed temperature gradients, non-uniform heating, oscillatory/shear inflow) were expected to govern cool-flame ignition, oscillation, transition to hot ignition, and extinction by shifting residence time and scalar dissipation. In microgravity, where buoyancy was suppressed, this forcing was anticipated to dominate transport. A multidimensional, multi-physics CFD model was used to map perturbation-dependent stability boundaries and predict observables for comparison with FLEX data.
research_impacts: Space Benefits: Potential to improve spacecraft fire-safety modeling by resolving cool-flame/extinction behavior in microgravity; leverages FLEX to define safer operating envelopes/materials. Earth Benefits: Advances low-temperature combustion understanding relevant to engine knock, efficiency, and emissions; delivers validated CFD tools transferrable to practical combustors.

title: PSI-119 Version 1 Enhanced Particle Tracking in STDC Data and Its Industrial Application of Marangoni Convection Investigation
objective: The primary objective this grant was to extract and understand the detailed thermo-fluid mechanics of the original NASA Surface Tension Driven Convection Experiment (STDCE-1) performed in microgravity, using modern diagnostic and computational tools. The study aims to revitalize the original video data found in PSI by applying advanced Particle Image Velocimetry (PIV) and Particle Tracking Velocimetry (PTV) methods, which provide higher resolution, sub-pixel accuracy, and robust flow field extraction compared to the limited analyses available in the early 1990s. By systematically comparing velocity and pressure fields obtained from these reanalyzed datasets with theoretical perturbation methods and COMSOL Multiphysics computational models, the project seeks to isolate the fundamental role of Marangoni convection and interfacial curvature in driving oscillatory and steady-state flows. Complementary ground-based experiments incorporating gravitational effects will be conducted to disentangle the relative contributions of buoyancy and surface tension-driven convection. These objectives ultimately support both NASA’s PSI solicitation by expanding the scientific return from legacy datasets and advancing applied understanding for industrial processes that rely on controlled Marangoni flows, such as wafer drying, thin-film coating, and microfluidic device operation.
approach: The approach combined archival microgravity data analysis, computational modeling, and ground experiments to study surface tension driven convection (STDC). Video data from the original NASA STDCE-1 experiments were re-analyzed using several modern particle tracking techniques, including four MATLAB-based codes, three ImageJ-based codes, and sub-pixel localization methods, to produce velocity and pressure fields. These flow fields were compared with theoretical models derived from perturbation methods and with computational simulations performed in COMSOL Multiphysics® v5.6 that incorporated boundary conditions and curved free-surface geometries. In parallel, ground-based STDC experiments were carried out to examine gravitational effects and to distinguish buoyancy-driven flows from thermocapillary convection. This combination of data reanalysis, numerical simulation, and experimental testing provided a means to identify the influence of interfacial curvature, surface stresses, and geometry on Marangoni convection.
hypothesis: Re-analyzing NASA’s STDCE-1 microgravity video data with advanced particle tracking and computational modeling to reveal previously inaccessible details of thermo-fluid mechanics in surface tension driven convection. These insights, validated against ground-based experiments, aimed to clarify the interplay between Marangoni forces, interfacial curvature, and flow instabilities, leading to improved predictive models of thermocapillary flows.
research_impacts: Space Benefits: Improves understanding of thermocapillary convection in microgravity, critical for designing reliable thermal management and materials processing systems aboard spacecraft. Provides validated numerical and theoretical models that can guide future ISS and space-based fluid physics experiments, reducing uncertainty from prior low-resolution analyses. Earth Benefits: Supports industrial applications such as semiconductor wafer cleaning, thin-film coatings, welding, and liquid crystal display fabrication. Findings also translate to emerging fields like active matter and micro/nano robotics, where Marangoni flows and surface interactions could be harnessed for medical diagnostics, targeted drug delivery, and microplastics removal.

title: PSI-12 Version 2 Growth of Large, Perfect Protein Crystals for Neutron Crystallography(Perfect Crystals) Investigation
objective: The Perfect Crystals investigation uses microgravity environment on the International Space Station to grow crystals of human manganese superoxide dismutase (MnSOD). This sheds light on how the antioxidant protein helps protect the human body from oxidizing radiation and oxides created as a byproduct of metabolism. For best results, the analysis technique requires large crystals with minimal imperfections, which are more easily produced in the microgravity environment of the space station.
approach: The Growth of Large, Perfect Protein Crystals for Neutron Crystallography investigation grows perfect, large-volume crystal suitable for neutron macromolecular crystallography of large unit cell protein crystals in microgravity. The protein of study in this investigation is human manganese superoxide dismutase (MnSOD or SOD2), which has an enzymatic mechanism that relies on a proton shuttling pattern that has yet to be fully elucidated. Neutron macromolecular crystallography allows for visualization of protons that cannot be achieved by XRay Diffraction or Cryo-EM, but requires large-volume crystals minimal imperfection for best results. Gravity has been implicated as a cause of defects in crystals grown on Earth. The marriage of the liquid-liquid capillary diffusion crystal growth technique to the microgravity environment aboard the International Space Station (ISS) allows for the growth of multiple greater than 1 mm3 crystals with very few defects. Please refer to AccessingPerfectCrystalData.pdf under the Science Documents section.
hypothesis: In 2001, the Borgstahl laboratory successfully grew large crystals of SOD using microgravity conditions on the International Space Station (ISS). Using existing crystallization hardware that uses the Granada Crystallization Boxes (GCB) for capillary counter diffusion protocols will be used to achieve microgravity crystallization results for SOD. The principal outcome will be to identify the role of hydrogen atoms in enzymatic activity, discern superoxide from peroxide, and water from hydroxide ion by their protonation state and decipher a structure-based mechanism for human MnSOD more precisely than from previous X-ray crystallographic models determined from Earth-grown crystals.
research_impacts: Manganese superoxide dismutase (MnSOD) is implicated in a number of human diseases, including non-Hodgkins lymphoma, lung cancer and colorectal cancer. Understanding how it works is an important step toward developing better prevention and treatment methods for such diseases. In space application, MnSOD could help researchers protect astronauts on future long-term missions. Astronauts receive significantly more exposure to oxidizing radiation than people on Earth, and on long journeys such as to Mars may receive dangerous doses that create Reactive Oxygen Species (ROS). These can damage DNA and other biomolecules, causing diseases such as cancer. The manganese superoxide dismutase (MnSOD) enzyme converts ROS into molecular oxygen and hydrogen peroxide, which other enzymes can then break down. Studies on MnSOD can help researchers can develop artificial techniques to reduce ROS and help protect astronauts on future long-term missions.

title: PSI-125 Version 2 Light Microscopy Module Biophysics-2,5(LMMBIO-2) Investigation
objective: The primary objective of this investigation was to understand why protein crystallization experiments in microgravity have generated unexpectedly low or high numbers of crystals. Each outcome may cause experiments designed to obtain a small number of well-separated crystals to fail. The objective of the proposed investigations is to explore the effects of a hitherto unstudied factor for the nucleation of protein crystals: solution shear flow. Besides providing a novel tool for nucleation control for protein crystallization experiments, the correlation between solution flows and protein crystal nucleation, to be tested in the proposed investigation, will shed light on one of the major mysteries of current space biophysics: the finding that in many cases the number of crystals nucleated in microgravity was greater or smaller than those nucleated on earth.
approach: Three cassettes containing five capillaries each were loaded with one of three proteins; (1) Lysozyme, (2) p53, and (3) hnRNPA-LC. The observation of these protein clusters were observed with a newly developed technique, called differential dynamic microscopy (DDM). DDM improves a recent method used to study and quantify the dynamics of sub-micrometer particles in solutions from fluctuations in intensity in optical micrographs. All samples were frozen to a temperature of -80C before flight to the ISS. The proteins were thawed and observed over several weeks in the ISS LMM module where they were filmed and photographed. Sample details and experimental parameters are summarized in LMMBio2_Experimental Table in the science document section.
hypothesis: Hypothesis: The behavior of dense liquid clusters at different rates of convection will have a profound effect on crystal growth. The main hypothesis underlying the proposed investigations consists of two parts: 1. The existence of nucleation precursors and the correlation between their properties and the nucleation rate can be used to control protein crystal nucleation via solution flow. 2. Enhancement or suppression of nucleation via solution flow, i.e., independently of solution supersaturation, can be used to achieve higher perfection of the grown crystals. 3. A very small fraction of the protein exists in a dense liquid phase in the form of Brownian particles, each a cluster of roughly 105 protein molecules undergoing liquid-like dynamics. 4. Crystal nucleation occurs when a small, ordered domain forms within the highly concentrated liquid-state environment of one of these particles.
research_impacts: These images provide data that help scientists and engineers understand the forces that control organization and dynamics of matter at microscopic scales. The organization and movement of matter on the microscopic level profoundly affects the macroscopic world and understanding such processes contributes to development of more efficient materials and machines for application on Earth.

title: PSI-13 Version 6 Advanced Colloids Experiment- Microscopy(ACE-M1) Investigation
objective: The ACE-M1 investigation aims to study the behavior of microscopic particles in colloidal mixtures such as gels and creams. Objectives include the study of the physics of colloidal coarsening and the role of polydispersity (variation in particle size) in determining the stability of colloidal systems. Previous Earth-based experiments show that polydispersity dramatically affects the time it takes for these gels to collapse. The imaging goal was to observe crystallites and resolve particle centroid positions with less than 20% error.
approach: The ACE-M1 investigation utilized a Sample Cartridge disk with 10 Sample Wells for 10 samples. Samples were colloidal fluids of small and large particles in varying concentration over .5 to 2.0 mg/ml. Protocols included Homogenization and microscopic Observation and Imaging. A crew member used magnetic stir bars embedded in the sample well to homogenized each sample. Fluorescent microscopy and Imaging of the colloidal crystallites in each well as they developed over time allowed observation of particle movements and interactions to characterize and quantify rates of growth of structures formed.
hypothesis: Polydispersity significantly affects the time scale and dynamics of coarsening. It is believed that polydispersity can lead to a substantial difference in the collapse time of weak gels, and understanding this effect in a microgravity environment can provide critical insights into product design and stability.
research_impacts: Space Benefits: By conducting colloidal research in microgravity, the ACE-M1 experiment can obtain clearer data on the dynamics of liquid mixtures, free from the effects of gravitational forces. This research can improve the manufacturing processes for creating new, longer-lasting products for use both in space and on Earth. Earth Benefits: Understanding the behavior of colloidal mixtures and the coarsening process can help materials scientists design products with longer shelf lives. This has significant implications for a wide range of products, including food, medicine, cosmetics, gels, and cleaning solutions, potentially leading to reduced waste and enhanced product performance​.
hardware: Light Microscopy Module (LMM) Fluids Integrated Rack (FIR)

title: PSI-137 Version 1 Phase Transitions in Colloid-Polymer Mixtures in Microgravity Investigation
objective: The objective of this PSI grant was to advance the understanding of phase transitions in colloid–polymer mixtures under microgravity conditions by integrating experimental observations with predictive modeling. Specifically, the research sought to determine how depletion interactions, arising from non-adsorbing polymers, influence the kinetics and morphology of phase separation and crystallization in complex fluids. By analyzing image data from NASA’s Binary Colloidal Alloy Test (BCAT-3 through BCAT-6) experiments conducted on the International Space Station, the project aimed to isolate the effects of gravity on phase behavior, quantify domain growth over multiple orders of magnitude in time and length scale, and develop a theoretical framework that connects these dynamics to hydrodynamic and thermodynamic parameters. Ultimately, this work sought to establish colloidal systems as model analogues for atomic and molecular phase transitions, providing insight relevant to both fundamental soft-matter physics and applied materials design.
approach: The approach combined data-driven analysis of PSI-archived BCAT imagery with a phase-field modeling framework that coupled the Cahn–Hilliard and Stokes equations to simulate phase separation in colloid–polymer mixtures. Experimental image sequences were processed for BCAT-3, -4 and -5, using algorithms in ImageJ and MATLAB to remove background noise, enhance contrast, and compute spatial autocorrelation functions for extracting characteristic domain length scales. Theoretical modeling of BCAT-5 incorporated concentration-dependent mobility and viscosity, along with Korteweg stresses to represent interfacial tension effects, allowing for the inclusion of hydrodynamic interactions that influenced domain coarsening. The governing equations were solved using a pseudospectral semi-implicit numerical scheme, and simulation results were quantitatively compared to flight data from the BCAT experiments. Model parameters were tuned using physical data from PSI to validate predictions and refine understanding of hydrodynamic coupling, phase-domain morphology, and kinetic arrest in colloid–polymer systems. This integrated experimental–theoretical approach yielded a comprehensive, microgravity-validated description of soft-matter phase transformation mechanisms.
hypothesis: Introducing non-adsorbing polymers into colloidal suspensions generates depletion-induced attractions that alter phase-transition kinetics; in microgravity, free from sedimentation and convection, these interactions can be directly modeled to reveal the intrinsic role of hydrodynamics in phase separation.
research_impacts: This research provided benchmark insight into soft-matter phase transitions without gravitational interference, improving predictive capability for self-assembly, crystallization, and gelation relevant to materials manufacturing and fluids research aboard the ISS. It has also improved understanding of phase-transition kinetics and rheology in colloid–polymer mixtures, informing materials science, pharmaceutical, and chemical engineering applications, and advancing the design of next-generation coatings, gels, and nanostructured materials.

title: PSI-138 Version 2 Pool Boiling Heat Transfer Mechanisms in Low Gravity: Numerical Experiments of MABE and NPBX Data Investigation
objective: The primary objectives for this PSI grant include establishing a deeper mechanistic understanding of nucleate boiling under low-gravity conditions by conducting high-fidelity numerical simulations that replicate the flight conditions of prior ISS-based boiling experiments, specifically MABE and NPBX. The investigation seeks to characterize key mechanisms governing bubble growth, waiting time, vapor spreading, coalescence, and detachment under variable gravity levels, degrees of wall superheat, and levels of liquid subcooling. Central to the objectives is quantifying how heat flux divides between nucleate boiling and natural convection modes, evaluating how the contact angle modulates wall adhesion forces, and determining the precise contribution of microlayer evaporation to heat transfer during low-gravity operation. By leveraging validated direct-numerical-simulation approaches tied to empirical MABE and NPBX measurements, this objective generates fundamental physics-based insights that enable predictive modeling of boiling processes relevant to spacecraft systems and advanced thermal architectures.
approach: The project approach was to use validated high-fidelity Direct Numerical Simulation (DNS) ground-based computational simulations to numerically reproduce MABE- and NPBX-like boiling environments over a controlled range of heater temperatures, wall superheat conditions, and fluid subcooling levels. The research draws directly from ISS-acquired datasets that include detailed bubble growth dynamics, heat-flux profiles, and heater-surface imaging, which serve as reference benchmarks that guide simulation fidelity. Multiphase DNS simulations incorporate fluid phase-change physics, contact-line motion, interphase mass transport, and three-dimensional flow-field resolution to connect bubble behavior to instantaneous and time-averaged heat transfer. Iterative simulation campaigns then probe how variable gravitational acceleration, wettability contrast, bubble confinement, and microlayer evaporation influence overall heat-flux partitioning. The resulting database enables first-principles analysis of changes in boiling performance between terrestrial and microgravity settings while supporting quantitative model development applicable to spaceflight hardware, thermal architectures, and advanced electronic cooling systems.
hypothesis: The research was based on the hypothesis that, in microgravity, shifts in the relative influence of buoyancy, capillary forces, and microlayer evaporation fundamentally alter bubble-growth behavior and reduce heat-flux performance. It further hypothesized that these low-gravity effects can be accurately captured using high-fidelity Direct Numerical Simulations (DNS) validated against historic ISS boiling data from the MABE and NPBX experiments. By exploring variations in gravity, surface wettability, and thermal conditions, the study aimed to test the mechanisms governing bubble dynamics and heat transfer for application to spacecraft thermal management.
research_impacts: Space Benefits: This investigation provides high-resolution insight into how boiling heat-transfer efficiency degrades under reduced gravity, enabling the development of more reliable spacecraft thermal-management systems that do not depend solely on buoyancy-driven vapor removal.
