Improved understanding of microlayer-based transport, contact-line wetting, spatial heat-flux distribution, and boiling-mode transition directly supports the design of future ISS and deep-space thermal architectures, power-electronics packaging, life-support thermal management, and compact, energy-efficient cooling platforms for extended-duration missions. Earth Benefits: The computational foundations and physics-based insights gained through this study directly advance terrestrial thermal-management strategies for high-power electronic systems, including server-class processors, power-dense computing architectures, and high-performance energy-conversion systems. The work improves predictive control of boiling-induced heat removal, enabling higher operating throughput, greater component longevity, and reduced power consumption in heat-intensive commercial and defense electronics.

title: PSI-142 Version 2 Quantitative Studies of Cool Flame Transitions at Radiation / Stretch Extinction Using Counterflow Flames Investigation
objective: By using the Flame Extinguishment (FLEX) experimental data from the Physical Sciences Informatics (PSI) system of combustion science, the purpose of this grant was to conduct new simulations and ground-based experiments using ozone-sensitized counterflow flames to: 1) Develop a new diagram of the flammability limits of diffusional cool flames affected by radiation, diffusion, and convection. 2) Bridge the knowledge gap between the flammability limits and extinction limits of hot flames and cool flames. 3) Verify the phenomena observed on the ISS flame extinguishment experiments. 4) Obtain new, quantitative data of extinction limit, flame temperature, and species distribution for the validation of kinetic and radiation models involving cool flames. 5) Extend the cool flame experiments from the original ISS droplet experiments to a more general ground-based combustion system involving radiation, diffusion, convection, and low-temperature chemistry while maintaining a one-dimensional geometry.
approach: Using the experimental conditions of FLEX flight, a comparative studies of the oxygen concentration effects on the extinction limits of cool flames was conducted using three different numerical modeling schemes, (a) spark-assisted flame propagation of a n-heptane/air mixture, (b) one dimensional freely-propagating dimethyl ether (DME) flames using an arc-length continuation method and (c) simulated cool flame regimes and burning limits at elevated pressure (up to 20 atm) using DME/air mixtures. Specific research details are outlined in the publication, ''Dynamics of cool flames'' [https://doi.org/10.1016/j.pecs.2019.100787]; '' Understanding Cool Flames and Warm Flames'', [https://doi.org/10.1016/j.proci.2020.09.019] and ''Study of the low-temperature reactivity of large n-alkanes through cool diffusion flame extinction'', [https://doi.org/10.1016/j.combustflame.2017.01.028].
hypothesis: This investigation attempts to answer the critical question as to what conditions causes the hot flames transfer to cool flames and how the cool flame flammable region is related to hot flame flammability limit and extinction limit. The investigation hypothesizes that factors such as oxygen concentration, dilution, pressure, diffusion, and convection transport processes affect the cool flame transition.
research_impacts: Obtaining a fundamental understanding of the warm diffusion flame is particularly relevant to combustion in highly turbulent flow fields and in microgravity environments, owing to the possibility of long residence times. The results showed that the warm flame has a double reaction zone structure and plays a critical role in the transition between cool flames and hot flames. At elevated pressures, it was found that the flammable region of warm flames and cool flames expands due to the increase in low-temperature and intermediate-temperature reactivity with pressure. Since many real engines operate in the 20-40 atm pressure range, therefore, cool flames and warm flames are relevant and important flame regimes for high-pressure near-limit combustion applications. These calculations from this investigation will serve to advance the understanding of near-limit flame dynamics and provide guidance for experimental observation of different flame regimes.

title: PSI-148 Version 2 Spurious Grain Formation in Alloys Directionally Solidified on the Space Station Due to Marangoni Convection Investigation
objective: Develop a three dimensional solidification model incorporating Marangoni convection and thermosolutal convection which can predict formation of spurious grains during DS. Extract data, such as, fluid velocities along stream lines as a function of distance from the surface-void, angular rotation of the fragmented side arms due to Marangoni flow lines, etc. from PFMI (Pore Formation and Mobility Investigation) videos, and then compare these observations with the simulations in order to quantitatively validate our numerical model. Use that model to predict formation of spurious grains in a totally different alloy, Al-7Si (MICAST), under varying processing conditions, such as, during re-melting prior to DS, after a step increase or decrease in growth speed vs at constant speed, etc.
approach: Use the PFMI and MICAST experimental flight data available in PSI to validate a three dimensional solidification model to predict that formation of spurious grains during DS.
hypothesis: Columnar and dendritic growth experiments in a predominantly diffusive microgravity environment have shown the presence of voids at the melt-crucible interface which are the likely the source of Marangoni convective flows. It is hypothesized that it is this flow that is responsible for fragmentation of the dendrite-side arm, and its rotation which creates the nucleus for the subsequent growth and formation of spurious grains. This hypothesis was tested by numerically simulating the influence of the Marangoni convection on the trajectory of such a dendrite fragment in the alloy melt and comparing with the experimental observations.
research_impacts: Results from this research are valuable not only for terrestrial technologies involving solidification, such as repairing gas turbine blade tips by laser cladding, but also for any future space manufacture or repair which involves solidification.

title: PSI-15 Version 2 Advanced Colloids Experiment-Microscopy 2 Reflight(ACE-M2R) Investigation
objective: Sometimes its hard to tell a gas from a liquid. ACE-M2R observes the microscopic behavior of liquids and gases separating from each other. The investigation examines the behavior of model (colloid rich) liquids and model (colloid poor) gases near the critical point, or the point at which there is no distinct boundary between the two phases. ACE-M2R uses a new microscope to record micro-scale events on short time scales, while previous experiments observed large-scale behavior over many weeks. Liquids and gases of the same material usually have different densities, so they would behave differently under the influence of gravity, making the microgravity environment of the International Space Station ideal for these experiments. This investigation is a re-flight of the original ACE-M2 with the intent to resolve issues from the original flight.
approach: The ACE-M2 investigation utilized 2 Sample Modules (1 is duplicate for back-up) with 15 Sample Wells each for a total of 30 samples, 15 flight and 15 slight identical for back-up. Samples were colloidal fluids varying concentrations of two different types of fluorescent dye and particle size; large and small. Magnetic stir bars embedded in each sample well were used to homogenized each sample. Fluorescent microscopy and Imaging of the colloidal crystallites in each well as they developed over time allowed observation of particle movements and interactions to characterize and quantify rates of growth of structures formed.
hypothesis: Near the critical point, variations in density and effective temperature will significantly influence particle interactions, leading to observable changes in phase stability and transition behavior. These changes are expected to reveal underlying mechanisms governing critical phenomena in colloidal systems, enhancing the predictability of particle dynamics in similar environments.
research_impacts: Space Applications: On Earth, gravity plays a big role in how liquids and gases interact: The heavier liquid phase settles beneath a lighter gas phase, and these differences in density enable easy separation. But the flow and behavior of complex fluids and phase separation where there is little or no gravity is not well understood. A greater understanding of liquid-gas interaction in microgravity could benefit a wide range of fluid storage, transport and processing systems for future spacecraft. Earth Applications: Particle separation and behavior in liquids, gels, and creams is important for developing consumer and household products, which are worth billions of dollars annually to the U.S. economy. Many consumer products are complex fluids, combining microscopic particles in gel or liquid, which are similar to the model colloidal system used in the ACE investigations which give insight into product formulations that could be used to maximize stability and shelf life.
hardware: Light Microscopy Module (LMM) Fluids Integrated Rack (FIR)

title: PSI-153 Version 1 Fabrication of Amorphous Metals in Space(FAMIS) Investigation
objective: The primary objective of this investigation was to understand the effect of microgravity processing on composition and microstructure evolution in metallic glass forming alloys or bulk metallic glass (BMG). Specific questions to be answered were: (a) How does processing in microgravity change the composition of the matrix of the glass-forming alloys compared to processing in gravity? (b) How does the volume fraction of the W spheres affect the composition and properties of the matrix? (c) How does the composition and viscosity of the glass-forming alloy affect the diffusion of W in microgravity? (d) How do the different diameter of W spheres affect the diffusion of W into the matrix? (e) Does the dissolved W provide a mechanism to improve the wear resistance and toughness of the matrix by providing reinforcement for brittle phases?
approach: The objective of the flight experiment is to process 12 samples of two glass-forming alloys (Vitreloy 106 and Zr48Cu47.5Al4Co0.5) in microgravity with three different volume fractions of W spheres (5%, 15% and 30%) with two different diameters of W spheres (25-36 μm diameter and 140-150 μm diameter). The cast composite samples were 15 mm in diameter and 12 mm long cylinders. The W particles were distributed as homogeneously as possible without sedimentation. On orbit, the samples were loaded into the Low Gradient Furnace (LGF) on the Materials Science Research Rack. They were held for 120 minutes at 1,200 °C (1,473 K) in microgravity with the intent to dissolve the W particles into the matrix and to create a fine distribution of W dendrites homogenously distributed throughout. The samples were then cooled back to room temperature slowly, solidifying the morphology and composition. The Vitreloy 106 samples were compared with Zr48Cu47.5Al4Co0.5 in terms of composition of the matrix, morphology of the W dendrites, and mechanical properties, with comparisons drawn between samples produced on-orbit and on the ground to distinguish the effects of microgravity.
hypothesis: The hypothesis for the experiment is that microgravity promotes composite formation by stabilizing the interface between the W nano-particle nuclei and the bulk liquid. In contrast, on Earth, the heavy W particles would fall out of the system as they form. Therefore, the composition of the solid formed on Earth will differ from that formed in microgravity. On Earth, the samples should solidify in a manner consistent with the Scheil solidification approximation meaning: (a) liquid diffusion is instant over experimental timescales (b) solid-state diffusion does not occur (solid falls out of the system as it forms) (c) the solid composition profile will follow the solidus as the system cools, until all the liquid is consumed. In contrast, in microgravity, the solid/liquid interface lifetime is much longer, so there is more opportunity for solid back-diffusion. For this case, the composition profile will approach (but not reach) that of the equilibrium solidification case. After processing in both gravity and microgravity, experimental compositional data at the matrix-sphere interface will be obtained. It is expected that composites formed on Earth will solidify consistent with Scheil solidification and composites formed in microgravity will deviate from Scheil, approaching equilibrium solidification.
research_impacts: The development of innovative new materials is a fundamental part of future terrestrial and space technologies. These materials have a tremendous benefit towards improving life on Earth, from improving the accessibility and cost of solar power, to making cars safer and stronger, to reducing the mass of aircraft, for example. Innovative technologies typically require new materials tailored for those applications. This drives materials development.

title: PSI-159 Version 1 Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments / Cool Flames Investigation with Gases(ACME CFI-G) Investigation
objective: 1. Plan and support flight testing on the International Space Station (ISS). 2. Determine the conditions for which cool diffusion flames occur for propane, n-butane, and n-pentane; normal and inverse flames; and a broad range of Zst, Tad, and fluent flow rate. 3. Support the flight tests with advanced CFD simulations. 4. Identify or develop a chemical kinetics mechanism that yields good agreement between the CFD predictions and the ISS measurements. 5. Disseminate the results as widely as possible.
approach: Perform spherical diffusion flame tests aboard the International Space Station. Consider multiple fuels, a range of reactant dilutions, flow rates, and pressures for normal and inverse convection directions. Observe the flames with a broad suite of cameras, radiometers, photomultiplier tubes, and thermocouples.
hypothesis: The hypotheses of this research are that testing aboard the ISS can demonstrate the following for the first time, contributing to an improved understanding of cool flame kinetics. 1. Steady-state cool diffusion flames on spherical porous burners. 2. Cool diffusion flames burning propane, n-butane, and n-pentane. 3. Cool diffusion flames for a wide range of Zst, Tad, and pressures. 4. Inverse cool diffusion flames. 5. Cool diffusion flames for which a decrease in fluent flow rate will cause extinction, whereas an increase will cause a transition to a hot diffusion flame, with oscillation possible between hot and cool flames.
research_impacts: Combustion provides 86% of the world’s energy and an even higher fraction of the energy used for transportation. The internal combustion engines used for transportation generally have thermal efficiencies of 38% or lower because of thermal losses. These efficiencies may increase to 60% if future engines can take advantage of ultra-lean combustion. However, this progress is being impeded by the limited understanding of the chemistry of cool flames. Research into cool diffusion flames (whose peak temperatures are 500 – 1000 K) has grown exponentially since they were discovered in 2012. The measurements performed for this project will help to test and advance cool flame kinetics mechanisms. This should facilitate the development of more efficient internal combustion engines.

title: PSI-16 Version 4 Advanced Colloids Experiment - Temperature 1(ACE-T1) Investigation
objective: The ACE-T1 investigation seeks to answer fundamental questions about behaviors of colloids, helping scientists to understand how to control, change, and even reverse interactions between tiny particles. The objective is to build a fundamental understanding of the behavior of antisotropic (directionally dependent) Janus particles and their 3D self-assembly in microgravity. For decades, important advances have been reported in the literature regarding the effects of directionally dependent particles, both the chemical and morphological aspects, that provide the potential to extend the complexity of the self-assembled structures.
approach: The ACE-T1 investigation was executed in 2 phases and utilized 3 Sample Modules (SM), each having 3 temperature controlled capillary cells with 20 ml sample fluid each. Phase 2 was a re-run of the T1-103 SM and employed confocal microscopy, which uses a 532-nm frequency-doubled Nd:YAG laser, a confocal scanner, and an 8- to 12-bit digital CCD camera. The scanner allowed 30 frames per second of confocal images to be taken by the CCD camera. A sample’s 3D crystal structure was reconstructed by assembling individual slices with an image analysis program, from which colloidal growth, structure, and dynamics can be observed and measured. To obtain statistically meaningful data, at least ten colloidal structures in one capillary cell was imaged, at least ~400 minutes of observation on each capillary.
hypothesis: Fundamental science and colloidal engineering can be pursued and understood directly at a particle level. Microscopy enables scientists to directly observe what is happening at a colloid particle level - one no longer requires a theoretical model to hope to connect macroscopic experimental observations to microscopic ones (as when observing experiments at the size scale seen with a photograph taken of a BCAT or PCS sample).
research_impacts: SPACE APPLICATIONS Observing colloidal interactions without the influence of gravity provides new insight into how unhindered particles form network and structures. Results from ACE-T1 lay a foundation for understanding this mechanism. Very small scale self-assembly of materials can be an efficient method to build new materials and equipment in space. EARTH APPLICATIONS The ACE-T1 investigation seeks to answer fundamental questions about behaviors of colloids, helping scientists to understand how to control, change, and even reverse interactions between tiny particles. This knowledge is crucial for developing self-assembling, self-moving, and self-replicating technologies for use on Earth. It is anticipated that this novel fabrication approach can be applied to produce novel functional material in various applications such as self-assembly, photonics, diagnostics, and drug-delivery.
hardware: ACE-T and 3 Sample Modules Light Microscopy Module (LMM) Fluids Integrated Rack (FIR)

title: PSI-160 Version 1 Ring-Sheared Drop - Interfacial Bioprocessing of Pharmaceuticals(RSD-IBP-I) Investigation
objective: The Ring-Sheared Drop (RSD) is a Microgravity Science Glovebox experiment that launched in July 2019 to the ISS to study shearing flow in the absence of solid walls. The major goals of this project were to adapt and use the RSD module to develop and test predictive models of non-Newtonian flow of high-concentration proteins at the interface. Incorporating non-Newtonian constitutive equations for both interfacial and bulk flows and coupling the interfacial and bulk stresses is essential for mechanistic models that would be capable of predicting behavior under flow conditions of practical interest. The coupled problem is intrinsically nonlinear and there is a need to develop robust and accurate numerical techniques to interrogate flow dynamics and experimentally validate and verify results. The ring-sheared drop interfacial bioprocessing of pharmaceuticals-I (RSD-IBP-I) campaign aimed to study non-Newtonian interfacial hydrodynamics of the blood transport proteins bovine serum albumin (BSA) and human serum albumin (HSA) in microgravity. Specifically, scientific aims focus on the effects of protein primary structure (BSA or HSA), protein concentration (4, 40, or 400 mg/mL), and interfacial shear rate (3, 10, or 30 rpm) on microgravity fluid flow, measured using velocimetry of hollow glass microsphere tracer particles within protein samples. This campaign intended to confer improved understanding of interfacial protein flows in relation to physiology, the environment, and industry relevant to both spaceflight and Earth.
approach: Preflight preparation included refurbishment of all test cells including modification of test cells S/N 101-106 to include the flight tested (both parabolic and ISS with the assistance of NASA MSFC) integrated deployment tube and upper ring design by TBE, refurbishment of all test cells used in the previous RSD-BPS campaign by TBE, preparation of protein samples and methodological ground controls. Following sample installation, the RSD drop was deployed by extruding a drop from the deployment tube until pinning is achieved at the far ring. Shearing was then commenced by rotation of the far ring, measurements recorded for startup, steady, and stop flows each at 3, 10, and 30 rpm. Each 1.5 min. image sequence was then compressed to a portable video file and downlinked to the ground computer at RPI. ISS flight campaigns occurred Summer 2022 and Spring 2023, achieving 92% of proposed science objectives with 121.5/132 sample videos successfully collected, meeting the criteria for complete success. Additionally, 27 videos of interfacial aging and 24 micrographs of extra data were collected. The RSD hardware concluded the campaign in a nominal configuration with good health and status after four years in space aboard the ISS. Postflight: Test cells were returned June 30th 2023 on SpX-28 to TBE. Test cells appear to be in nominal pre-refurbishment configuration. RSD hardware remains in nominal configuration and good health.
hypothesis: The study of fluid interfaces coupled to bulk flows, including non-Newtonian response of either the interfacial or the bulk fluid can be uniquely advanced through experimentation in microgravity, where surface tension containment can be achieved at relatively large length scales. If the hydrodynamics of concentrated protein solutions are precisely measured, then sufficiently descriptive viscosity constitutive relations can be selected or developed from fundamental physics to describe fluid behavior.
research_impacts: Coupled bulk and interfacial flow in the RSD, developed under this grant is currently being analyzed to aid in formulating a model of non-Newtonian interfacial hydrodynamics coupled to a Newtonian bulk flow. These results were recently submitted for publication in a special issue of the journal Fluids, entitled ''Non-Newtonian Flow: Interfacial and Bulk Phenomena.'' While all cases examined remain at least weakly coupled to the bulk flow, this investigation established the effective ranges of model parameters. Bulk flow profiles demonstrate moderate sensitivity of the bulk flow to the behavior of the air-liquid interface, in general increasing with higher Boussinesq number Bq (non-dimensionalized surface viscosity) while maintaining interface to bulk flow coupling. Furthermore, investigation of dissipation may be useful for gauging the interchange between the hydrodynamics and energetics of flow constituents. The change in Bq by the shear-thinning model is indicative of a change in structure of an constituent material. As such, changes in the shape of a constituent of a complex fluid induced by flow are reciprocal with the changes that manifest in flow behavior. Describing the stability of such reciprocal changes could lead to a better understanding of natural systems as well as improved control of transport phenomena.

title: PSI-165 Version 1 Advanced Colloids Experiment -Temperature controlled- 2(ACE-T2) Investigation
objective: The objective of this experiment is the investigation of the assembly of complex structures from micron-scale colloidal particles interacting via tunable attractive interactions. Regulating temperature enables control of particle interactions. This simple reversible process is controlled by adjusting the size of the tunable temperature fluctuations in a two-component fluid (solvent). In principle, the ingredients are simple: particles suspended in a binary solvent, without the addition of any other components. By studying this process based on critical Casimir forces in microgravity, where sedimentation and convection are essentially removed, we will learn how to adjust complex attractive particle interactions. This simple reversible process is controlled by adjusting the size of the tunable temperature fluctuations in a two-component fluid (solvent). In principle, the ingredients are simple: particles suspended in a binary solvent, without the addition of any other components. Understanding self-assembly processes like the critical Casimir effect will teach ways to grow complex nanostructured materials. Furthermore, these experiments will provide fundamental insight into the nature of temperature-controlled super structure assembly, the relation between complex interactions and complex equilibrium and non-equilibrium structures, and the dynamics of both equilibrium and non-equilibrium growth processes.
approach: The ACE-T2 experiment utilizes the Fluids Integrated Rack (FIR) and the Light Microscopy Module (LMM). Accordingly, the ACE-T2 experiment will use a camera which scans at 30 frames per second of confocal images. ACE-T2 utilizes capillary cells. One set of three capillary cells is provided for each sample module. Each capillary contains 1 ml of a binary solution consisting of Lutidine and aqueous mixture of. The samples also contained polystyrene 3-(trimethoxysilyl) propylmethacrylate (PS/TPM) spheres. The difference between capillaries are as follows: Sample Module: S/N 2011: Capillary 1 Composition: -32% Lutidine -68% H₂O with 40% wt sucrose in H₂O fraction + 2 mM salt (KCl) Particle Size Ratio: 1:1 Number Ratio of Particle Sizes: 20/80 Capillary 2 Composition: -32% Lutidine -68% H₂O with 40% wt sucrose in H₂O fraction + 2 mM salt (KCl) Particle Size Ratio: 1:1 Number Ratio of Particle Sizes: 50/50 Capillary 3 Composition: -32% Lutidine -68% H₂O with 40% wt sucrose in H₂O fraction + 2 mM salt (KCl) Particle Size Ratio: 1:1 Number Ratio of Particle Sizes: 80/20 Sample Module: S/N 2012: Capillary 1 Composition: -32% Lutidine -68% H₂O with 40% wt sucrose in H₂O fraction + 2 mM salt (KCl) Particle Size Ratio: 1:1.2 Number Ratio of Particle Sizes: 20/80 Capillary 2 Composition: -32% Lutidine -68% H₂O with 40% wt sucrose in H₂O fraction + 2 mM salt (KCl) Particle Size Ratio: 1:1.2 Number Ratio of Particle Sizes: 50/50 Capillary 3 Composition: S/N 2018 Particle Size Ratio: 1:1.2 Number Ratio of Particle Sizes: 80/20 Sample Module: S/N 2018: Capillary 1 Composition: -25% Lutidine -75% H₂O + 1 mM salt (MgSO₄) Particle: 1.2 μm diameter *Note: Dipatch and Tetrapatch Capillary 2 Composition: -25% Lutidine -75% H₂O + 1 mM salt (MgSO₄) Particle: 3.8 μm diameter *Note: Dipatch and Tetrapatch Capillary 3 Composition: -25% Lutidine -75% H₂O + 1 mM salt (MgSO₄) Particle: 1.2 μm diameter *Note: Tetrapatch Here is a brief high-level descriptive outline of the investigation on-orbit procedures that gives general experiment steps for each capillary. 1- Short mix of sample. 2- Ramp temperature to find critical temperature and reduce temperature and initiate a very long mix of sample. 3- Determine Region of Interest (ROI). 4- Ramp temperature continuously while imaging. 5- Mix sample followed by Single temperature step visits. 6- Mix sample followed by stepwise temperature ramp with image stacks.
hypothesis: The critical Casimir effect is affected by temperature, particle size and relative concentrations and will impact the growth of complex nanostructured materials.
research_impacts: Understanding self-assembly processes will teach ways to grow complex nanostructured materials. Furthermore, these experiments will provide fundamental insight into the nature of self-assembly, the relation between complex interactions and complex equilibrium and non-equilibrium structures, and the dynamics of both equilibrium and non-equilibrium growth processes. Ultimately, it is hoped that these insights can be applied to advances in in photonic and optoelectronic technologies.
hardware: Fluids Integrated Rack (FIR) Light Microscopy Module (LMM)

title: PSI-166 Version 2 Unified Support for THERMOLAB - ISS, ICOPROSOL and PARSEC(EML USTIP Batch 2) Investigation
objective: Specific objectives of this investigation were as follows: • Plan and develop experiment parameter sets to investigate anomalous nucleation events in zirconium samples during ISS-EML experiments • Analyze cavitation-induced nucleation experiments on zirconium and zirconium-nickel alloys • Analyze fluid flow during ISS-EML experiments to support collaborators investigations • Continue flight preparations and development of experimental parameter sets for upcoming experiments in Batch 3 • Provide magnetohydrodynamic (MHD) modeling support of macroconvection in various materials for three ESA sponsored projects: PARSEC, THERMOLAB - ISS, ICOPROSOL.
approach: • The anomalous nucleation events of interest are hypothesized to be caused by cavitation in the melt. Experiments replicated the conditions in which the nucleation events were previously observed and explored similar experimental conditions. • Magnetohydrodynamic modeling of fluid flow is to be used to determine the flow conditions during ISS-EML experiments. Relevant parameters include fluid velocity, shear rates, turbulence intensity, and their distribution. Such data is critical for control of experiments and input to other theoretical and modeling efforts.
hypothesis: • Dynamic nucleation is an effect of the fluid flow and not reliant on classical nucleation theory. • Thermophysical property measurements may require appropriate flow conditions, which should be quantified • Flow conditions may affect solidification and nucleation behavior • Oxygen may influence surface tension measurements in metallic melts
research_impacts: Containerless processing provides access to the deeply undercooled region of metallic melts. Using this unique processing environement we are able to investigate fundamental solidification behaivor and meausure thermophysical properties of metallic melts including density, surface tension, viscosity, thermal expansion, heat capacity, thermal conductivity, and electrical conductivity. More specifically, impacts and benefits are broken out by the 3 associated flight experiments. In PARSEC, the effect of fluid flow on the solidification path of certain alloys is investigated. Control of the solidification path would enable tailoring of the microstructure and properties of metal parts for specific applications. In ThermoLAB, the thermophysical properties of high-temperature materials is investigated. Many of these materials are used commercially. A better understanding of the physical properties will allow more efficient and more reliable production of metallic parts using these alloys. Other alloys are chosen because of scientific interest in their properties, which may illuminate fundamental physics related to the formation of bulk metallic glasses and quasicrystals. The nucleation and growth of quasicrystals, and the effect of atomic-scale order on the macroscopic properties of these alloys is investigated in ICOPROSOL. This fundamental investigation may improve our ability to tailor the microstructure of metals for commercial applications.

title: PSI-167 Version 1 Advanced Colloids Experiment - Imaging, Folding and Assembly of Colloidal Molecules(ACE-T9) Investigation
objective: In ACE-T9, the imaging capability, folding dynamics, and assembly behavior of linear colloidal chains, colloidal dimers, and lock-and-key particles were studied by the combination of a proper design of particle architecture and tunable colloidal interactions (e.g., double layer repulsion and hydrophobic attraction). In the case of colloidal chains, for example, the single chain dynamics should sensitively depend on the chain flexibility and monomer-solvent interactions. Under the microgravity environment, we hoped to observe qualitative three-dimensional, real-time dynamics of single colloidal chains (using pre-confocal - bright field and fluorescent microscopy. We also aimed to observe three-dimensional structures assembled from colloidal dimers and lock-and-key particles and to measure the binding equilibrium constants that are impossible to measure in earth experiments due to the effect of sedimentation.
approach: The imaging goal is to observe (1) real-time and three-dimensional particle centroid positions of colloidal chains over both short (30 minutes) and long period (one week); (2) assembled structures, crystallites, and resolve particle centroid positions for colloidal dimers and Janus spheres. For short-time imaging, the video should be taken with 5 fps over 30 minutes. For both cases, the x-y positions of particles should be determined with less than 5% error (with respect to particle diameter). The z-positions should be determined within 1 micron. For fluorescence imaging, lamp should be shuttered between image sets to prevent sample bleaching.
hypothesis: In the microgravity environment, we will study the folding dynamics of single colloidal chains where the chain architecture can be varied systematically, and the monomer-solvent interaction can be tuned by varying salt concentrations. Furthermore, by tuning the balance between electric double layer repulsion and hydrophobic attraction on both colloidal dimers and lock-and-key particles, we aim to study the assembly of those colloidal molecules into complex three-dimensional structures and measure the binding equilibrium constants. This set of experiments provide insight into the relation between particle shape, colloidal interaction and structure. With the wide variety of attributes that characterize anisotropic interactions, we will probe previously inaccessible regions of complex phase space. Our studies will move significantly beyond hard spheres and towards experimental models appropriate for studying fundamental questions associated with complex symmetries.
research_impacts: In-situ manipulation of anisotropic interactions and dynamic pathways, based on rational colloidal particle design and proper use of external fields, could lead to crystalline and a periodic structures beyond those seen in nature. Results from this study will lead to improved control of non-covalent assembly of molecules, efficient tailoring of lattice symmetries, and the scalable processing of nano-structured materials. The development of new colloidal molecules and their associated assembled structures have considerable technological impact as well. Such structures will generally lead to arrays with reduced symmetry and enhanced directionality. They can interact with a broad range of electromagnetic radiation in unique ways and can exhibit collective photonic, plasmonic, mechanical, electronic, or magnetic properties that are not manifested at the level of single particles. As a result, they have significant potential as next-generation functional materials.
hardware: Light Microscopy Module (LMM) Fluids Integrated Rack (FIR)

title: PSI-168 Version 1 Advanced Colloids Experiment - Aging Dynamics and Stress-Relaxation in Colloidal Gels Studied in Microgravity(ACE-T10) Investigation
objective: Colloidal stability is critical to soft matter systems, especially to consumer products. These structures change in time, by processes know as coarsening - meaning the spacing between particles compact. This compaction continually changes this structure. When the structures created in the products can longer resist the gravitational stresses (e.g. buoyancy) on the structures, they collapse. The collapse, such as those that occur in geological formations during earthquakes, is often abrupt and without warning (delayed collapse). This is the essence of product instability. For some systems, the gel collapse can be anticipated by precursors, that can potentially be detected and forecasted. This research will have significant impacts in two areas: • It is not clear how the microscopic structure and its dynamics are related to the gel mechanical properties. The structure evolution controls the aging of the gel, and, on earth, this eventually leads to collapse. This work may significantly enhance the knowledge necessary to advance this important area of science. • Second, relaxation of localized stresses in an amorphous solid brought by a rapid solidification process is ubiquitous in nature and can damage and destroy the materials. Besides affecting the rheological properties of the materials, these dynamics rule the aging of the thermal systems at rest. The detection of failure precursors, as the ones discovered in our colloidal gel, can potentially allow us to forecast the material failure before catastrophic rupture.
approach: The ACE-T10 experiment exploited the Fluids Integrated Rack (FIR) and the Light Microscopy Module (LMM). The Light Microscopy Module (LMM) is an automated microscope. It permitted flexible imaging (e.g., bright field, dark field, phase contrast, confocal microscopy) for physics experiments and can be controlled remotely from the ground. The LMM accommodated sample change-out and fluid containment and included a glove box for on-orbit sample manipulation. The ACE-T10 experiment used include confocal microscopy, which utilized a 532-nm frequency-doubled Nd:YAG laser, a confocal scanner, and an 8- to 12-bit digital CCD camera. The scanner captured 30 frames per second of confocal images by the CCD camera. A sample’s three-dimensional crystal structure can thus be reconstructed by assembling individual slices with an image analysis program. This information, in turn, enabled the observation and measurement of the colloidal growth, structure, and dynamics. The confocal module was attached and aligned to the side of the LMM. The microscope used a reflecting mirror to direct the light to and from the sample. ACE-T10 utilized 6 capillary cells in 2 holding modules. The capillary cells, each contained about 20 microliters of the sample fluid and a magnetic stainless steel stir bar. Samples were stirred prior to example. The sample temperature was adjusted between 20 – 60 °C in order to find the transition temperature where the sample became a gel.
hypothesis: ACE-T10 delivered unique insights into the restructuring behavior of thermo-reversible colloidal gels, a topic of noticeable interest for the community of scientists dealing with soft materials. In normal gravity experiments, the ACE-T10 science team found evidence that the aging of these soft gels proceed via a sequence of sudden intermittent bursts of dynamical activity that resembles the ‘critical avalanche’ phenomena observed in several driven systems. The evidence collected suggests that, in a soft solid, these avalanches may be triggered by thermal agitation and occur spontaneously, even in the absence of other external forces. However, because of the density difference between the fluid and the particles in the gel network, gravity may play a role as well. Performing the ACE-T10 experiment in microgravity provided a unique opportunity to determine the gravity contribution.
research_impacts: Earth benefits/spin-off applications include understanding the behavior of weak gels and their aging can help materials scientists to make consumer product with longer shelf lives. In addition, because several features of the failure dynamics of disordered materials are system independent, the results obtained using this model colloidal system can be generalized to other materials. This potentially can help to develop new way to characterize aging material and suggest their replacement before catastrophic failure.
hardware: Fluids Integrated Rack (FIR) Light Microscopy Module (LMM)

title: PSI-169 Version 1 Advanced Colloids Experiment-Nanoparticle Haloing(ACE-T12) Investigation
objective: Nanoparticle Haloing (NPH) is a colloidal stabilization technique that has been discovered relatively recently. In NPH, highly charged nanoparticles are used to stabilize much larger (by 2 orders of magnitude or more), non-charged particles. To accomplish this stabilization, the volume fraction of nanoparticles within the suspension need only be on the order of 1e-5 up to 1e-4 to stabilize at 1 to 2 vol% suspension of the larger particles. The objective of this work is to gain fundamental insight into the physics of NPH with the aim of addressing the following unresolved questions: • How will NPH suspensions behave in thermal or electrical field gradients as they do under gravity? • How does the halo form or re-form if disturbed? • Can NPH (and manipulation thereof) be used to assemble and reconfigure colloidal crystals? • How does the nanoparticle charge impact halo formation?
approach: The ACE-T12 experiment utilizes the Fluids Integrated Rack (FIR) and the Light Microscopy Module (LMM). The FIR is built to accommodate a wide range of experiments. Accordingly, the ACE-T12 experiment included confocal microscopy, which used a 532-nm frequency-doubled Nd:YAG laser, a confocal scanner, and an 8- to 12-bit digital CCD camera on a Leica DM-RXA microscope. The scanner captured 30 frames per second of confocal images by the CCD camera. ACE-T12 utilizes capillary cells. Three capillary cells with different concentrations of nanoparticles were provided in a sample module. Here is a brief high-level descriptive outline of the investigation on-orbit procedures that gives general experiment steps for each capillary. 1- Short mix of sample. 2- Ramp temperature to find critical temperature and reduce temperature and initiate a very long mix of sample. 3- Determine Region of Interest (ROI). 4- Ramp temperature continuously while imaging. 5- Mix sample followed by Single temperature step visits. 6- Mix sample followed by stepwise temperature ramp with image stacks.
hypothesis: When NPH suspensions were allowed to settle under gravity, those that were stabilized (while in suspension) formed highly ordered, 3-dimensional colloidal crystal structures. Current theory suggests that nanoparticles create a charge layer by forming a cage, or Halo, around the larger particles. Another hypothesis regarding the NPH stabilization mechanism focuses entirely on nanoparticle adsorption to the surface of the larger particle. Based on the measurement of the interaction forces between two larger colloidal surfaces in a nanoparticle suspension, it was found that the force curves obtained could be fitted using a model based on nanoparticle adsorption.
research_impacts: Ultimately, the ability to design colloidal particles with a variety of well-controlled three-dimensional bonding symmetries opens a wide spectrum of new structures for colloidal self-assembly, beyond particle assemblies whose structures are defined primarily by repulsive interactions and shape. Such materials might include photonic crystals with programmed distributions of defects. Optical technology utilizing such materials may offer intriguing solutions to unavoidable heat generation and bandwidth limitations facing the computer industry.
hardware: Fluids Integrated Rack (FIR) Light Microscopy Module (LMM)

title: PSI-17 Version 3 Advanced Colloids Experiment - Temperature 6(ACE-T6) Investigation
objective: ACE-T6 studies the microscopic behavior of colloids in gels and creams. Consumer products are often required to be ‘structured’ by colloidal gels to prevent instability - or bulk separation of dispersed benefit actives. Benefit actives are generally dispersed as micron-size drops in liquid products to impart a consumer benefit, such as fabric softness. This leads to a fundamental challenge- how do you preventing bulk separation of the actives (i.e. maintain shelf life) while at the same time maintaining the relative ease-of-flow characteristics of the products. The objective of ACE-T6 is to use confocal microscopy to study the 3D behavior of microscopic particles in gels and creams, to advance knowledge of the fundamental physics associated with gel coarsening to improve the shelf-life stability of products. The microgravity environment on ISS was required to detach phase separation from coarsening.
approach: The ACE-T6 investigation utilized a single Sample Module (SM) having 3 temperature controlled capillary cells with 20 ml colloidal sample fluid and each having differing particle concentration. The capillary cells were situated on the temperature gradient stage (typical range: 20 – 60 °C, 10 °C temperature differential over the full length). The experiment employed confocal microscopy, which uses a 532-nm frequency-doubled Nd:YAG laser, a confocal scanner, and an 8- to 12-bit digital CCD camera. The scanner allowed 30 frames per second of confocal images to be taken by the CCD camera. A sample’s 3D crystal structure was reconstructed by assembling individual slices with an image analysis program, from which colloidal growth, structure, and dynamics can be observed and measured. To obtain statistically meaningful data, at least ten colloidal structures in each capillary was imaged, for at least ~400 minutes of observation on each capillary.
hypothesis: ACE-T6 addresses the effect of polydispersity on coarsening in colloidal systems. It is hypothesized that polydispersity in the polymer makes order-of-magnitude differences in the time scale of collapse of weak gels. The investigation attempts to make benchmark microgravity measurements and advance theories that allow a more comprehensive understanding of the role of polydispersity in the coarsening process.
research_impacts: This research will have significant impact in two areas. First, in the scientific community, there is a large disconnect between microscopic structure and dynamics of these mixtures to the macroscopic changes in the structure which lead to collapse. This work will significantly enhance the knowledge necessary to advance this important area of science. Second, understanding this relationship should enable us to anticipate instability in products, directly impacting the development of multi-billion dollar products and initiatives which improve the lives of 4.8 billion people on Earth per day from products originating from Procter and Gamble alone. Understanding the behavior of mixtures and coarsening can help materials scientists to make colloidal mixtures with longer shelf lives. This has great potentials in creating a wide range of products from food, medicine, cosmetics, gels, and cleaning solutions which do not expire quickly.
hardware: ACE-T and 3 Sample Modules Light Microscopy Module (LMM) Fluids Integrated Rack (FIR)

title: PSI-174 Version 1 Micromechanics Based Modeling of Cement Solidified in the Microgravity Investigation
objective: Micromechanics‑Based Modeling of Cement Solidified in the Microgravity aimed to advance knowledge of the mechanical properties of cement binders formed in reduced gravity by leveraging microgravity materials data, such as SEM/BSE micrographs, available in the PSI database. This project sought to connect microstructure (e.g., porosity, phase morphology such as portlandite) observed in ISS‑cured tricalcium silicate (C3S) pastes to bulk mechanical/transport behavior through modeling, thereby informing design and engineering of cementitious materials for extraterrestrial construction and providing validated simulation data that scale sparse flight samples to application‑relevant sizes.
approach: In this work, the micromechanics analysis code with generalized method of cells (MAC/GMC) was used to predict the structure-property relationship of these unique cement samples. First, the sparse data of cement hydrated in microgravity environment was converted to high-fidelity 3D microstructure with the aid of a deep learning-based microstructure methodology. The reconstructed sub-volumes were compared against micro-CT data using statistical descriptors. Second, the sub-volumes (partitioned based on individual constituents) of such reconstructed 3D structures were fed into the NASA Multiscale Analysis Tool (NASMAT) to obtain homogenized properties of the cement. A semi-automated Python script was developed to complete the workflow. Owing to the high computational demand, the analyses were carried out in NASA Advanced Supercomputing (NAS) servers. Phase‑discerned ISS and ground BSE/SEM images were segmented and reconstructed into 3D volumes using a deep learning microstructure framework; these Representative Volume Elements (RVEs) were then analyzed with NASA’s Multiscale Analysis Tool (NASMAT) to homogenize and predict effective properties. Reconstruction quality was validated against statistical descriptors and micro‑CT data, and the modeling spans length‑scale partitioning to capture porous, multiphase behavior. The experimental basis originated from the MICS investigation (PSI‑84 in the database), which conducted controlled ISS/ground hydration in sealed Burst Pouches, keeping temperature/pressure/humidity constant so gravity is the sole variable, followed by porosimetry, TGA, XRD, EDS/EMPA, and image analysis to quantify phase fractions and pore structures that feed the modeling pipeline.
hypothesis: Consistent with the microgravity MICS investigation, the central hypothesis was that minimizing gravity‑driven transport (buoyancy, sedimentation, convection) yields a diffusion‑controlled hydration process in microgravity, producing more uniform phase distributions and distinct microstructures (e.g., higher porosity, altered portlandite morphology) relative to 1g; these differences are expected to translate into measurably different mechanical properties for µg‑hardened cement paste versus terrestrial cement. The grant tested this by quantifying microstructural features from flight/ground samples and propagating them through micromechanics to predict property deltas attributable to gravity effects.
research_impacts: This research provides the first reference simulation data and a practical route to predict how cement (including regolith‑based mixes) behaves when fabricated in space, which can inform Artemis‑aligned or other space-based habitat concepts and construction logistics where transporting bulk materials is prohibitive. On Earth, the deep-learning-assisted reconstruction and micromechanics workflow developed can be applied to other multiphase materials, enabling materials-by-design even when only a limited samples are available. By clarifying how processing conditions in microgravity affect cement structure and performance, such as the ~70% porosity and plate-like portlandite observed in ISS samples, this work improves predictive models for optimizing mix designs and curing conditions in constrained environments. These advances also benefit low-resource or extreme-environment construction on Earth and contribute more broadly to the ICME community.

title: PSI-177 Version 1 Investigating the Structure of Paramagnetic Aggregates from Colloidal Emulsions - 4(InSPACE-4) Investigation
objective: The overall objective of the InSPACE-4 investigation was to study the effects of particle shape and toggle duty cycle on the phase separation kinetics of particles in toggled fields. Three specific objectives include: (1) investigation of phase separation kinetics of anisotropic particles in toggled fields, (2) study the effect of toggle duty-cycle on the phase diagram, and (3) perform concurrent ground-based self-assembly experiments using the same magnetic colloids and extend the work to dielectric (insulating) particles driven by toggled alternating current (AC) electric fields.Concurrent ground-based experiments help translate International Space Station (ISS) discoveries to Earth-based manufacture by providing additional insights into the structure of equilibrated phases.
approach: This ISS investigation was conducted using magnetic prolate ellipsoids with aspect ratios ranging from 2:1 to 4:1. Experiments involving spheres was also be conducted for comparison purposes. The sample material consisted of randomly oriented nano Fe3O4 coated polymer beads within a fluid filled vial, creating a magnetorheological fluid (MR). The vials were subjected to a pulsed magnetic field, which created a configuration of three-dimensional structures.The particle orientation was determined from birefringence measurements using crossed polarizers. The effects of particle shape, anisotropy, and magnetic field toggling frequency on the phase separation of particles was examined. Relatively short duration, ground-based experiments was conducted using the same magnetic particles to provide additional details about structure formation from particle-level to mesoscale structure.
hypothesis: Due to their anisotropic dynamics and interactions, investigators hypothesize that particle shape, in particular anisotropy (having different physical properties along different molecular axes), affects the phase separation kinetics of suspensions in toggled fields. Theoretical and simulation results suggesting that dynamic self-assembly can access a broad range of states analogous to equilibrium phases, even metastable ones, was also tested.
research_impacts: Discoveries from this work could lead to advanced materials for space applications such as better thermal shields, protection from micrometeorites, materials for energy production, energy-transfer devices, control systems and new mechanical actuators and sensors for robotic and human missions. This investigation helps advance the manufacture of next-generation nanomaterials for applications on Earth such as thermal shields, sound damping devices, shock absorbers, camouflage, medical diagnostic and environmental sensors, display technologies and advanced coatings. The technology also is expanding into larger-scale applications such as building foundation stabilizers for areas prone to earthquakes.

title: PSI-178 Version 2 The origin of fragility in high-temperature oxide liquids - towards fabrication of novel non-equilibrium oxides(ELF-6 PRONTO) Investigation
objective: This project investigated the high-temperature thermophysical properties of molten metal oxides, with a particular focus on molten titanates. These property measurements were used to establish correlations with atomic structure and glass formation. The research exploits the unique capabilities in microgravity to measure the thermophysical properties – density, thermal expansion coefficient, viscosity and surface tension – over a wide temperature range. Samples, including glasses, were recovered after melt processing in microgravity for ground-based analysis and comparison with materials made on Earth. The work underpins development of a materials property-structure data set that can help in development of new materials and in meeting requirements of material utilization, processing in space, and exploration.
approach: Density, thermal expansion, viscosity, and surface tension of molten oxides were measured using the Electrostatic Levitation Furnace (ELF) onboard the ISS. Measurements included silhouette imaging and drop oscillation over a wide range of temperatures, including deep supercooling. Recovered samples included glasses and polycrystalline materials, which were characterized post-flight using a combination of X-ray scattering, neutron scattering, X-ray tomography, Raman spectroscopy, calorimetry, and electron microscopy. Space-made glasses were compared with terrestrial analogues to investigate how changes in fluid transport may influence structure and properties.
hypothesis: Glasses are inherently non-equilibrium materials. Their structure and properties depend directly on the processing route used to form them. Because gravity affects fluid convection, glass formation and resulting structure may differ between different gravity conditions. We hypothesize that the superior control of fluid and thermal transport possible in microgravity will enable improved glass forming ability via melt quenching in containerless conditions, particularly for highly fragile liquid oxides. We hypothesize that the differences in thermal history - between microgravity and Earth-based processing - will manifest as differences in structure and thermodynamic properties.
research_impacts: This project advances the understanding of oxide melt properties, atomic structure, and glass formation. This builds a foundation for the development of new functional glasses and related technologies, with applications on Earth and in space for exploration and utilization of local resources. The project was successful on several fronts: 1. Microgravity experiments enabled melting, drop imaging, drop oscillation and measurements of properties of approximately 30 samples. 2. First experiments in ELF that used melt processing to make and recover glass in space. 3. First publications that compare the structure of glasses made in microgravity vs. terrestrially. 4. First demonstration of laser action in a titanate-network glass and of a glass made by containerless processing. 5. Results were analyzed in collaboration with a variety of researchers leading to 12 peer-reviewed publications and more than 20 presentations. 6. Two patents are pending based on results of the work. These have a high impact on glass materials processing in space and development of new glass products both on-Earth and in reduced gravity. 7. The project met all of the stated goals: perform basic research in microgravity, develop applied knowledge to make new materials, build collaborations to advance the field, and establish the basis for new glass materials products made in reduced gravity. 8. The results are relevant to the applied research mission of NASA's Biological and Physical Sciences (BPS) to enable space exploration and utilize materials based on natural resources that are available in space. 9. Developed and fostered a productive international collaboration.

title: PSI-179 Version 1 Aerosol Sampling Experiment(ASE) Investigation
objective: Aerosols are small particles suspended in the air, and in Earth’s atmosphere, aerosols include soot, dust, pollen and a wide range of other natural and human-made materials. Smoke does not rise and dust does not settle in microgravity the way they do on Earth, causing aerosols to behave differently and pose hazards for crew members breathing the air. The Aerosol Sampling Experiment (ASE) collects airborne particles in the International Space Station’s (ISS) cabin air, and returns them to Earth for scientists to study. The objectives of ASE were: 1- Characterize airborne particulate matter aboard the ISS to assess air quality for crew health and hardware longevity. 2- Identify particle sources (e.g., human skin, equipment wear, biological contaminants) in the spacecraft environment. 3- Improve understanding of particle transport and accumulation in microgravity conditions. 4- Support design of future spacecraft air filtration systems, ensuring they are appropriately targeted for actual airborne particle profiles.
approach: The ASE approach involved passive aerosol sampling in multiple ISS modules using filters placed in air ducts and cabin areas (especially near high-traffic zones and vents) by deploying commercial off-the-shelf (COTS) samplers for long-duration exposure (3 months–1 year). The sampled filters were returned to Earth for ground-based analysis using: 1- Scanning Electron Microscopy (SEM), 2- Energy-Dispersive X-ray Spectroscopy (EDS) and 3- Gravimetric analysis. The ISS samples were compared to terrestrial cleanroom and indoor environments to assess relative cleanliness and particle source uniqueness. Data collected was cross-referenced with previous ISS air monitoring efforts (e.g., TOCA, CCAA) to inform models of contaminant accumulation and mitigation.
hypothesis: Airborne particulate matter aboard the ISS exhibits a different size distribution, composition, and transport behavior in microgravity compared to Earth-based environments, and that particles from crew activity and hardware wear contribute significantly to the aerosol burden as well as the assumption that microgravity reduces sedimentation, allowing finer particles to stay suspended longer and accumulate in regions not typically affected by gravity-based settling on Earth.
research_impacts: Crew members on the ISS are breathing more or less the same fixed volume of air that has been on the ISS for years. There is no chance to get ‘fresh air’ as we do on Earth, but an advanced air revitalization system processes and cleans the air continuously. Crew members in space have complained of allergies and nose and eye irritation, which suggests the ISS cabin air has a high concentration of tiny particles that can be inhaled. The ISS filtration system is designed to remove these particles, but researchers have no way to verify the efficiency or cleanliness of the air. This investigation generates new data to characterize the quality of the air on the ISS, in terms of particles. Future space travelers may benefit from this data, as they can be used in the design and selection of particle detectors appropriate for low gravity. Long-term manned space missions need aerosol measurement capability to ensure crew health and comfort

title: PSI-18 Version 4 Advanced Colloids Experiment - Temperature 7(ACE-T7) Investigation
objective: The ACE-T7 experiment involves the design and assembly of complex 3D structures from small particles suspended within a fluid medium. These so-called “self-assembled colloidal structures”, are vital to the design of advanced optical materials and active devices. The objective of ACE-T7 was to utilize confocal microscopy for time- and space-resolved, 3D imaging of non-spherical colloids whose phases can be controlled by adding depletants and/or adjusting spatial temperature changes around a particular location. The research goal is to produce cubic colloidal structures, and study the dynamics of crystal nucleation and growth. ACE-T7 varied the size of the depletant in different samples with the goal of seeing the effect on crystallization. The imaging goal was to observe crystallites and resolve particle centroid positions with less than 20% error.
approach: The ACE-T7 experiment used the Fluids Integrated Rack (FIR) and the Light Microscopy Module (LMM) with enhancements. ACE-T7 utilized two sample cartridges, each having three temperature-controlled capillaries for a total of six samples; each capillary volume has 50 mm length, 2.0 mm ID width, and 0.2 mm ID height, with automated mixing capabilities using magnetic stir bars embedded in the capillaries. Each sample volume was about 20 μl. Each cartridge could be heated or cooled uniformly via Peltier temperature control. The concentrations of hollow silica microcubes and silica nanoparticle depletants are varied to study the effect that each of these parameters have on the dynamics of crystal nucleation and growth in microgravity. In total, six capillaries are prepared, numbered C1-C6. In capillaries C1-C4, the depletant concentration is kept constant at a concentration that produces cubic crystals in a timely manner on Earth (within 1 hour), while the concentration of hollow silica cubes is varied. In capillaries C5 and C6, the depletant concentration is increased and two different concentration of hollow silica cubes are used. After homogenization of each sample using the magnetic stirrer, the particles are left undisturbed to crystallize. Samples were preliminarily observed with a 2.5X objective, followed by measurements with 10X, 63X (air), 63X (oil), and 100X (oil) objectives.
hypothesis: It is hypothesized that under certain conditions, the particles should self-organize into crystals with simple cubic symmetry, which is set by the size of the nano-size depletant. Increasing particle number density using a temperature gradient, i.e., thermophoresis, is expected to induce formation of crystallites. Three-dimensional structures that are impossible to create or reform on earth due to sedimentation issues (high density contrast between particles and fluid) should be observed in microgravity.
research_impacts: Future space exploration may use self-assembly and self-replication to make materials and devices that can repair themselves. Self-assembly and evolutionarily optimized functional units are key to long-duration space voyages which will require use self-assembly and self-replication to make materials and devices that can repair themselves. This research will enable design and development of functional colloidal structures for new devices for chemical energy, communication, and photonics, including photonic materials to control and manipulate light. Such materials might include photonic crystals with programmed distributions of defects. Optical technology utilizing such materials may offer intriguing solutions to unavoidable heat generation and bandwidth limitations facing the computer industry. The beginning of this process is understanding the basic interactions between micro- and nanoscale particles, and how to control them using external sources such as temperature and light.
hardware: ACE-T and 1 Sample Module Light Microscopy Module (LMM) Fluids Integrated Rack (FIR)

title: PSI-181 Version 1 Structure and Properties of Pb-Sn and Pb-free Sn-Ag-Cu Solders Produced in Terrestrial vs. Microgravity Environments under Extremes of Elevated and Cryo Temperatures Investigation
objective: This study addresses the reliability of solder joints in space by pursuing two principal objectives: (1) Characterization of solder-joint formation under microgravity conditions aboard the International Space Station, specifically examining the impact of suppressed convective flow and buoyancy on 40Pb-60Sn alloys utilized in the In-Space Soldering Investigation (ISSI). (2) Evaluation of the solder’s material and mechanical properties under extreme thermal environments, including elevated and cryogenic temperature exposures characteristic of spaceflight conditions.
approach: The study examined three distinct solder alloys: the ISSI lead-based (40Pb-60Sn) composition, an off-eutectic 50Pb-50Sn formulation, and a lead-free alloy consisting of 95.5Sn-3.8Ag-0.7Cu. Microstructural characterization was performed on four solder specimens processed in microgravity from the ISSI investigation, one terrestrial ISSI solder, and a freshly fabricated terrestrial 40wt%Pb-60wt%Sn sample. These analyses elucidated the role of suppressed buoyancy and natural convection in void formation within microgravity environments. Evidence of void-induced Marangoni convection influencing microstructure development was demonstrated using wire-feed solder processed in space. The micromechanical response of solders fabricated under both terrestrial and microgravity conditions was further evaluated across a broad thermal range (–157ºC to +121ºC), simulating the conditions encountered externally on the International Space Station. Investigations under cryogenic conditions focused on the β-to-α phase transformation in Sn below 13ºC, examining associated volumetric expansion, internal stress evolution, and the ductile-to-brittle transition phenomena observed in Sn-based alloys. At ambient temperature, the influence of accelerated aging on both microstructural stability and mechanical performance was assessed.
hypothesis: In microgravity environments, fluid dynamics are markedly constrained, predominantly governed by solidification-induced volumetric changes, thermally driven density gradients, and Marangoni convection. This suppression of fluid motion results in diminished mixing, causing voids and gas bubbles to remain entrapped within the solder joint during the solidification process. Such internal porosity critically impairs the solder’s thermal and electrical conductivity, while also compromising the mechanical robustness of the joint. To advance the feasibility of extended space missions, this study seeks to elucidate the fundamental mechanisms, observable phenomena, and process parameters that influence the structural and functional integrity of solder joints fabricated under terrestrial and microgravity conditions.
research_impacts: The research presented in this project offers significant contributions across multiple space exploration initiatives: (i) The project objectives are closely aligned with ongoing NASA initiatives focused on metal joining techniques in reduced gravity environments. The three solder alloys investigated—selected in collaboration with NASA partners, underscoring the relevance of the study to future space exploration efforts, (ii) The findings are expected to inform the design of future experiments responsive to forthcoming NASA proposal calls, including those associated with the Artemis program, which aims to return humans to the lunar surface, (iii) The insights gained into microgravity fluid behavior and surface tension variation can be extended to a broad range of spaceflight-enabling technologies, such as boiling, heat transfer, combustion, welding, brazing, and soldering. This research enhances the understanding of gravity-driven separation processes—such as gas bubble removal—that must be accomplished via alternative mechanisms in microgravity conditions. (iv) The gravity-level-specific protocols (GLSPs) developed for various soldering configurations serve as practical guidance for future investigations into metal joining techniques under reduced gravity. These protocols may be adopted by scientists and flight personnel for welding, brazing, and soldering applications in spaceflight environments.

title: PSI-182 Version 2 Colloidal gels: Aging in microgravity, Structure of highly polydisperse gels Investigation
objective: Data are from two projects: one related to aging, one related to polydispersity. The first project has data under folders with a name containing AGING. The second has data under folders with a name containing POLYDISPERSE. ------- Project 1: Objectives specific to aging of colloid gels •Quantify coarsening of colloidal gels under microgravity conditions. •Quantify changes in thermal fluctuations of colloidal gels under microgravity conditions. •Understand aging of colloidal gels over time scales range from seconds to tens of hours. Project 2: Objectives related to structure of polydisperse colloidal gels •Measure fractal dimension of polydisperse colloidal gels (on Earth) •Understand how particle size relates to contact number •Quantify tetrahedral structures, and how particle size influences tetrahedral structure in colloidal gels
approach: Project 1: We studied colloidal gels using the data from the Advanced Colloids Experiment-Microscopy-1 (ACE-M1) experiments. Colloidal gels are formed from sticky micron-sized solid particles in a liquid, where over time the particles stick together and form random clumps that eventually bridge across the entire sample chamber in tangled networks. The ACE-M1 data set consists of a large number of optical microscopy movies of colloidal gels. In microgravity, these gels are long-lived, rather than collapsing under their own weight as happens in ground-based experiments. We have analyzed these microscopy movies using particle tracking, studying the visible thermal fluctuations and the gel structure as it evolves over time. Some gels have thick aggregated regions, while others have more tenuous gel strands and free particles. We show that the structure and dynamics change over the several-day period of each experiment. Project 2: In a second project, we did ground-based experiments to study the structure of colloidal gels composed of polydisperse particles. In particular, we used confocal microscopy to image colloidal gels formed from highly polydisperse particles. We suspended our polydisperse particles in a density matched solvent, and let the particles spontaneously aggregate through the van der Waals force. The largest particles were more than 15 times the size of the smallest particles. As expected, larger particles have more nearest neighbors than small ones. This leads to an over-representation of large particles in tetrahedral structures where four particles are mutually nearest neighbors, showing that large particles help provide rigidity to the gel structure. The tetrahedral structures also suggest that particles are able to rearrange somewhat during the gelation process, until their motion is stabilized by the multiple contacts with their neighbors.
hypothesis: Project 1: Colloidal gels in microgravity conditions will coarsen over time, and their thermal fluctuations will diminish over time as the gel gets coarser; the coarsening will continue indefinitely because gravitational collapse will not be possible. Project 2: Large particles play significant roles in highly polydisperse colloidal gels, as they serve as highly connected nodes in the structure.
research_impacts: This research helps us understand the technical challenge of keeping particles dispersed in a colloidal suspension. A gel is one way to prevent particles from settling, although the long-time behavior of a gel is challenging to study under Earth gravity.

title: PSI-184 Version 1 Flow Boiling Heat Transfer Using Temperature Sensitive Paints(Flow Boiling TSP) Investigation
objective: Obtain spatiotemporal data in Zero-G flights during up-flow and down-flow in varying gravities (lunar, martian, 0-g) to obtain heat transfer coefficients along the tube.
research_impacts: The flight data is being used to develop and validate sub-models of the flow within each flow regime. Understanding of the heat transfer mechanisms will enable space-based heat exchangers to be designed with much more confidence. Although this work is primarily aimed at thermal management subsystems and development of lightweight evaporators, it also impacts other systems for novel power and transmission, advanced chemical propulsion, and energy storage.

title: PSI-185 Version 1 Testing Analytical and Numerical Models in Phase Coarsening using NASA Physical Sciences Informatics System Investigation
objective: NASA has supported “coarsening in solid–liquid mixtures” (CSLM) experiments, performed in microgravity on the International Space Station (ISS), with greatly reduced sedimentation rate in partially molten alloys. CSLM experimental data are stored in NASA’s Physical Sciences Informatics (PSI). Microgravity experiments offer a unique opportunity to test existing numerical modeling and theories of phase coarsening. The objective of this research is to test existing numerical modeling methods for simulation of the microstructure evolution that occurs during phase coarsening, using experimental data for Sn-Pb mixtures currently held in PSI. Results from this research can be found in the following publications: Wang, K.G., Glicksman, M.E. Testing Numerical Modeling of Phase Coarsening by Microgravity Experiments. JOM 69, 2825–2830 (2017). https://doi.org/10.1007/s11837-017-2553-x
approach: (1) use data archived in NASA's PSI system from the Coarsening in Solid-Liquid Mixtures (CSLM) microgravity experiments to determine mean and maximum particle sizes in each sample processed through the CSLM microgravity experiments; (2) apply a two-dimensional (2-D) phase-field simulation code to allow simulation and evolution of initial microstructures that were observed in the CSLM experiments for Sn-Pb solid-liquid phase mixtures, and which provide input data for our phase-field code to numerically evolve coarsened microstructures over time; (3) calculate particle size distributions (PSDs) from the prior NASA CSLM experiments, our phase-field and multiparticle diffusion simulations, and from diffusion screening theory.
hypothesis: Phase-field and multiparticle diffusion numerical methods can be applied to simulate the evolution of the microstructure during phase coarsening, delivering accurate statistical physical quantities such as the particle size distribution (PSD). Phase-field modeling can adequately capture the complexity of the microstructures developed during phase coarsening at large volume fraction. In contrast, multiparticle diffusion modeling can track the evolution of microstructures consisting of nearly spherical particles that develop during phase coarsening at lower volume fraction.
research_impacts: The contributions from our research activities improved the understanding of fundamental materials phenomena, i.e., phase coarsening. We advanced the state of the art in both theory and simulation. Better understanding of two-phase microstructures will help engineers improve process designs in economically important areas, including liquid-phase sintering for the production of hard tool materials. The theory and simulation tools developed herein that are tested by microgravity experiments, will provide technical pointers for the improvement of important processes, microstructures, and materials properties. The improved knowledge of microstructure evolution in this project will have significant impact on alloy design and service-life strategies for alloy materials. The theory and simulation tools developed will provide guidance toward exploring the structure and properties of alloys. Finally, the theoretical and computational tools will save money and time for alloy modification.

title: PSI-186 Version 2 Coupled Growth in Hypermonotectics(CGH) Investigation
objective: The overall objective of the Coupled Growth in Hypermonotectics is to understand the fundamental physics controlling solidification in immiscible alloy systems. Specific experimental goals were (1) to show that production of an aligned fibrous microstructure is possible in hypermonotectic alloys by achieving interfacial stability and steady state coupled growth through microgravity processing, (2) to determine the influence of alloy composition and growth velocity on microstructure, and (3) to determine the growth velocity and composition range over which interface stability is possible in a hypermonotectic alloy system.
approach: The CGH experiment investigation flew aboard the Life and Microgravity Spacelab (LMS) mission during the summer of 1996. Processing conditions were controlled in an attempt to force the production of an aligned fibrous phase in the microstructure of processed samples. The Advanced Gradient Heating Facility (AGHF) was used to directionally solidify the immiscible alloys. Aluminum (Al)-Indium (In) alloys were studied and specialized aluminum nitride (AlN) ampoules were used in order to control several undesirable effects that are sometimes observed during low gravity processing. Three alloy compositions, namely 17.3 weight % In monotectic, and 18.5 and 19.7 weight percent In hypermonotectic alloys were processed during this mission. A thermal gradient of 67 C/cm was achieved and all flight samples were processes at a translation velocity of 1 micrometer/s. Ground based control samples were subsequently processed under conditions identical to those of two of the flight samples in order to allow a direct comparison of the results.
