title: PSI-31 Version 5 Cold Atom Lab - Microgravity Dynamics of Bubble-Geometry Bose-Einstein Condensates(CAL-BEC Bubble Dynamics) Investigation
objective: Microgravity Dynamics of Bubble-geometry Bose-Einstein Condensates (Cold Atom Lab - BEC Bubble Dynamics) aims to study Bose-Einstein Condensates (BECs) and degenerate Fermi gases (DFGs) confined to a the surface of an experimentally-controlled topologically-connected ''bubble.'' The limitations of gravitational sag have prevented terrestrial exploration of a quantum gas confined to such as surface. This investigation aims to test fundamental ideas in quantum mechanics, statistical mechanics, and strongly-correlated many-body physics in condensed matter. Studying the behavior of quantum gas bubbles could provide insights for next-generation quantum sensors and simulators.
approach: This investigation uses rubidium (87 Rb) and potassium (39K and 41K) samples in the Cold Atom Laboratory (CAL) aboard the International Space Station (ISS). The approach for the investigation comprises two main aspects: the creation of ultracold atomic gases and the subsequent manipulation and probing of these gases to study systematic mitigations. Creation of Ultracold Atomic Gas: Laser Cooling: Atoms are released into a vacuum chamber and collected into a magneto-optical trap (MOT), where they are initially cooled using laser cooling techniques. This technique cools the sample by essentially ‘pushing’ the laser against the motion of the atoms effectively lowering the momentum, and therefore the velocity, kinetic energy, and temperature, of the sample. This is followed by a brief stage of “optical molasses” during which the quadrupole magnetic field is turned off and the laser frequency is further detuned. State Preparation: The sample is optically pumped to a low magnetic field-seeking quantum state. The state is then subjected to an intermediate quadrupole magnetic field which allows for the transferred from the MOT, located at the bottom of the science region, to an atom-chip-based trap, located at the top of the science region. Evaporative Cooling: The atoms undergo evaporative cooling to below the critical temperature, leading to the formation of a Bose-Einstein Condensate (BEC). Evaporative cooling cools the sample by removing the highest-energy atom from the trap so that the remaining atoms re-thermalize at progressively lower temperatures. Decompression and Release: The atom trap is slightly relaxed to further cool the atoms, eventually releasing them completely to allow free expansion. At this point, investigators can search for the primary signatures of a BECs for confirmation that one was formed. Formation of a BEC is typically associated with the behavior of the velocity distribution, such as the presence of a narrow peak centered at near zero velocity and the low velocity peak growing (greater fraction of atoms in this domain) as the temperature decreases. Manipulation and Probing: Probing Techniques: The ultracold gas is probed using laser, radiofrequency, and/or microwave pulses. These techniques are designed to investigate the pairwise interactions and molecular dynamics crucial for mitigating systematics in high-precision measurements. Time-of-Flight Imaging: After a predetermined time of flight, the sample is imaged using absorption imaging techniques. This process involves taking two images: one of the sample and a reference image post-destruction of the sample. As implied, this is the end of the experimental cycle for this specific BEC as the measurement process destroys the sample. The manipulation and probing aspect is particularly important for this specific investigation as the ultracold atomic gas must be treated with certain fields to achieve the bubble topology. To do this, a locally harmonic spin-dependent trapping potential originating from inside an applied magnetic field is combined with a near-resonance oscillatory magnetic field with a certain radiofrequency. Together these two magnetic fields produce atoms in spatially dependent dressed atomic states that experience dressed or adiabatic dressed potentials. These potentials can then be manipulated via tuning the radiofrequency field so that the atoms take on an ellipsoid or bubble-like geometry.
hypothesis: This investigation hypothesizes that radiofrequency dressing can be used to create a trap formed by a spherical or ellipsoidal shell structure capable of confining quantum gases to a “bubble” topology. Due to gravitational sag and trap distortion present in terrestrial experiments this trap topology has not been explored, and further, it is only able to be explored in the microgravity environment unique to the Cold Atom Laboratory (CAL). The low-energy excitations of such systems, as well as various theories on the physics of phase transitions will be investigated using this bubble-geometry.
research_impacts: This work, while focused on the fundamental physics of ultracold atoms and not directly connected to human life, has a similar impact to life on Earth as that of all fundamental physics; it broadens our understanding of the physical world and helps us further cement our collective picture of quantum mechanics as ''the way the world works.'' It explores the limits of how large Bose-Einstein condensates can be made, and to what extent the gravity-well of terrestrial labs render certain investigations difficult or impossible. The observations made aboard CAL through this project are a clear demonstration that physical insight can sometimes require microgravity facilities to be fully developed, and that space borne atomic physics experiments can be valuable contributions to our collective scientific efforts. Additionally, insight into fundamental laws of quantum mechanics can have many applications in many on Earth. Quantum computers continue to exponentially accelerate as a field of study and in industry, and research into these fundamentals can support scientific workforce development, public science outreach and research and development.

title: PSI-32 Version 4 Cold Atom Lab - Consortium for Ultracold Atoms in Space(CAL-CUAS) Investigation
objective: The Consortium’s work is described in the context of four Tasks. Task 1: Advanced Clocks in Space and Time Transfer Task 2: Maturing and Advancing Atom Interferometer Technology for Space Task 3: Precision Atom Interferometric Measurement in Space Task 4: Strategies for the Frontier of Ultracold Atoms in Space. The Consortium is: N. P. Bigelow, M. Kasevick, W. Ketterle, M. Lukin, H. Müller, W. D. Phillips, D. Pritchard, D. Stamper-Kurn, V. Vuletic, and J. Ye. Berkeley and Stanford lead Tasks 2 and 3. MIT, U.C./JILA, and Harvard lead Task 1. U. Md., Rochester, and MIT lead Task 4. Members of the Consortium can and often will contribute to all four tasks with priorities being set by the lead institutions.
approach: The Consortium for Ultracold Atoms in Space (CUAS), led by Nicholas Bigelow, conducted groundbreaking experiments in atomic clocks, atom interferometry, and quantum gases, with a strong focus on the application of these quantum technologies in space environments. The consortium's research was guided by the objectives outlined in the National Research Council (NRC) report and NASA's Research Announcement (NRA), particularly in precision measurement and quantum gas studies. The Consortium fostered a collaborative approach, bringing together scientists from top institutions like MIT, Stanford, Berkeley, and Harvard, as well as international partners such as those from the DLR (German Space Agency). This collaboration allowed the group to pool expertise, regularly refine their goals, and push forward only the most promising space experiments. The procedure for the creation of an ultracold gas is fairly standardized. The atoms are released into a vacuum chamber, collected into a magneto-optical trap (MOT), and cooled via laser cooling. The sample is then optically pumped to a low magnetic field seeking quantum state and transfer from the MOT to an atom-chip based trap. The atoms are then evaporatively cooled to below the critical temperature so that a Bose-Einstein Condensate (BEC) begins to form. The atom trap is slightly relaxed to further cool the atoms, and eventually the atoms are completely released from the trap and allowed to expand freely. At this point, the ultracold gas is probed using laser, radiofrequency, and/or microwave pulses. After a prespecified time of flight, the sample is imaged using absorption imaging techniques. This is the end of the experimental cycle for this specific BEC because the measurement process destroys the sample. A total of two images are taken, the first being an image of the sample and the second being a reference image that is taken after the destructive absorption imaging process. This general process was followed by the Consortium for experiments requiring the production or probing of ultracold quantum gases. In their work on atom interferometry, the Consortium conducted experiments to detect dark-energy scalar fields with unprecedented sensitivity. The team also focused on measuring the fine structure constant with high accuracy, which involved overcoming systematic effects that could be amplified in the space environment. Collaborations with the Bose-Einstein Condensate and Cold Atom Laboratory (BECCAL) science definition team and other international partners were essential for demonstrating long coherence times in microgravity, testing the equivalence principle, and searching for dark-energy candidates. These experiments were conducted with a focus on utilizing the microgravity conditions available aboard the International Space Station (ISS) and other space-based platforms, which provided a unique environment to achieve results unattainable on Earth. In the realm of atomic clocks and quantum sensors, the Consortium developed new configurations for optical lattice clocks and achieved precision at the 19th decimal place, setting a new record for stable laser performance with a linewidth of 10 mHz. These experiments were designed to improve the accuracy of space-based timekeeping and navigation systems, which are critical for the success of space missions. The Consortium also explored innovative cooling methods, such as direct optical cooling to achieve Bose-Einstein condensation, which simplified the setup for quantum experiments in space. These methods were tested and refined in microgravity environments, demonstrating their potential to enhance the performance of quantum technologies in space. Overall, the Consortium’s approach to conducting experiments was characterized by a strong emphasis on leveraging the unique conditions of space, particularly microgravity, to achieve results that would be impossible on Earth. Their collaborative efforts, cutting-edge experimental designs, and focus on precision allowed them to make significant contributions to the field of quantum technologies in space, laying the groundwork for future space missions and advancing our understanding of fundamental physics.
hypothesis: This consortium aims to provide a space for the world’s experts on Bose-Einstein Condensates (BEC), atom optics, atom interferometry, and related quantum realms to push the current boundaries of quantum gas and atomic physics space experiments. It is hypothesized that with the realization of a space atom laser and precision atomic interferometry there is potential for significant scientific advancement by testing the equivalence principle with quantum test masses and pushing the limits of the standard model. A space atom laser is expected to provide truly novel investigations of the wave-like nature of matter. Varied experiments and manipulation of quantum gases (both single-species and dual-species) including deep cooling, condensate mixture phases, and precision motional control are hypothesized to mature the technology of quantum gases and provide first of its kind opportunity to investigate interacting quantum gases in space.
research_impacts: Significant progress has been made on atomic interferometry and atomic clocks in terrestrial experiments. The work has long-term impact for fundamental science, navigation technologies, and global clock synchronization. Clocks are vital to navigation, communication, and security. ATOM INTERFEROMETRY We have pushed atom interferometry for space applications forward in many ways: 1. We have shown that atom interferometry can detect dark-energy scalar fields with unprecedented sensitivity. There is a chance to cover all the relevant parameter space so as to detect them or to rule them out once and for all. This work has been published in Science, Nature Physics, and Physical Review D. 2. We have demonstrated a theoretically predicted, but never observed, attractive force on atoms from blackbody radiation. It is an important limitation that has to be taken into account in the design of atomic-physics space missions. 3. We have pushed forward the accuracy of atom interferometry for measuring the fine structure constant, which has resulted in a measurement of this constant with an accuracy about three times better than the best previous one. The agreement of this measurement with others sets very strong constraints on hypothesized particles from the dark sector, such as dark photons. 4. We have developed atom interferometry with lithium atoms, opening up the possibility to do interferometry with a much wider class of atoms than available previously. We will continue to develop atom interferometry for demonstrating the gravitational Aharonov-Bohm effect, and measuring fundamental constants very precisely. We will also work with the Bose-Einstein Condensate Cold Atom Laboratory (BECCAL) science definition team and other teams to identify future targets for spaceborne fundamental physics. The interferometry work has several main thrusts. In the first thrust, we have been investigating how spaceborne atom interferometry can probe models for dark matter and dark energy. This has resulted in experimental demonstrations of such tests for so-called chameleon and symmetron models, and theoretical studies on how to make detailed predictions of the putative signals. In the second thrust, we have developed strategies to overcome systematic effects in atom interferometers that use Bragg diffraction, as the one planned for the Cold Atom lab. In the third, we have developed specific plans for spaceborne atom interferometry. We have collaborated with the German team Document for atom interferometry on the Cold Atom Lab and BECCAL. Plans include demonstrating long coherence times thanks to microgravity, tests of the equivalence principle, and searches for dark-energy candidates. They have also collaborated with Nan Yu (Jet Propulsion Laboratory-JPL) on a concept study QTEST (Quantum test of the Equivalence Principle and Spacer-Time) for testing the equivalence principle in space. CLOCKS AND QUANTUM SENSORS TECHNOLOGIES We have demonstrated the first direct optical cooling to Bose-Einstein condensation, without any evaporative cooling. This has promising impact of simplifying spaceborne experiments. The Bose-Einstein condensation by direct optical cooling was achieved for small ensembles of ~1000 atom. We will attempt to make substantially larger condensates with the same method by using a more powerful trapping laser. We have been working on spin squeezing in the optical-transition clock with trapped ytterbium atoms. By implementing both frequency and intensity feedback loops for the magical wavelength trap inside an optical cavity, we have now lengthened the trap lifetime for the Yb sample from 200 ms to 2 seconds. We have also started non-destructive state-dependent measurements for spin squeezing by observing the light transmitted through the cavity, and we can already more than resolve the shot-noise limit. In the Rb experiment, we are working towards using Rydberg states for increasing the light-atom interaction in cavity QED. We have frequency-stabilized the control laser coupling the P state to high-lying Rydberg states. We have demonstrated a new optical lattice clock configuration using a three-dimensional optical lattice, leading to measurement precision in the 19th decimal place. We have also demonstrated another record-breaking performance on stable lasers, with the narrowest laser linewidth at 10 mHz. We will perform a clock comparison between this JILA Sr clock and the NIST (National Institute of Standards and Technology) Yb clock and Search for ultralight dark matter by comparing the Sr transition frequency with the resonance frequency of a crystalline cavity.2022 Update: Our team aims to study: o The realization of a space atom laser o Precision atom interferometry in space o The investigation and manipulation of quantum gas sample control including deep cooling, condensate mixture phases, and precision motional control Relevance: Potential for significant scientific advancement from interferometric tests of the equivalence principle with quantum test masses and pushing the limits of the standard model. Space atom laser provides truly novel investigations of the wave-like nature of matter. Varied experiments of the investigation and manipulation of quantum gases (both single-species and dual-species) mature the technology of quantum gases and provide first of its kind investigations for interacting quantum gases in space.

research_impacts: The development of precision inertial sensing techniques is useful for Earth-based as well as space-based navigation. Besides using direct sensing for inertial navigation, rotation sensing can also be useful for north-finding while gravity sensing can be used to tabulate local gravity variations and form a type of three-dimensional map for navigating. These techniques also have many applications in geophysics. Gravity sensing can be used for oil and mineral exploration, while rotation sensing can detect dynamics in the Earth's core. Gravity sensing also has defense applications such as locating underground tunnels and potential screening cargo for high-density contraband or weapons. Other precision measurement applications have less direct impact, but advance scientific knowledge. For instance, precision tune-out spectroscopy measurements of atomic matrix elements can be used to improve the interpretation of atomic parity violation experiments. These in turn impact our understanding of the standard model of particle physics and thus the nature of our universe. Direct benefits of such understanding can be hard to trace, but in general the continued advance of technological applications builds on advances in our fundamental knowledge.

title: PSI-35 Version 8 Cold Atom Lab - Fundamental Interactions for Atom Interferometry with Ultracold Quantum Gases in a Microgravity Environment(CAL-Fundamental Interactions) Investigation
objective: Precision atom interferometers (AI) in space promise exciting technical capabilities with diverse applications of interest to NASA. These quantum sensors are particularly relevant for fundamental physics research, with proposals including unprecedented tests of the validity of the weak equivalence principle, precision measurements of the fine structure and gravitational constants, and detection of gravity waves and dark matter/dark energy. This investigation will utilize the capabilities of NASA's multi-user Cold Atom Laboratory (CAL), in the microgravity environment onboard the International Space Station (ISS), to study mitigation schemes for the leading-order systematics expected to limit future high-precision measurements of fundamental physics with AIs in microgravity. The flight experiments, supported by theoretical investigations and ground studies at Jet Propulsion Laboratory (JPL), will concentrate on the physics of pairwise interactions and molecular dynamics in ultracold quantum gases as a means to overcome uncontrolled AI shifts associated with the gravity gradient and few-particle collisions. A space-based dual-species AI will be further developed and used, which is planned as an on-orbit upgrade to the CAL science module after approximately a year of science investigations, for proof-of-principle tests of systematic mitigations and phase-readout techniques for use in the next-generation of precision metrology experiments based on AIs in microgravity. The proposed studies require the effective position invariance, long free fall times, and extremely low temperature samples uniquely available with the CAL apparatus. It is anticipated that these studies can lead to the unprecedented level of control and accuracy necessary for AIs to explore some of the most fundamental physical concepts in nature.
approach: Investigation comprises two main aspects: the creation of ultracold atomic gases and the subsequent manipulation and probing of these gases to study systematic mitigations. For dual-species operations the process is slightly more complicated, especially with the addition of a sympathetic cooling step, however, the general process is fairly standardized. Creation of Ultracold Atomic Gas: -Laser Cooling: Atoms are released into a vacuum chamber and collected into a magneto-optical trap (MOT), where they are initially cooled using laser cooling techniques. This technique cools the sample by essentially ‘pushing’ the laser against the motion of the atoms effectively lowering the momentum, and therefore the velocity, kinetic energy, and temperature, of the sample. This is followed by brief stages of “compressed MOT”, in which the trapping force of the MOT is increased to compress the gas, and then an “optical molasses” stage, during which the quadrupole magnetic field is turned off and the laser frequency is further detuned to minimize the temperature of the gases. -State Preparation: The sample is optically pumped to a low magnetic field-seeking quantum state. The atoms in this state are then subjected to an intermediate quadrupole magnetic field which traps the atoms from the MOT and allows for the transfer from the MOT, located at the bottom of the science region, to an atom-chip-based trap, located at the top of the science region. -Evaporative Cooling: The atoms undergo forced evaporative cooling, using frequency sweeps of either RF or microwave fields, to bring the gases below the critical temperature, leading to the formation of a Bose-Einstein Condensate (BEC). Evaporative cooling cools the sample by removing the highest-energy atom from the trap so that the remaining atoms re-thermalize at progressively lower temperatures. -Decompression and Release: The tightness of the atom trap is adiabatically relaxed to further cool the atoms via decompression colling. After a short hold time in the relaxed trap, the atoms are released by rapidly turning the atom-chip and bias coil currents to zero to allow the atoms to expand in freefall. At this point, investigators can search for the primary signatures of a BECs for confirmation that one was formed. Formation of a BEC is typically associated with the behavior of the velocity distribution, such as the presence of a narrow peak centered at near zero velocity and the low velocity peak growing (greater fraction of atoms in this domain) as the temperature decreases. Manipulation and Probing: -Probing Techniques: The ultracold gas is probed in freefall using laser, magnetic field, radiofrequency, and/or microwave pulses. These techniques are designed to establish atoms in the proper state, perform atom interferometry, or establish and investigate the pairwise interactions and molecular dynamics crucial for mitigating systematics in high-precision measurements. -Time-of-Flight Imaging: After a predetermined time of flight, the sample is imaged using absorption imaging techniques. This process involves shining resonant light on the atoms and taking two images, per atomic species, of the shadow cast in the light: one of the sample and a reference image post-destruction of the sample. As implied, this is the end of the experimental cycle for this specific BEC as the measurement process destroys the sample. This approach is particularly suited for studying mitigation schemes for leading-order systematics that can affect future high-precision measurements with atom interferometers (AIs) in microgravity. By leveraging the unique microgravity environment provided by NASA’s Cold Atom Laboratory (CAL) on the International Space Station, this investigation aims to achieve the level of control and accuracy required for groundbreaking tests of fundamental physics principles, such as the weak equivalence principle, and precision measurements of the fine structure and gravitational constants. The integration of theoretical investigations and ground studies at JPL supports these flight experiments, enabling comprehensive understanding and development of systematic mitigation techniques.
hypothesis: This investigation hypothesizes that the control of interactions and association/dissociation of weakly-bound molecules in ultracold quantum gases can overcome uncontrolled Atomic Interference (AI) shifts in space which are caused by the gravity gradient and few-particle collisions. Investigators will interrogate this hypothesis by conducting tests using ultracold quantum gases and exploring Feshbach resonances at new energy regimes. Investigators expect unprecedented levels of control and accuracy in the AI that will enable exploration of some of the most fundamental physical concepts in nature and open up venues for exploration of novel quantum phases in exotic dynamical regimes.
research_impacts: Our studies are designed to achieve technological advances in precision metrology that can only be realized in the microgravity environment of the Cold Atom Laboratory (CAL). The tools of ultracold atomic and molecular physics are utilized (namely Feshbach resonances) for exquisite control of the differential center-of-mass distributions of the dual-species quantum gases and on methods to use the fundamentals of few-body interactions to maintain coherence in atomic ensembles for enhanced precision sensor capabilities. Subsequent proof-of-principle studies with the dual-species atom interferometer on CAL will further advance the state of the art for precision interferometry with ultracold matter waves. The impact of such research to the field of metrology can be seen through its potential to increase precision for atom-interferometry and also the possibility of engineering highly efficient system-specific devices based on the fundamental nature of few-body interactions. The microgravity environment of the CAL facility strongly favors such explorations and allow for the possibility of uncovering novel effects and quantum phases of matter, a major goal in ultracold quantum gases and other disciplines of fundamental physics. These studies can benefit life on Earth by providing both fundamental understanding of nature in previously inaccessible environments and energy regimes, and by enhancing the tools available for scientific exploration at the highest precision.

title: PSI-36 Version 4 Cold Atom Lab - Zero-G Studies of Few Body and Many-Body Physics(CAL - Few Body Physics) Investigation
objective: Zero-G Studies of Few-Body and Many-Body Physics (Cold Atom Lab - Few-Body Physics) investigates the dynamics of interacting ultracold atoms under varying conditions. The dynamics of few-body systems comprised of just three or four atoms can strongly influence the collective behavior of quantum gases and play an important role in development of quantum gas applications. Modern laser cooling techniques are used to chill atoms to near absolute zero temperatures. At these temperatures, atoms behave like matter waves, according to the laws of quantum mechanics. Fully automated data runs, each lasting about one minute, acquire images of ultracold atom clouds under varying conditions. The acquired data fills a critical need for the development of detailed and precise atomic physics models. The development of these models is performed in theoretical studies accompanying the data gathering campaigns with the CAL instrument. Studying the behavior and interaction of few atoms in microgravity could provide important data for developing a precise theory describing quantum gases on a microscopic level. The knowledge gained in this study also aids in the development of future quantum technologies for which a detailed microscopic understanding of few-body physics is essential. Examples of future quantum technologies include, among others, atom interferometers for inertial navigation or precision measurements of gravity and sensitive Terahertz (THz) detectors for astronomy.
approach: The Zero-G Studies of Few-Body and Many-Body Physics investigation uses rubidium (87Rb) and potassium (39K and 41K) samples in the Cold Atom Laboratory (CAL) aboard the International Space Station (ISS). The approach for the investigation comprises two main aspects: the creation of ultracold atomic gases and the subsequent manipulation and probing of these gases to study few-body physics and exotic quantum states. Modern laser-cooling techniques are used to cool atoms to near absolute zero temperatures. At these temperatures, atoms behave like matter waves, according to the laws of quantum mechanics. Fully automated data runs, each lasting about one minute, acquire images of ultracold atom clouds under varying conditions. 1. Creation of Ultracold Atomic Gas: • Laser Cooling: Atoms are released into a vacuum chamber and collected into a magneto-optical trap (MOT), where they are initially cooled using laser cooling techniques. This technique is based on the rapid scattering of light off atoms and can cool a cloud of atoms to temperatures below 1x10-3 K. An additional magnetic field applied in conjunction with the lasers concentrates the cold atoms in a specific region of the vacuum apparatus, called the source chamber. The MOT is the starting point for further cooling and experimental preparation. • State Preparation: Using further laser manipulations, the atoms are then prepared in a state that seeks to occupy regions of low magnetic fields. By applying a suitable magnetic field geometry with a moving magnetic minimum, the cloud of atoms is transported to a so-called “science region.” Magnetic fields generated by a chip with current-carrying traces provide a trap for the atoms in the science region. • Evaporative Cooling: With the atoms trapped in the science region, evaporative cooling is performed by selectively removing the hottest rubidium atoms from the cloud. The remaining atoms then rethermalize at a lower temperature. The selective removal of the hottest rubidium atoms is achieved by applying suitably tuned radiofrequency radiation. Potassium atoms are cooled by being in thermal contact with the actively cooled rubidium atoms, in a process called sympathetic cooling, where rubidium atoms act as a cold bath of atoms. With sufficient evaporative cooling, the clouds of rubidium and potassium atoms can undergo a phase transition to a Bose-Einstein condensate (BEC), providing a macroscopic, quantum mechanical object. However, pronounced quantum mechanical effects can already be observed before reaching this phase transition. • Further sample preparation: After the preparation of the ultracold sample, further preparation steps are employed for the proposed studies. These steps include changes to the trapping strength, changes of the internal states of the atoms, and the application of suitable homogeneous magnetic fields. 2. Manipulation and Detection: • Manipulation Techniques: The ultracold gas is manipulated using laser, radiofrequency, and/or microwave pulses. In addition, homogeneous magnetic fields are used to shift internal energy levels of the atoms. These techniques are designed to adjust the pairwise interactions as needed for the preparation of exotic quantum states. • Time-of-Flight Imaging: After a predetermined time-of-flight during which the cloud is released from the trap and can expand freely, the sample is imaged using absorption imaging techniques. For this, a short laser pulse is flashed onto the atoms, and the shadow cast by the atoms is imaged on a CCD camera using a custom microscope setup. This imaging process typically destroys the “quantumness” of the sample and concludes an experimental cycle. The apparatus then starts over with the preparation of a new sample. Many cycles are performed during a typical data-taking campaign, with a time scale of approximately one minute per run.
hypothesis: Ultracold atoms in microgravity provide a unique environment for the study of complex few-body phenomena. One of the surprising predictions for quantum mechanical few-body systems is the existence of universality, i.e. the idea that highly intricate phenomena can be governed by underlying principles that are agnostic to specific microscopic realizations. As a concrete example, Efimov physics predicts the emergence of an infinite series of exotic three-body bound states when the interactions between the atoms are made stronger and stronger. It is predicted that these Efimov states are connected by universal scaling relations governing their energy and their size. Our experiments aim to provide essential benchmark data to test this universality hypothesis. By measuring two members of this infinite series, scaling relations can be probed and can be compared to some of the most advanced few-body theories to date. This will be a steppingstone towards the investigation of a plethora of associated few-body phenomena, with the ultimate goal of significantly advancing the boundary of our understanding and paving the way for the development of new quantum technologies.
research_impacts: Physics is the discipline that provides understanding of biology and chemistry at the most microscopic level, and the area within physics most relevant to chemistry and biology is “few-body physics.” It is an often neglected portion of physics, because it is so difficult to do. An important way to make progress is to simplify, simplify, simplify: to come up with model systems in which we can make progress that can later be applied to human-centric disciplines like biology, and develop exotic and useful new materials. A promising way to simplify is to study matter at lower temperature, and lower densities. The Cold-Atom Lab (CAL) flying in the International Space Station (ISS) is where we will reach the lowest possible temperatures, and low densities, to perform studies of simple, yet intricate (think “snowflakes”) clusters of three or four atoms. Ultracold atomic gases are a key platform for a broad range of future quantum technologies, including ultraprecise sensing and timekeeping, novel medical imaging methods, secure communication schemes, high-performance computing, and development of exotic materials. A precise knowledge of few-body physics is necessary to fully realize the potential of quantum technologies. This project supports development of a detailed understanding of quantum mechanical few-body physics at the microscopic level, which may open new avenues for quantum gas applications in future space exploration. Such applications include inertial navigation and precision measurements using atom interferometry, or calibration standards for detectors used in astronomy.

title: PSI-37 Version 4 Capillary Flow Experiment - 2(CFE-2) Investigation
objective: Liquids behave differently in space than they do on Earth, so containers that can process, hold or transport them must be designed carefully to work in microgravity. The Capillary Flow Experiment-2 furthers research on wetting, which is a liquid’s ability to spread across a surface, and its impact over large length scales in strange container shapes in microgravity environments. This work will improve our capabilities to quickly and accurately predict how related processes occur, and allow us to design better systems to process liquids aboard spacecraft (i.e., liquid fuel tanks, thermals fluids, and water processing for life support).
approach: Wetting describes how well a liquid is attracted to a solid surface. Understanding the impact of wetting over large length scales in microgravity is important for a wide variety of engineering systems being developed for human spaceflight.Studies from CFE-2 may serve to demonstrate how liquids can be efficiently and passively separated from gases in the absence of gravity. This is a key operation in fluid systems aboard spacecraft such as water purification systems for life support.
hypothesis: This research hypothesizes that capillary flows in microgravity are strongly influenced by container geometry, particularly interior corners and gaps. For vane gaps, a critical wetting condition, dependent on gap size and vane design, is expected. In interior corners, imbibition rates, phase separation, and bubble dynamics should be highly sensitive to 3D geometry, with long-duration microgravity being crucial for observing subtle, slow processes. Experiments are designed to quantify these relationships and validate theoretical models.
research_impacts: The Capillary Flow Experiments demonstrate how capillary forces work in space, how differently shaped containers change the wicking behavior of a wetting fluid, and how such can be used to passively separate liquids and gases. Understanding how microgravity amplifies these behaviors could improve the reliability of such key processes as water purification fuel storage and supply, and general liquid transport aboard spacecraft. On Earth capillary action allows small amounts of liquid to flow up and into tight spaces despite the effects of gravity. New miniature medical devices, known as lab-on-a-chip technologies, exploit this phenomenon to draw blood or other fluids into essentially miniature l diagnostic systems. CFE-2 improves our understanding of how capillary forces work in a variety of system geometries including the open spaces within porous materials such as sand and soil, wicks and sponges.

title: PSI-38 Version 3 Capillary Flow Experiment(CFE) Investigation
objective: 1. The primary objective of the CL unit experiments is to identify the extent the role of the boundary condition at the contact line plays in the natural dynamic response of a large capillary interface to a variety of disturbances. 2. The primary objective of the ICF units is to experimentally determine secondary imbibition rates in complex containers due to spontaneous large length scale capillary flows along interior corners in weakly 3-dimensional containers. Secondary objectives of the experiments are to quantify such flows in closed loop cycles, and to identify the passive phase separation characteristics of certain capillary driven multiphase-flows (e.g. bubbly flow) along interior corners. 3. The primary objective of the VG units is to determine equilibrium interface configurations and critical wetting conditions for interfaces between interior corners separated by a gap. A secondary objective is to validate numerical predictions of the large length scale discontinuous or nearly discontinuous wetting phenomena.
approach: Without gravity, it is more difficult to control the flow of fluids and this is a challenge for designing spacecraft systems such as liquid propellants/cryogens, thermal control systems, wastewater management and recycling.Capillary forces (the interaction of liquid with solid that can draw a fluid up a narrow tube) continue to act in the absence of gravity and can be exploited to control fluid orientation so that fluid systems on spacecraft perform predictably.CFE uses the low-gravity environment provided by the International Space Station to understand the special dynamics of capillary flow and will aid in the design of fluid transport systems on future spacecraft.
hypothesis: The CFE investigations operate under the hypothesis that capillary phenomena in microgravity, specifically contact line dynamics, interior corner flows, and vane-gap wetting, deviate significantly from idealized theoretical predictions based on simplified geometries and boundary conditions. This deviation is anticipated to manifest as measurable differences in dynamic interface response (frequency and damping) for varying contact line conditions, geometry-dependent secondary imbibition rates in complex containers, and distinct critical wetting conditions in vane-wall gaps influenced by gap size and wettability. The CFE experiments are designed to quantify these deviations, providing empirical data to refine existing theoretical models and enhance the predictive capabilities for low-gravity fluid management systems.
research_impacts: The knowledge gained from this payload has the potential to be instrumental in the design of future fluid systems for spacecraft-impacting fluid bearing containers such as propellant and cryogenic fluids tanks, thermal control system coolant reservoirs, water storage and management systems, liquid state low-gravity materials processing equipment, and biofluids handling instruments for inflight human health systems. By performing this experiment, researchers will gain information that will lead to improvements in system reliability with reductions in system mass and complexity. These applications of CFE are in direct support of NASA's mission to develop safe, reliable, and affordable spacecraft to pursue the greater exploration of our solar system and universe. The results of the flight experiments are also expected to provide insights into terrestrial interfacial phenomena and may lead to models predicting fluid flows in porous media (i.e. ground water transport), complex capillary structures (i.e. high performance wicks for heat pipes employed in electronics cooling), and Lab-On-Chip technologies (i.e., microscale biofluids processing).

title: PSI-39 Version 4 Cool Flames Investigation(CFI) Investigation
objective: The objectives of this investigation are to: 1) Examine the combustion behavior of n-dodecane and mixtures of n-dodecane/iso-dodecane at pressures ranging from 0.25 atm to 5 atm. 2) Analyze the effects of helium dilution on cool flame behavior. 3) Examine the behavior of combustion characteristics. 4) Investigate the relationship between droplet size, pressure, and flame extinction, and (5) understand the consequence of soot formation during cool flame combustion.
approach: The Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR) contains the Multi-User Droplet Combustion Apparatus (MDCA) which facilitates the controlled combustion of fuel droplets. A system of gas bottles and fuel syringes delivers the desired gas mixture to the combustion chamber ranging from 0.25 to 0.5 atm. Droplets of fuel are dispensed and suspended between hypodermic needles or tethered using silicon-carbide fibers. A hot-wire igniter is positioned near the droplet for ignition. After ignition the wire is retracted. Fuels observed include n-dodecane, farnesane, and mixtures of n-dodecane/iso-dodecane. Fuels diluted with molecular oxygen, atomic nitrogen, and helium to study the influence on flame extinction and dynamics. Flames were observed with a black-and-white camera for droplet size measurements. A UV camera was used for capturing the OH* radical emissions and flame size. Other high resolution cameras were used for monitoring and documentation. Narrow-band and wide-band radiometers for analyzed flame radiation.
hypothesis: Flame combustion of liquid hydrocarbon fuels such as n-dodecane, n-dodecane/iso-dodecane mixtures, and faresane in microgravity can provide insights into low-temperature chemical kinetics, revealing critical parameters like droplet extinction diameters and flame dynamics that are not observable on Earth.
research_impacts: A basic understanding of cool flames is important for understanding ignition phenomena of practical fuels and fuel additives. Cool flames play a key role in the development and selection of new fuels and the design of advanced engines such as clean, high-efficiency Homogeneous Charge Compression Ignition (HCCI) engines. The research will also help combustion chemists to develop new computational models to compute combustion performance in for many practical applications on earth, including an understanding of how cool flame reactivity determines octane and cetane number for fuels in spark ignition and diesel engines. Cool Flames Investigation (CFI) will provide critical validation for complex chemical kinetic mechanisms, advance the understanding of flame dynamics and instabilities in low-temperature combustion, and support the design of safer spacecraft systems by refining knowledge of combustion in microgravity environments.
hardware: Multi-User Droplet Combustion Apparatus (MDCA) Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR)

title: PSI-4 Version 2 Flow Boiling and Condensation Experiment Flow Boiling Module(FBCE FBM) Investigation
objective: The proposed research aims to develop an integrated two-phase flow boiling/condensation facility for the International Space Station (ISS) to serve as a primary platform for obtaining two-phase flow and heat transfer data in microgravity. By comparing the microgravity data against those obtained in Earth’s gravity, it will be possible to ascertain the influence of body force on two-phase transport phenomena in pursuit of mechanistic models as well as correlations, and to help determine the minimum flow criteria to ensure gravity independent flow boiling and condensation. This research is a joint effort between the Purdue University Boiling and Two-Phase Flow Laboratory (PU-BTPFL) and the NASA Glenn Research Center. Personnel from the two organizations combine extensive experience in research and development of both flow boiling and condensation systems, and in conducting microgravity experiments. The objectives of the Flow Boiling and the Flow Condensation Experiment (FBCE) in the long duration microgravity environment of the ISS are to: 1. Develop experimentally validated, mechanistic model for microgravity flow boiling critical heat flux (CHF) and dimensionless criteria to predict minimum flow velocity required to ensure gravity independent CHF. 2. Develop experimentally validated, mechanistic model for microgravity annular condensation and dimensionless criteria to predict minimum flow velocity required to ensure gravity independent annular condensation. Also, develop correlations for other condensation regimes in microgravity. 3. Obtain flow boiling data (heat flux, flow visualization, the wall temperature difference) in long duration microgravity environments for a well characterized heating surface as functions of liquid inlet mass velocity and subcooling. 4. Obtain flow condensation data (heat flux, flow visualization, the wall temperature difference) in long duration microgravity environments for a well-characterized condensing surface as functions of inlet quality and flow rate of condensing vapor. Specific tasks for the study will be as follows.
approach: The approach used in this project is to perform the following sequential series of tasks: 1. Provide detailed design and instrumentation requirements for the Flow Boiling Module (FBM). 2. Provide design and instrumentation requirements for the entire flow loop. 3. Generate test matrix for operating conditions of the study. 4. Perform initial validation tests in both terrestrial gravity and parabolic flight. 5. Perform tests on board the ISS. 6. Based on both the ISS and terrestrial data, develop a series of predictive tools, including empirical correlations as well as theoretical, computational, and machine learning models.
hypothesis: In literature spanning many decades, body force in terrestrial gravity is identified as having a profound influence on two-phase transport behavior. This behavior is drastically altered In the absence of gravity, wherein flow fluid and heat transfer are dictated by flow inertia and surface tension. This implies predictive tools from terrestrial gravity studies are inapplicable for design of NASA's reduced gravity systems. This limitation points to a need for performing two-phase flow and heat transfer experiments on board the ISS as basis for formulating relevant reduced gravity predictive tools.
research_impacts: The proposed research will lay the foundation for development of advanced high power to weight ratio thermal management systems for NASA's future space vehicles and planetary bases. Purdue University research has also shown tremendous value in findings from this projects to numerous other applications including ultra-fast charging of electric vehicles, fusion reactors, hydrogen storage, avionics, high-Mach turbine engines, and advanced electronics in laser, microwave, and radar systems.

title: PSI-40 Version 4 Coarsening in Solid Liquid Mixtures-2(CSLM-2) Investigation
objective: The objective of the CSLM-2 investigation was essentially the same as the original CSLM investigation with the addition of higher solid volume percent samples requiring longer times to reach steady state coarsening rates.
approach: The CSLM-2 approach and hardware was identical to the predecessor CSLM investigation. The solid volume fraction of the 4 samples for CSLM-2 were 0.3. 0.5, 0.7, and 0.8.
hypothesis: The theory of coarsening has been described by Lifshitz, Slyozov and Wagner (LSW) predicts that for the limit of zero volume fraction particles grow with time as the cube root of the average radius, and the particle size distribution becomes independent of time. The investigation hypothesizes that finding a system which satisfies all the constraints of LSW theory such as particles are infinitely separated and there is no diffusional interaction between them is prohibitive for ground-based laboratory condition due to effects of particle sedimentation and buoyancy-induced convection and therefore the theory can only be tested by performing experiments in a microgravity environment, For CSLM-2 it is hypothesized that for large volume fraction solid samples the transient coarsening process will be longer and steady state will be reached much later compared to low volume fraction solid particles.
research_impacts: Coarsening occurs on Earth during the processing of any metal alloy and thus the coarsening process affects a large spectrum of products from dental fillings to turbine blades. Since the properties of an alloy are linked to the size of the particles within the solid, coarsening can be used to strengthen materials. This is the case with the majority of aluminum alloys used commercially today. Conversely, if the coarsening process proceeds too long the material can weaken. This occurs in jet turbine blades and is one of the reasons why turbine blades must be replaced after a certain number of hours of service. Thus developing accurate models of the coarsening process is central to creating a wide range of new materials encompassing those used in automobiles to those used in space applications.
hardware: CSLM Sample Processing Unit (SPU) and Electronic Control Unit (ECU)

title: PSI-42 Version 4 Coarsening in Solid-Liquid Mixtures(CSLM-3) Investigation
objective: The objective of this investigation was to study dendritic coarsening in solid-liquid mixtures at low volume fractions of solid. Specific interest was in examining dendritic structure close to the dendrite tip. Additional objectives included measuring the rate at which topological singularities occur when a secondary dendrite arm separates from the main dendrite stem or when two arms fuse together.
approach: The CSLM-3 approach and hardware was essentially identical to the predecessor CSLM and CSLM-2 investigations. The solid volume fraction of the 4 Pb-Sn samples for CSLM-3 were 0.1, 0.2, 0.3 and 0.4. Isothermal holding times between 10 minutes and 48 hours were employed. After the requisite holding times the samples were quenched using pressurized gas. Upon receipt of the samples they were analyzed using three-dimensional reconstructions of the microstructure. The 3D reconstructions was used to determine the interfacial curvatures, the genus and the spatial distribution of curvature in the system. The experimentally measured structures were used to compare phase field simulations and experiment.
hypothesis: The fundamental questions that this investigation attempts to answer are as follows: Does the Interface Shape Distribution (ISD) vary with position from the tip of the dendrite? If so, as is likely the case, does the ISD scale with time, as is usually the case during coarsening? How important is the spatial distribution of curvature in setting the evolution of the structure? How do diffusional interactions between the secondary, and perhaps tertiary, arms on different dendrites affect the evolution of the system? How does the ISD evolve when there are multiple dendrites in the system? Does scaling exist?
research_impacts: Coarsening occurs on Earth during the processing of any metal alloy and thus the coarsening process affects a large spectrum of products from dental fillings to turbine blades. Since the properties of an alloy are linked to the size of the particles within the solid, coarsening can be used to strengthen materials. This is the case with the majority of aluminum alloys used commercially today. Conversely, if the coarsening process proceeds too long the material can weaken. This occurs in jet turbine blades and is one of the reasons why turbine blades must be replaced after a certain number of hours of service. This investigation will provide insights into the dynamics of dendritic morphological evolution and will point the way to the formulation of models of this technologically important coarsening process. Thus developing accurate models of the coarsening process and validating them using benchmark experimental data is central to creating a wide range of new materials encompassing those used in automobiles to those used in space applications.
