title: PSI-44 Version 6 Coarsening in Solid-Liquid Mixtures(CSLM) Investigation
objective: The primary objective of the microgravity experiment was to measure the temporal evolution of the average size-scale of a solid-liquid mixture during solidification. Specifically, the objective was to measure the average intercept length and the average section area of the solid particles at various times and for various volume fractions of solid. Using this data the amplitude of the temporal power law for the average section area. and intercept length was to be determined. Once the amplitude of the temporal power law is known, the objective is to compare the result to the theoretical predictions on the dependence of the amplitude of the power law on the volume fraction of the coarsening phase. The objective was also to determine the steady-state particle size distribution by measuring the distribution of section area of of the particles in a plane and the intercept length distribution.
approach: The sample holder in the Sample Processing Unit (SPU) contained four Lead-Tin samples of 12 mm diameter and 6 mm thickness for various volume fractions of Tin. The SPU heated the samples up to 185 degree C in less than 9.5 min, held the temperature for a predetermined time at 185 ± 0.1 degree C ranging from 0.25 to 48hrs (coarsening phase). The heating system consists of two disc resistance heaters and one ring heater to insure uniform heating with four resistance temperature devices (RTD) installed mid-way between the discs 1 to measure temperature of the samples. Subsequent to the predetermined coarsening time the samples were quenched using pressurized air to nearly room temperature in approximately 1 minute. Once the samples were returned to earth they were sectioned and the measurements of particle size and distribution was performed.
hypothesis: The theory of coarsening has been described by Lifshitz, Slyozov and Wagner (LSW) predicts that for the limit of zero volume fraction particles grow with time as the cube root of the average radius, and the particle size distribution becomes independent of time. The investigation hypothesizes that finding a system which satisfies all the constraints of LSW theory such as particles are infinitely separated and there is no diffusional interaction between them is prohibitive for ground-based laboratory condition due to effects of particle sedimentation and buoyancy-induced convection and therefore the theory can only be tested by performing experiments in a microgravity environment.
research_impacts: The importance of coarsening from a commercial perspective arises from the major effect that coarsening has on the properties of materials, for example materials can become stronger while undergoing coarsening. The CSLM experiment will assess the validity of the theory of coarsening that has been used to design materials. The result will be a more rational design of materials using a first-principles approach, reduced development cost for the production of new materials and better materials properties. Such a first-principles design of materials will enable NASA and industry to create materials in a rapid cost-efficient manner with the superior properties that are needed for space exploration.
hardware: CSLM Sample Processing Unit (SPU) and Electronic Control Unit (ECU)

title: PSI-45 Version 3 Constrained Vapor Bubble-2(CVB-2) Investigation
objective: The primary objective of CVB-2 is to determine the overall interfacial stability, characterize the hydrodynamics, measure heat transfer coefficients, and determine the overall conductance of a complex fluid (94% Pentane/6% Isohexane) in a microgravity environment.
approach: The Constrained Vapor Bubble (CVB) Experiment was conducted on the International Space Station (ISS) and the temperature data have been used to analyze the heat transfer mechanisms operating within the quartz cuvette for 40 mm and 30 mm modules. Even with the large millimeter dimensions of the CVB, interfacial forces dominate in these exceedingly small Bond Number systems with small viscous losses. A comparison of the modeling results obtained using a simple one-dimensional analysis of the temperature fields found with the dry and partially liquid pentane filled cuvettes allowed the phase change and radiation fields to be determined in both microgravity and earth gravity. Unique visual observation of the shape of the liquid flow field through a microscope enhanced the understanding of the temperature and vapor pressure [1],[2] measurements. The internal heat transfer processes were very complicated, multidimensional, and the length of the closed system strongly affected the average internal heat transfer processes. Internal radiation was shown to be more significant than originally anticipated as well as the effect of Marangoni convection. The competing processes of capillary flow driving liquid from the cold to the hot end and Marangoni flow driving liquid from the hot end to the cold end resulted in the formation of a central drop and a pinch point in the film thickness profile. The results also indicate that the study of the constrained vapor bubble in an open loop heat pipe configuration would allow the passive bubble more freedom to respond.
hypothesis: In microgravity environments, the introduction of a higher boiling point, higher surface tension component into a low-boiling-point fluid within a constrained vapor bubble suppresses temperature-induced Marangoni convection, thereby enhancing heat transfer performance and system stability.
research_impacts: Most liquids have a surface tension that decreases as temperature rises. This causes fluid to flow in the direction of higher surface tension, a phenomenon known as Marangoni flow. This reduces the effectiveness of a heat pipe, because liquid cannot return to the hot end. CVB-2 investigates whether a mixture of two fuels (pentane and isohexane) that can reduce Marangoni flow and improve the efficiency of the CVB system on the International Space Station. In addition, the investigation provides insight into how heat transfer functions in microgravity. Most satellites use heat pipes to keep critical parts cool, and improved understanding of fluid mixtures could enable future heat pipes that are smaller, lighter and less expensive to launch. A wide range of high-performance devices must be perpetually cooled in order to function, from supercomputers to personal laptops and LED light bulbs. Fluid mixtures circulating through heat pipes can passively dissipate heat, using less energy than fans or cooling systems. But heat pipe transport systems are sensitive to small differences in temperature, pressure, and gravity. Studying how fluid mixtures and heat pipes function in microgravity provides insight into the fundamental principles of thermodynamics. This also provides insight into how mixtures of fluids behave during boiling, condensation, evaporation, distillation, and stripping. These processes are used in a variety of industries and environmental cleanup.

title: PSI-46 Version 4 Constrained Vapor Bubble(CVB) Investigation
objective: The immediate macroscopic objectives are to determine the overall stability, the fluid flow characteristics, the average heat transfer coefficient in the evaporator, and the heat conductance of the CVB as a function of vapor volume and heat flow rate. On the microscopic scale, the scientific objective is to evaluate the local details of the Kelvin-Clapeyron model of change-of-phase heat transfer under microgravity conditions where the extended Young-Laplace equation predominates.
approach: The CVB-1 investigation used a variety of methods to study the behavior of the constrained vapor bubble (CVB) in a microgravity environment. This approach involved conducting experiments, creating mathematical models, and using insights from past CVB experiments to analyze the findings after the flight. 1. Experimental Design and Testing: -Customized CVB Cells: Five CVB cells were fabricated from quartz. Each cell featured a square cross-section (3 x 3 mm) and varying lengths to achieve specific liquid-to-vapor volume ratios. One cell was a ''dry'' cell, evacuated to 5 torr, to establish baseline thermal behavior. The remaining four cells were filled with either pentane (a completely wetting fluid) or ethanol (a partially wetting fluid) before launch. Three cells utilized pentane at different volume ratios, while one was intended for ethanol. -Controlled Thermal Environment: The CVB cells were integrated into a system that allowed for precise control of heat input at the evaporator end and heat rejection at the condenser end. The system maintained a stable and uniform thermal environment for the cells. -Microgravity Environment: The CVB experiments were conducted on the International Space Station (ISS) to provide the necessary microgravity conditions. 2. Data Acquisition: -Macroscopic Measurements: Throughout the experiment, macroscopic data were recorded, including temperature profiles along the cell, vapor pressure, heat input and rejection rates, and visual observations of the vapor bubble. These observations were used to assess the overall performance and stability of the CVB system. -Microscopic Measurements: The investigation utilized an Image Analyzing Interferometer (IAI) to acquire detailed, microscopic measurements of the liquid film profile. These measurements included curvature profiles, film thickness profiles, and adsorbed film thickness. These data were crucial for understanding the local transport processes within the CVB. -Acceleration Measurements: The system monitored residual accelerations to assess their potential impact on the CVB's stability and behavior. Time Correlation: All acquired data were meticulously time-correlated to ensure accurate analysis and interpretation. 3. Mathematical Modeling and Analysis: - Extended Young-Laplace Equation: This equation, incorporating both capillary and van der Waals forces, was employed to model the equilibrium shape of the liquid-vapor interface. Kelvin-Clapeyron Transport Model: This model was used to analyze the non-equilibrium behavior of the CVB. It incorporated conservation equations for mass, momentum, and energy, along with the extended Young-Laplace equation. The model was considered for refinement to account for internal radiative heat transfer, observed in previous experiments. -Numerical Modeling: Two- and three-dimensional numerical thermal modeling were considered to evaluate and refine the Kelvin-Clapeyron model, particularly to capture the complex interplay between capillary and Marangoni convection. -Internal Heat Analysis: Temperature data were analyzed to quantify the contributions of conduction, external radiation, and internal radiation to the overall heat transfer within the CVB system. This analysis built upon previous ground-based studies and included a detailed examination of the role of Marangoni convection. 4. Comparison with Ground-Based Studies: -Equilibrium Studies: The microgravity equilibrium data, including film thickness and curvature profiles, were compared with ground-based measurements to confirm the validity of the extended Young-Laplace equation under these conditions. -Non-Equilibrium Studies: Comparison of microgravity non-equilibrium data with results from ground-based studies illuminated the influence of gravity on CVB behavior. Specifically, this comparison focused on the differences in flow field symmetry and the magnitude of heat transfer. 5. Stability Analysis: -Macroscopic Stability: The investigation evaluated the overall stability of the CVB system, considering the occurrence of dryout, oscillations, and cavitation, as a function of heat flux, liquid-to-vapor volume ratio, and working fluid. -Microscopic Stability: A stability analysis was performed, leveraging experimental observations and mathematical modeling, to understand the conditions and mechanisms that lead to instability within the thin liquid film. 6. Post-Flight Analysis: -Reflectivity and Image Data: Detailed analysis of the raw reflectivity and image data was conducted to extract information about the adsorbed film thickness and its influence on CVB behavior.
hypothesis: It is hypothesized that the isothermal equilibrium liquid film shape depends on the gravitational field and the intermolecular force field which changes rapidly in the vicinity of the liquid-vapor and liquid-solid interfaces. This equilibrium shape in a particular gravitational field can be controlled by fixing the container shape, the liquid-substrate system, and the relative volume of the liquid to that of the vapor. It is further hypothesized that the extended Young-Laplace equation can describe this shape over a large range of conditions. Under non-equilibrium conditions resulting from an imposed temperature gradient, fluid flow and change-of-phase heat transfer are a function of further changes in the shape of the liquid volume. It is postulated that these non-equilibrium effects can be analyzed using a Kelvin-Clapeyron transport model that includes the use of the conservation of heat, mass and momentum and the extended Young-Laplace equation.
research_impacts: CVB has performed ground-based studies in a thermal vacuum chamber to determine the efficiency of the heater and cooler configuration. Large thermal response times that have been experimentally observed in space-based experiments cannot be obtained from these ground-based studies. Space-based experimentation is the only method available to ascertain internal low-gravity fluid mechanics within a heat pipe. The project aims to achieve an improved understanding of microscale heat transfer, improved designs for wickless heat pipes, and an increased efficiency in heat transfer devices for cooling critical components. Targeted users are existing microelectronics industry and perhaps military applications. New designs should be able to be developed several months following the analysis and presentation of the results from the experiment.

title: PSI-47 Version 5 Dust and Aerosol Measurement Feasibility Test / Dust and Aerosol Measurement Feasibility Test-2(DAFT / DAFT-2) Investigation
objective: The focus of DAFT / DAFT-2 was to mitigate the risk for the Smoke Aerosol Measurement Experiment (SAME). SAME relied on a commercially available condensate nuclei counter, the TSI P-Trak, to quantify smoke aerosols in a microgravity environment, however there were concerns that th P-Trak would not be reliable in microgravity as it relies on gravity to recycle isopropyl alcohol used in the measurement process. DAFT / DAFT-2 tests that a modified P-Trak particulate counter would be accurate in microgravity. Summarized objectives include: 1) Demonstrate the Functionality of the Modified TSI P-Trak in Microgravity 2) Compare the TSI P-Trak Performance against the DustTrak control 3) Create and Analyze Aerosol Standards in Microgravity 4) Ensure the reliability of future aerosol experiments
approach: The experimental approach consists of the following components: 1) Modification of Instrumentation: TSI P-Trak was modified for use in microgravity by redesigning the condenser tube to use capillary forces for recycling isopropyl alcohol and removing the mercury switch responsible for detecting instrument orientation. 2) Aerosol Generation: Arizona Red Dust (ARD) was chosen as an aerosol standard due to its ease of dispersion. The ARD was aerosolized with GN2 to create particle samples. The aerosol was contained within 15-liter Mylar bags. 3) On-Orbit Testing: The modified P-Trak gathered data from counting aerosol particles and these data were compared to the DustTrak CNC specifically designed to work in microgravity.
hypothesis: The TSI P-Trak operates by condensing isopropanol around aerosol particulates that are subsequently laser counted. It was hypothesized that the P-Trak would not work in microgravity due to two potential failure modes that exist. 1) the system would clog or become obscured by isopropanol, and 2) the internal air-flow dynamics of the optics chamber of the device will cause an over counting of particulates. The TSI P-Trak was modified for microgravity use via using capillary action to recycle the isopropanol. Therefore, there are two basic hypotheses: 1) that the P-Trak, as modified for use in SAME, would function normally in microgravity. 2) that the aerosol created and filtered per the experiment design would be within the measurement capabilities of the test devices.
research_impacts: Extended duration space flight missions with larger vessels will require fire detection systems with increased reliability and sensitivity. This research will impact the development of novel fire and smoke detection systems for the International Space Station and future spacecrafts. Additionally, the successful adaptation of the TSI P-Trak for microgravity can inform the design of instruments for use in other challenging Earth environments, such as submarines or underwater laboratories where accurate detection of smoke can save lives.

title: PSI-48 Version 9 DEvice for the study of Critical LIquids and Crystallization Directional Solidification Insert-Reflight(DECLIC DSI-R) Investigation
objective: The main objective of the DSI-R investigation was to quantitatively establish the fundamental physics controlling the spatiotemporal organization of the secondary sidebranch structure and its interaction with the array structure of primary branches under directional solidification conditions. This investigation particularly focused on the origin of sidebranches that occur when columnar solidification patterns transform from cellular to dendritic as a function of thermal gradient and solidification velocity and study the potential for the formation of an intermediate multiplet pattern. The dynamics and stability of cellular and dendritic growth patterns, and the relationship between the tip geometry and growth pattern were also to be investigated as well. This intent of this investigation was to directly address outstanding issues that remain open in the understanding of complex dendritic microstructures.
approach: The DSI-R investigation utilized a Bridgman type furnace and an experimental cartridge containing the organic transparent alloy of succinonitrile (SCN) - camphor. The nominal concentration was 0.46 wt% camphor. A single crystalline solid seed with a 100 direction parallel to the pulling axial direction is kept unmelted during all experiments. Solidification is performed by pulling the experimental cartridge containing the alloy inside a thermal gradient G at a pulling rate V. The G and V were the primary variable for each experimental run. Images obtained by the direct axial observation, providing top-view interface images, and transverse observations, providing side-view interface images, were analyzed.
hypothesis: Bridgman solidification of transparent binary alloys in a diffusion controlled growth regime can yield benchmark data required for establishing the detailed dynamics of interface pattern selection. The ''SPAtiotemporal evolution of three-dimensional DEndritic array Structures'' (SPADES) investigation conducted during the reflight of the Directional Solidification Insert (DSI-R) campaign targeted the columnar dendritic growth regime to quantitatively establish the fundamental physics controlling the spatiotemporal organization of the secondary sidebranch structure and its interaction with the array structure of primary branches under directional solidification conditions. SPADES focused on the origin of sidebranches that occur when columnar solidification patterns transform from cellular to dendritic as a function of thermal gradient and solidification velocity. The “Effects of Curvature and Unsteady Dynamics on Alloy Solidification Patterns” (CUSP) investigation extended the DSIP and SPADES project into a new direction that addressed the critical effects of the macroscopic curvature of the solidification front and the unsteady dynamics that occurs in response to changes of growth conditions or that is associated with side-branching. A weak macroscopic interface curvature can have a major effect on both the array pattern evolution and grain structure. The convex and concave interfaces lead to a continuous increase and decrease of the average primary spacing, respectively, and it only attains a stationary value for a flat interface.
research_impacts: By providing a reduced gravity environment where fluid convection is suppressed, space enables the direct experimental observation of the solid-liquid interface dynamics during the solidification process under long-duration and purely diffusive conditions. The acquired benchmark data will make it uniquely possible to critically test computational models of alloy microstructures by quantitative comparisons of modeling predictions and experimental observations, thereby contributing to the development of Integrated Computational Materials and Engineering (ICME) tools for both space and earth applications. Those tools are expected to “shorten development time, optimize designs and reduce costs relative to more traditional strategies involving building prototypes, testing and redesigning philosophies. In addition, understanding alloy solidification in the microgravity environment of space is important to improve in-space processing (manufacturing, joining, and welding) of structural materials that will be used for future space exploration.
hardware: DEvice for the study of Critical LIquids and Crystallization (DECLIC) – Directional Solidification Insert (DSI)

title: PSI-49 Version 3 DEvice for the study of Critical LIquids and Crystallization - Alice Like Insert(DECLIC-ALI) Investigation
objective: Primary scientific goals Study phase separation and critical boiling Measure turbidity thermal diffusivity and heat capacity near the critical point SRD
approach: The investigation approach for DECLIC-ALI centers on conducting experiments within the microgravity environment of the ISS, utilizing the DECLIC facility and its specialized Alice-Like Insert (ALI, ALI-R, and ALI-2). The approach involves precise control of the temperature and density of the SF6 sample, including temperature and mechanical quenches, as well as heat pulse techniques. A suite of optical diagnostics (Interferometry, shadowgraphy, light scattering, and direct observation) is used to visualize and quantify the SF6 fluid behavior. Different sample cell configurations, including fixed and variable volume cells, are employed within the ALI insert. Data acquisition is performed at high frequencies, and the data are analyzed quantitatively, with a strong emphasis on comparing experimental results with theoretical predictions. The overall approach is iterative, building upon previous space-based experiments and refining both experimental techniques and theoretical models, all focused on understanding the critical phenomena of SF6.
hypothesis: It is hypothesized that fluctuating hydrodynamics will dominate domain growth at low volume fractions, challenging classical theories. A sharp transition between growth regimes is expected. Mechanical quenches are hypothesized to be a viable method for inducing phase ordering. The vapor recoil force is believed to significantly influence bubble dynamics and wetting near the critical point. Adiabatic volume changes are expected to reveal the dynamics of the Piston Effect. Critical water is hypothesized to follow the same universality class, and external vibration will affect the dynamics.
research_impacts: The DECLIC facility provides power, communications, command, control, data storage, and multiple, flexible optical capabilities in support of each experiment. The knowledge gained will assist in the understanding of the behavior of cryogenic (of or relating to very low temperatures) rocket propellants for the study of dynamics regarding near-ambient temperature critical fluids. DECLIC is designed for telescience from the ground and will offer scientists the capability to remotely control experiment conditions onboard the ISS provided by DECLIC lockers. The use of near-critical fluids allows important parameters (e.g., compressibility of supercritical fluids, density of gas and liquid phases, surface tension) to be easily varied in a scaled way by using small changes in temperature. The readily variable properties of near-critical fluids makes them appealing candidates for studying numerous interesting phenomena valid for all fluids, which will ultimately leads to the development of improved solvents for chemistry and the environment.
hardware: Device for the Study of Critical Liquids and Crystallization (DECLIC)

title: PSI-5 Version 3 Plasma Kristall 4(PK-4) Investigation
objective: PK-4 is not an apparatus dedicated for specific experiments but rather a laboratory which shall offer the possibility to perform a large variety of experiments with complex plasmas and to react to new developments in this field in a manner as flexible as possible. The main interest lies in the investigation of the liquid phase and flow phenomena of complex plasmas for which PK-4 is especially suited thanks to a DC-discharge and its geometry (elongated glass tube with a large observational access). The experiments for PK-4 can be divided into research in three classes of fundamental questions: 1. Microscopic properties of complex plasmas This category comprises the charging of the particles, the external forces on the particles (e.g. ion drag), the fundamental interactions between the particles, agglomeration, and particle growth. 2. Macroscopic properties of complex plasmas In this category belong hydrodynamics (e.g. viscosity), thermodynamics (e.g. equation of state), and non-equilibriums aspects (e.g. lane formation, self-organisation) of complex plasmas. 3. Generic properties of classical many-body systems Complex plasmas are ideal model systems for studying various problems of strongly coupled many-body systems in solid state physics, fluid physics, plasma physics, nano-technology and even nuclear physics because complex plasmas can easily be produced and observed in real time on the microscopic and kinetic level. Hence dynamical processes can be investigated on the level of single particles which is not possible in most systems. Therefore new insights in the dynamics of those processes can be provided. Typical examples are crystallization and melting, phonons in plasma crystals, dust waves, Mach cones, nozzles, turbulence, and nano-fluidics.
approach: The basic experimental protocol starts with an evacuation of the plasma chamber for several hours (a minimum of 20 hours; base pressure: less than 10-3 Pa) to guarantee good plasma conditions, e.g. no striations. Then neon or argon gas is filled in with a gas flow of typically 2 sccm reaching pressures between 5 and 250 Pa. Afterwards the plasma is ignited by the high-voltage (about 1000 V) of the DC electrodes corresponding to a DC current of the order of 1 mA and a longitudinal electric field of about 2 V/cm. Then the micro-particles are injected. They get quickly charged in the plasma and drift from the cathode to the anode with a typical velocity between 1 and 10 cm/s. In addition, the electric fields from the two RF coils/electrodes or the fast polarity switching can be used to manipulate the particles, e.g. to capture and confine them. Gas flow, modulation of the DC and RF fields, the powerful manipulation laser, the thermal manipulator, and the EM electrode can also be used to manipulate the particles, e.g. to accelerate them or to introduce oscillations. A sketch of the PK-4 experiment is shown in Figure 1. The micro-particles are made visible by illumination with a laser beam, which is widened into a sheet by a cylindrical lens. The scattered light is recorded by one or two CCD cameras (e.g. up to 200 frames per second, with a maximum resolution of about e.g.10 microns/pixel). The light emission (“plasma glow”) from the plasma will be measured using the narrow band IF-filters. The basic measurements comprise the positions of the particles, their velocities (extracted from the track length of the particles or from their positions in consecutive images), and correlations between the particles. These quantities are determined from the images by using a dedicated IDL program or other methods for image analysis. At the end of each experiment run the particles will be removed by gas flow before the plasma is switched off in order to avoid the contamination of the glass walls
research_impacts: PK-4 enables fundamental investigation of flows and related instabilities, by mimicking molecular mechanisms at a scale which allows for real time in-situ optical observations. This requires on-orbit experiments to be undertaken in order to observe the processes at work, which are obviously disturbed by the influence of gravity on Earth. Even though PK-4 is principally a fundamental experiment, understanding the processes at work and understanding how complex plasmas can be influenced by varying research parameters gives a better understanding of how improvements can be made in areas and industries where plasmas are used. Understanding how dusty plasmas behave in microgravity could shed light on plasma phenomena in space, which could lead to new research methods or improved spacecraft designs.

title: PSI-50 Version 2 Development and Verification of a 3D Nucleate Pool Boiling Simulation Model Using PSI Data Investigation
objective: The primary objective of this investigation was to develop and validate a numerical model for further investigation of nucleate pool boiling problems under microgravity conditions.
approach: The moment-of-fluid (MOF) procedure is employed to reconstruct the interfaces of any number of material interfaces in a computational cell. The salient features of the overall approach includes: (i) Multi-material interfaces are represented by the piecewise linear moment-of-fluid (MOF) reconstruction, (ii) the time derivative part of the heat equation is discretized using the backward Euler method which is a discrete maximum principle preserving time discretization scheme, (iii) the spatial derivatives part of the heat equation is discretized using the finite volume method, (iv) the temperature field is discretized on a multi-material “supermesh” in which there is just one temperature variable per material per cell, (v) the discrete location for a given variable is at the materials' centroid, (vi) “connected centroid” method is used in order to approximate fluxes, (vii) at Dirichlet or Neumann embedded interfaces, a linear exact correction term is prescribed so that the method approximates the temperature gradient with second order accuracy.
hypothesis: It is hypothesized that the developed model will have the following advantages which can lead to a more accurate prediction: (1) the method can better resolve thermal boundary layers (away from triple points) using adaptive mesh refinement, (2) a novel Moment of Fluid multiphase flow algorithm will straightforwardly prescribe a microlayer model in 3D general geometries, (3) the moment of fluid interface capturing algorithm will enable better handling of 3D problems such as bubble merging, (4) the modeling method can better conserve the boiling mass flow rate by directly exploiting the moment-of-fluid (sharp) interface reconstruction for approximating the interface heat flux in the vicinity of multiple (greater than 2) materials.
research_impacts: The verified model can be used to further study scenarios not investigated on ISS such as vapor bubble departure and collapse. It can also be used to identify optimal heated surface configuration for better heat transfer characteristics. In addition, the model can be used to study other problems under microgravity such as packed bed reactors. The development of nucleate pool boiling simulation tool in microgravity based on the Navier-Stokes equations from this proposed work can be used to study other boiling problems in Earth gravity such as engine cooling and cooling in electronic devices.

title: PSI-51 Version 5 Electromagnetic Levitation Flight Support for Transient Observation of Nucleation Events(EML B1-ELFSTONE) Investigation
objective: The objective of this project is to understand phase selection in structural alloys and to investigate the effects of convection on time-dependent nucleation phenomena during rapid solidification from the melt. The ELFSTONE investigation involves a collaboration with the European Space Agency's (ESA) Thermolab Experiment which focuses on thermophysical properties data measurement of industrial alloys in the liquid phase as a function of temperature. The property values obtained are used to increase the accuracy of numerical modeling of casting and solidification processes of metal alloys. For access to data relating to the Thermolab Experiment, please consult ESA's HRE Data Archive (hreda.esac.esa.int)
approach: The samples are processed in the Electromagnetic Levitator (ISS-EML), a facility that has been operational since 2015 and is located in the Columbus module. The investigation is part of Sample Batch 1 - the first of six proposed 18-sample multi-user cartridges uploaded to the ISS. For the ELFSTONE Sample #09, a ternary FeCrNi analog steel sample, a process cycle is defined as (1) the melting of the sample, (2) the gathering of science data, and (3) the subsequent undercooling and rapid solidification of the sample. The next cycle starts with the re-melting of the sample. In any particular cycle, stirring may be induced at different levels to study the effect of convection on rapid solidification behavior. After all cycles are complete, final microstructure is preserved for return to earth.
hypothesis: The experimental hypothesis was that melt convection would significantly decrease the nucleation kinetics for transformation of metastable ferrite to stable austenite in ferrous structural steel alloys. The was successfully observed.
research_impacts: The value of this research is that the results have application to the design of industrial welding, spray forming, and casting operations for a commercially important class of structural materials. In addition, this research addresses fundamental issues relating to rapid solidification behavior, metastable phase selection, and analysis of the processes governing microstructural evolution. Experiments focus on the use of convection as a processing control parameter.

title: PSI-52 Version 3 Advanced Colloids Experiment - Temperature Control and Gradient Sample 11(ACE-T11) Investigation
objective: ACE-T11 studies the design and assembly of complex 3D structures from small particles suspended within a fluid medium with control of particle density, phase and behavior. Objectives included study of nucleation and growth of crystals within colloidal samples by varying the size and concentration of colloids and depletant, exploring the effect of temperature gradients, and demonstrating control of particle shape and density which is essential for creating high performance materials for 3D printing and advanced optical materials. The research goal is to produce various colloidal structures and study the dynamics of crystal nucleation and growth. The imaging goal is to observe crystallites and resolve particle centroid positions with less than 20% error.
approach: The ACE-T11 investigation used 2 Sample Modules (SM), each containing 3 capillary cells for a total of 6 samples. Confocal microscopy was employed for 3D imaging of non-spherical colloids, with phases controlled by adding depletants, adjusting spatial temperature changes, and applying temperature gradients. The size and concentration of both the particles and depletants were varied across different samples. After homogenization using a magnetic stirrer, the particles were left undisturbed to crystallize. Preliminary observations were made with a 2.5X objective, followed by detailed imaging using 10X, 63X, and 100X objectives.
hypothesis: Under microgravity conditions, colloidal particles would exhibit unique crystallization and self-assembly behaviors that differ from those observed under Earth's gravity. Researchers believed that without the effects of sedimentation, they would better understand the fundamental mechanisms governing colloidal phase transitions and self-organization​. This hypothesis also included the idea that controlling external factors like temperature and depletant concentration would enable precise manipulation of colloidal structures, allowing for the creation of more complex and functional materials.
research_impacts: Future space missions will require self-assembly and self-replication technologies for self-repairing materials and devices, essential for long-duration travel. 3D printing and additive manufacturing are crucial for creating replacement parts, with research focusing on developing particle slurries and pastes suited for both micro and regular gravity environments. This research advances soft matter science, with applications in medicine, electronics, and photonics. Self-assembly techniques will enable new devices for energy and communication, while 3D printing and additive manufacturing rely on optimizing high-density slurries and pastes with diverse mechanical properties.
hardware: ACE-T and Sample Module Light Microscopy Module (LMM) Fluids Integrated Rack (FIR)

title: PSI-57 Version 3 Capillary Channel Flow - Critical Velocities Experiment Unit 1(CCF-CV EU1) Investigation
objective: The investigation aims to characterize and quantify critical flow dynamics in open capillary channels of parallel plate and groove geometries. A primary objective is determining the critical flow rates at which free surface destabilization (''choking'') and gas ingestion occur, emphasizing the capillary-inertial regime. The investigation will examine the relationship between critical flow rate and channel length for complete and half-channel configurations. Controlled, low-frequency flow oscillations will be introduced to probe instability onset sensitivity across geometries and lengths. High-fidelity data on free surface shapes and critical velocities will be acquired to validate theoretical models and assess underlying assumptions, refining predictive capabilities for capillary flows relevant to spacecraft fluid management.
approach: The CCF experiment was operated on the ISS in the MSG. The CCF hardware consists of two experiment units, experiment unit number #1 for the parallel plate and groove geometry, and experiment unit number #2 for the wedge geometry. Initally, one experiment campaign for each experiment unit was planned. Due to the great success of the first two runs, two more additional runs were performed. The challenge for these runs was the commissioning of the fluid loop. The original design of the hardware did not foresee a commissioning from an undefined state, as it was the case after the first operation of each module. The fluid management technology builtinto the CCF hardware - however - was able to recover from an undefined fluid distribution state and allowed additional runs.
hypothesis: The primary hypothesis guiding CCF-CV EU1 is that a limiting flow rate, or 'choking' phenomenon, exists in open capillary channels with parallel plate and groove geometries. A relationship between the fluid velocity, the channel geometry, and the fluid properties governs this limit. Furthermore, it is hypothesized that the introduction of wave oscillations within the flow will impact the critical flow rate, with the amplitude and frequency of these oscillations playing a significant role in the flow behavior and the onset of choking.
research_impacts:
The knowledge of liquid management in space is important for any device which contain liquid and gas, and have one or many free liquid surfaces. The requirements for the device which experiences different acceleration levels down to fully compensated gravity conditions (weightlessness) during its operation may include the phase separation of liquid from gas, gas from liquid, and the transport of liquid through liquid acquisition devices. The results from the CCF experiments may help to design subsystems of future spacecrafts, such as the propulsion subsystem, the thermal control subsystem and the life support subsystem for crewed exploration. The data can be used to build mathematical models which can be applied to real fluids and real dimensions. The data can be used as well to validate computational fluid dynamics software packages which are state-of-the-art tools the design of spacecrafts.
Capillary forces on Earth are masked by gravity, but may become dominant in small scales. This can be encountered when a wetting liquid wicks into a porous structure. It may be a wanted - as in the case of cleaning - or an unwanted - as in buildings - effect. In a wider sense the CCF experiments contribute to this topic. The main difference is that the flow was not driven by the capillary forces. Instead, the capillary forces were used to stabilize the flow path. A variety of applications on Earth may have this requirement as well.

title: PSI-58 Version 3 Capillary Channel Flow - Critical Velocities Experiment Unit 2(CCF-CV EU2) Investigation
objective: The investigation aims to determine critical flow rates (choking) for wedge channels across various lengths and wedge angles. It explores choking behavior across capillary-inertial, visco-capillary, and overlap flow regimes. Bubble transport, migration, and phase separation within wedge geometries will also be investigated, focusing on the influence of flow rate, channel length, and bubble diameter.
approach: The CCF experiment was operated on the ISS in the MSG. The CCF hardware consists of two experiment units, experiment unit number #1 for the parallel plate and groove geometry, and experiment unit number #2 for the wedge geometry. Initially, one experiment campaign for each experiment unit was planned. Due to the great success of the first two runs, two more additional runs were performed. The challenge for these runs was the commissioning of the fluid loop. The original design of the hardware did not foresee a commissioning from an undefined state, as it was the case after the first operation of each module. The fluid management technology built into the CCF hardware - however - was able to recover from an undefined fluid distribution state and allowed additional runs.
hypothesis: The central hypothesis for CCF-CV EU2 is that a critical flow rate limit also exists in open capillary channels with wedge and gapped-wedge geometries, and it is governed by the interplay of capillary, viscous, and inertial forces. It is expected that the critical flow rate will be a function of the channel geometry, which includes the wedge angle and channel length, and that there will be different flow regimes which are linked to the governing flow forces. Furthermore, it is hypothesized that the nature of bubble transport, migration, and phase separation will depend on the flow conditions, such as flow rate and channel length, as well as bubble properties, such as the size and frequency.
