A variety of applications on Earth may have this requirement as well.

title: PSI-59 Version 3 Capillary Channel Flow - Phase Separation Experiment Unit 2(CCF-PS EU2) Investigation
objective: The objectives are to quantify phase separation efficiency in wedge channels as a function of flow parameters, bubble characteristics, and channel geometry; determine the influence of bubble size and injection frequency on separation efficiency; and optimize wedge geometry for passive phase separation.
approach: Building upon the CF-CV EU2 approach, the phase separation investigation utilizes a controlled bubble injection system to introduce bubbles of varying sizes and frequencies upstream of the wedge channel. The microgravity environment of the ISS ensures capillary-dominated flow conditions. Systematic variation of bubble injection parameters (size, frequency, location), flow rate, and channel geometry (wedge angle, length) enables comprehensive mapping of phase separation efficiency. High-speed imaging (HSHRC) coupled with wider-view video (MSGC) allows for detailed observation and quantification of bubble migration and coalescence. Image analysis techniques are employed to track bubble trajectories, quantify bubble size distributions before and after the wedge channel, and determine the overall degree of gas-liquid separation. This quantitative data is then correlated with the varied parameters to assess the effectiveness of the wedge geometry for passive phase separation and to optimize design parameters for enhanced performance.
hypothesis: The hypothesis underlying CCF-PS EU2 is that specific wedge and gapped-wedge channel designs can passively separate liquid and gas phases due to the complex interplay of capillary and inertial forces. Furthermore, it is hypothesized that by carefully adjusting flow conditions, such as flow rate and channel length as well as bubble properties, such as bubble size and frequency, it is possible to identify geometries and regimes suitable for gas-liquid separation, which can be used for spacecraft tank design and liquid supply.
research_impacts: Current spacecraft fuel tanks rely on an additional reservoir to prevent gases from entering the engines during firing. Capillary systems larger than a few millimeters in length are impossible to study on the ground, but the weightlessness on the International Space Station makes research on a variety of capillary channel sizes possible. The results are useful for the design and testing of liquid management systems in current use and for future missions. Rocket fuel tank designs and construction models from space research help to advance new technology and manufacturing capabilities on Earth.

title: PSI-6 Version 3 Foam Optics and Mechanics(FOAM) Investigation
objective: The objective is to take advantage of microgravity to eliminate drainage and to use imaging and multiple light scattering diagnostics in order to non-invasively measure and elucidate the time evolution of key features of the bubble-packing structure of wet foams – namely, the bubble size distribution and bubble rearrangement dynamics – and how they are affected by degree of wetness by systematically increasing the liquid content for sequences of otherwise identical foams. FOAM is divided into two experiments: FOAM Coarsening and FOAM Stability.
approach: Experiment Cells The FOAM-C experimental set-up comprises five segments with a total of 20 small test cells containing a variety of liquid mixtures. The Fluid Science Laboratory on the ISS Columbus module will automatically shake and analyze these mixtures using complex laser optics, highly sensitive photodiodes and high-resolution cameras that can take up to 10,000 images per second. Each test cell weighs only 20 grams and contains less than 2 cm³ of the liquid mixture, while each segment comprises four test cells and weighs a total of 320 grams. Diagnostics - Overview video, - Multiple light scattering spectroscopies (SVS - Speckle Variance Spectroscopy and/or DWS - Diffusing-Wave Spectroscopy) Example of Protocols - First, the foam is made at the time T0. Then the foam is left to age while optical diagnostics measure its dynamics during aging (up to 24 hours foam age). These cycles can be repeated several times. Another cell with a different composition (liquid fraction, concentration) is then subject of a new series of experiments. - Granular matter samples of defined volume concentration shall be agitated until a steady state is reached. Consequently, optical diagnostics measure the grains dynamics in the steady state and after turning the agitation off. Experiment Protocol For each foam sample, there are different sets of measurements that are to be repeated in sequence, for the total run duration. The maximum experiment duration shall be assumed with 24h per experiment run for each sample. At the beginning of a science campaign on orbit replaceable units shall be exchanged (if necessary) and the EC is installed in FSL by the Crew. Each run starts with the foaming process. Data acquisition shall start just at the end of the foaming process. After a run, either the same sample can be processed again, or another sample can be processed. After a run, data post processing and downlink of results can occur. The results can influence the experiment procedure of subsequent runs, and the possibility to change experiment parameters through telecommand shall be provided. At the end of a science campaign selected scientific data is downlinked and then the EC is uninstalled by the Crew. Runs Repetition Each sample shall be tested 3 times (one just needs to “re-foam” the sample after its first period of coarsening). Experiment Duration and amount of Data The measurements (alternatively SVS, DWS, DTS, Camera) shall be performed during the whole run duration. In the following the measurement time is a requirement. On the opposite, the resulting amount of data is based on the required scientific measurements and the specific data production of the instrument, it is an indication but not a requirement.
research_impacts: This experiment might provide useful insights for the manufacture, use and ageing behavior of foams, which are utilized in a wide range of areas, including in cosmetics and personal-hygiene products, in the food industry, in cleaning products, sealing products and for firefighting.

title: PSI-60 Version 1 Computational and Experimental Analysis of SPICE Data Sets Investigation
objective: This ground investigation sought to increase understanding of the issues that control the large discrepancy between soot formation in 1g and in 0g flames. The objective of this investigation was to integrate computational and experimental methods to derive temperature distributions and soot volume fractions from the Smoke Point in Coflow Experiment (SPICE) data available in PSI. By analyzing over 1600 raw DSLR images and incorporating advanced soot models, the study sought to improve understanding of soot formation, oxidation, radiative re-absorption, and aggregate growth in heavily sooting flames. The work further aimed to reconcile microgravity and normal gravity flame behavior, identify key physical and chemical processes influencing smoke point development, and provide a framework for evaluating model parameter sensitivity.
approach: The approach was to combine image processing, experimental diagnostics, and detailed soot modeling. Raw Nikon NEF images were decoded into three color channels and analyzed using color-ratio pyrometry to extract soot temperature fields. Absolute light calibration from SPICE was then used to calculate soot volume fractions. For computational modeling, a coupled flow–species–soot system was implemented, modified to include radiation re-absorption and discrete-sectional aggregate formation. Simulations were performed for both Yale and ACME burner configurations under normal and microgravity conditions. Comparisons between experimental data and computed results guided sensitivity analyses of soot evolution parameters, including the effects of radiation, scattering, boundary conditions, and heat transfer to the burner structure.
hypothesis: Microgravity conditions would produce longer, more diffuse flames with lower temperatures and increased soot concentrations compared to normal gravity, and that careful integration of experimental temperature fields into the simulations would reduce discrepancies between measured and predicted soot distributions.
research_impacts: This study sought to enhance understanding of soot formation, flame structure, and radiative transport under microgravity and normal gravity, improving predictive models for combustion in both spacecraft and terrestrial systems. For space applications, the results support safer fire detection, suppression, and cleaner combustion technologies critical for long-duration missions. On Earth, the insights help reduce pollutant emissions, optimize combustion efficiency, and inform the design of cleaner energy and industrial systems.

title: PSI-62 Version 1 Concurrent Flame Spread Modeling using Flamelet Generated Manifolds in Microgravity with Comparison to BASS Experiments using Two-Color Tomography Investigation
objective: The objective of this research was to develop and validate new flamelet generated manifold (FGM) modeling techniques for concurrent flame spread in microgravity. Concurrent flame spread presented one of the greatest modeling challenges in combustion science due to the intricate coupling between heat transfer, mass transport, and chemical kinetics near the solid-vapor interface. Traditional modeling strategies often relied on hybridized turbulence and chemistry models that were not fully consistent and failed to capture important intermediate reaction pathways. To overcome these shortcomings, this PSI grant advanced the use of an unsteady flamelet generated manifold (UFGM) framework that reduced the complexity of reacting systems by mapping them into lower-dimensional manifolds. The research aimed to leverage this methodology to simulate solid fuel combustion processes with high fidelity, using the NASA Burning and Suppression of Solids (BASS and BASS-II) experiments as benchmarks. Ultimately, the long-term goal was to enable accurate prediction of flammability limits for spacecraft materials and to provide a tool that could also serve as a subgrid-scale model in large-eddy simulations of fires, supporting spacecraft safety and hazard mitigation.
approach: The approach combined high-resolution computational modeling with experimental validation to study concurrent flame spread in microgravity. A previously developed computational framework was employed to run fully coupled simulations of fluid–solid responses, focusing on materials subject to charring and ablation. Within this framework, the unsteady FGM method was implemented and tested on various BASS geometries, including flat sheets, spheres, and rod-shaped polymethyl methacrylate (PMMA) samples, as well as wax cylinders. Experimental imagery found in PSI from the BASS and BASS-II investigations was post-processed using newly developed two-color tomography methods with DSLR cameras, enabling 3D reconstructions of soot and temperature fields for direct comparison to model predictions. The evaluation metrics included flame geometry, temperature distribution, soot volume fraction, and flame spread rate, with special emphasis on reproducing the “Goldilocks” flammability zone reported by Olson and Ferkul. Comparative analyses were also carried out with a parallel NSF-supported terrestrial flame spread project, ensuring that the predictive capabilities of the UFGM approach were assessed across both microgravity and normal-gravity conditions.
hypothesis: The unsteady flamelet generated manifold (UFGM) approach was believed to be able to accurately reproduce concurrent flame spread in microgravity, including phenomena such as the “Goldilocks” flammability zone, by coupling near-wall thermal, mass transport, and chemical processes with far-field flow dynamics.
research_impacts: This research provides predictive tools for screening new materials’ flammability limits, which can lead to the design of safer spacecrafts. The development of Large Eddy Simulation subgrid models is expected to improve hazard assessment capabilities critical for managing fire risks during long-duration space missions and within confined spacecraft habitats. On Earth, these advancements could improve combustion modeling by deepening our understanding of coupled thermal, chemical, and flow processes, which betters fire safety standards. The computational methods being refined have the potential to enable more effective fire prevention and mitigation strategies and foster innovations in diagnostics and simulations applicable across a variety of combustion scenarios. Overall, this research can contribute significantly to safer human exploration in space and improvements to fire safety protocols on Earth.

title: PSI-64 Version 3 DEvice for the study of Critical LIquids and Crystallization - Directional Solidification Insert(DECLIC DSI) Investigation
objective: The objective of this investigation was to obtain benchmark data on cellular and dendritic growth under diffusive growth conditions. Precise measurements of interface shape, cell/dendrite tip radius, tip composition and tip temperature will be carried out as a function of composition, growth rate and thermal gradient values. By systematically varying the process parameters in the absence of gravity-induced convection, the range of interface morphologies will be obtained, yielding insight into the underlying principles that govern dynamical pattern selection. Directional solidification experiments conducted in microgravity using transparent organic analogues will provide real time benchmark data to quantitatively determine conditions for the planar to cellular and cell to dendrite transitions and validate a predictive phase field 3D being developed as part of the investigation.
approach: Experiments were performed within the Directional Solidification Insert (DSI) of the Device for the study of Critical LIquids and Crystallization (DECLIC) aboard the International Space Station. Homogeneous 3D cylindrical samples in a classical Bridgman setup was processed with various pulling velocities V and temperature gradients G. The transparent succinonitrile (SCN)-0.24wt% camphor alloy was the sample material and it permitted in situ optical imaging of the solid/liquid interface. Experiments were typically initiated from a single crystal growing along the temperature gradient direction. The alloy solidified within a cylindrical crucible with an inner diameter of 10mm. The solid/liquid interface was located within a stable and well-controlled temperature gradient. The crucible was pulled through an axial adiabatic zone, allowing the interface to grow up to 100 mm in length at a controlled velocity. While independently controlling V and G experienced by the interface, in situ evolution of the solid/liquid interface morphology was imaged and analyzed. 3D phase-field simulations were specifically developed to identify ranges of primary spacings for the formation of the classically observed “fingers” (deep cells) with blunt tips and “needles” with parabolic tips.
hypothesis: When a planar solid-liquid becomes unstable, under certain growth conditions, complex interactions among perturbed regions can lead to different amplification rates of different wavelengths that determines the final selection of the reorganized pattern. This complex dynamical process selects a small range of wavelengths, from an unstable spectrum of wavelengths, to form a periodic array of cells.
research_impacts: From the technological viewpoint, the importance of cellular and dendritic microstructures is quite clear since these structures are exhibited in all important commercial solidification techniques. The proposed project will for the first time provide benchmark data for the dynamical evolution of three-dimensional cellular and dendritic patterns that will enable precise modeling of complex commercial processing technologies to give reliable products. The development of a reliable model will allow industries to design new materials and processing conditions that will have a significant impact on the economy in the US, since casting and welding industries are several billion dollars industries. In addition, the fundamental knowledge of pattern formation will allow the development of nano-scale patterns in polymers and electronic materials that will have significant impact on the development of high technology and advanced materials.
hardware: Device for the study of Crtical Liquids and Crystallization (DECLIC)

title: PSI-66 Version 1 Dynamic Response of Particle-Filled Polymeric Fluids in Flows with Complex Lagrangian Time Histories Investigation
objective: The primary objective of this ground investigation is to exploit the unique flight data from the Shear History Extensional Rheology (SHERE, SHERE-II, SHERE-R) investigations to better understand the dynamic rheology of particle-filled polymeric fluids in complex flows. These fluids, encountered in manufacturing processes such as fiber spinning, hydraulic fracturing, and roll-to-roll film production, experience alternating regimes of shear and extension in a Lagrangian frame. By using SHERE’s microgravity dataset, the study seeks to isolate the interplay between polymer stresses, particle orientation, and flow disturbances—effects that cannot be cleanly separated in Earth’s gravity. The overarching goal is to develop quantitative predictions and mechanistic insights into how particles alter extensional flow responses, strain hardening, and energy dissipation in viscoelastic suspensions.
approach: The investigation combines numerical simulations, theoretical modeling, and SHERE flight data validation. The SHERE experiments measured transient extensional responses of dilute particle suspensions in Boger fluids at moderate extension rates—regimes inaccessible on Earth due to sedimentation and buoyancy. To interpret these data, the project applies finite-difference methods in spheroidal coordinates to resolve inertia-less viscoelastic flows around suspended particles, capturing strong local stress gradients near particle surfaces. Semi-analytical theories are also employed to predict rheology in the limit of small polymer concentrations, allowing parameter sweeps that are computationally prohibitive in full simulations. Three flow classes are studied: (1) sphere suspensions in transient extension with/without pre-shear to directly compare with SHERE data; (2) spheroidal particle suspensions transitioning between shear and extension to mimic fiber-film processing; and (3) alternating shear/extension flows modeling turbulent drag reduction. Together, this multi-method approach bridges PSI experimental data with first-principles rheological predictions.
hypothesis: The central hypothesis is that particle-polymer interactions fundamentally alter the transient extensional rheology of polymer solutions in ways that cannot be predicted by simple additive models of particle and polymer stresses. Specifically, the particle-induced velocity disturbances are expected to modify local polymer stress distributions, suppress strain hardening at large deformations, and alter stress development depending on flow history (e.g., pre-shear orientation effects). Furthermore, anisotropic particles such as spheroids will introduce orientation-dependent rheological signatures, leading to different stress responses under alternating shear and extension. By validating these predictions with SHERE microgravity data, the study tests whether advanced numerical and theoretical models can accurately capture the coupled dynamics of particles and polymers across relevant industrial flow regimes.
research_impacts: In-Space Benefits: For space exploration and on-orbit manufacturing, understanding the rheology of particle-laden polymeric fluids is crucial for the design of efficient life-support systems, in-space fabrication, and thermal management technologies. Microgravity eliminates sedimentation, enabling stable suspensions and novel material processing methods, such as fiber spinning and advanced coatings. Insights from SHERE-based models improve predictability of fluid performance in spacecraft systems where multiphase, particle-laden fluids may be used. Earth Benefits: On Earth, particle-polymer suspensions underpin industries such as hydraulic fracturing, fiber spinning, extrusion molding, roll-to-roll manufacturing, and enhanced oil recovery. Adding particles imparts tailored mechanical or conductive properties but also increases energy demands due to altered rheology. This project provides mechanistic predictions for how particle orientation and polymer stress coupling influence flow resistance, helping optimize industrial processes, reduce energy consumption, and enable development of high-performance materials. By combining SHERE microgravity data with advanced modeling, this work addresses gaps in extensional rheology knowledge that hinder efficient design of complex fluid processing systems.

title: PSI-67 Version 5 Enhancement and Verification of Quantitative Phase-Field Crystal Modeling using NASA-PSI Coarsening in Solid- Liquid Mixtures Experiments Data Investigation
objective: The key objectives of this investigation were to develop 1) a binary Molecular Dynamics (MD) interatomic potential for Pb-Sn system, 2) Phase Field Crystal (PFC) models for coarsening of solid-liquid mixtures; 3) a highly-parallel semi-implicit spectral and operator splitting numerical algorithm to use on high performance computing facilities that will enable the necessary large-scale PFC simulations (comparable to CSLM data length-scale); (4) Data mining of NASA-PSI Coarsening in Solid-Liquid Mixtures (CSLM), CSLM-2, CSLM-2R, and CSLM-3 experiments and using them in series of simulations in the developed computational tool for enhancement and verification of the proposed modeling framework.
approach: The proposed multi-scale modeling framework is established around two atomistic computational material model of phase-field crystals (PFC) and molecular dynamics (MD). PFC is a unique computational model at diffusive time scale with the capability of simulating solid-liquid processes with atomistic resolutions while MD acts on the time scale of atomistic vibrations. A novel approach of modified-embedded-atom (MEAM) interatomic potential was adopted to obtain reliable interatomic potentials for Pb-Sn binary systems near or at the melting point (MP). The potentials were used to calculate relevant properties such as latent heat, expansion in melting, liquid structure factor, solid-liquid interface stiffness, solidus and liquidus lines, and solid-liquid interfacial free energy. The kinetics of coarsening in solid-liquid mixtures (Ostwald ripening of solid domains in the liquid phase) was simulated using a one mode phase field crystal (1PFC) model. The simulation results were compared to experimental data previously obtained in a microgravity environment. Simulations were carried out as a function of the difference in chemical potential between Pb and Sn. Please the data layout document (DLD) describing the data organization in folders for each delta chemical potential and underlying files as per temperature of simulation and each time step.
hypothesis: Modified-embedded-atom (MEAM) interatomic potential and a one mode phase field crystal (1PFC) model can be utilized to simulate the kinetics of coarsening of solid phases in solid-liquid mixtures.
research_impacts: The proposed computational tool verified/quantified based on CSLM data will establish a virtual laboratory that can be used to study coarsening as well as other material processing phenomena on Earth involving with solid-liquid coexistence; e.g., rapid solidification and grain growth. Since computational models are highly repeatable at lower cost, the proposed modeling framework will result in accelerated material process development and certification. Solid-liquid coexistence is the initial step in many manufacturing technologies such as casting, liquid infiltration, and additive manufacturing. Hence, this modeling framework can be used to investigate the relations between these manufacturing processes and the material properties in order to optimize/control the manufacturing processes parameters. In addition, the results of this research will be disseminated to the public in forms of peer-reviewed articles, scientific reports, a project-specific website, and data uploaded to NASA-PSI website.

title: PSI-68 Version 6 Flame Extinguishment Experiment - 2(FLEX-2) Investigation
objective: The primary goal of the FLEX-2 flight experiments is to extend the results of FLEX-1 to fuels and environmental conditions that mimic real combustor conditions, as well as, provide benchmark experimental data on bi-component droplet combustion over a wide range of initial conditions in order to validate numerical simulations and to develop new theoretical models. Detailed experimental objectives can be further itemized as: 1. Investigate the role of liquid-phase mixing on the burning characteristics of bi-component fuel droplets. 2. Examine the steady and unsteady liquid and gas-phase phenomena in pure fuel combustion. 3. Study flame extinction mechanisms and their boundaries. 4. Analyze the soot formation process, including soot volume fraction soot-shell dynamics. 5. Determine the influence of droplet interactions on the flammability limits and extinction behavior of droplet arrays. 6. Validate theoretical models of droplet combustion through comprehensive experimental data collection in microgravity environments.
approach: The chamber was filled with the appropriate atmosphere, which was varied in pressure between 0.5 atm to 3.0 atm and O2 concentration between 0.1 to 0.4 mole fraction with the diluent gas making up the balance. A settling time of approximately 2 minutes elapsed prior to initiating the test in order to ensure that the temperature and pressure of the chamber gases have stabilized. This settling time was followed by the dispensing of a predetermined amount of fuel (based on the target droplet size) onto the support fiber for those tests in which the droplet is not freely deployed. When sufficient fuel has been dispensed the dispensing needles were retracted and a dwell period of at least 10 seconds was allowed for the droplet internal fluid motion induced by deployment to subside. This was then followed by initiating power to the ignitor for a selectable amount of time ranging from 1 second to 5 seconds after which the ignitor was retracted from the field of view. If the flow field is to be generated by translating the droplet then droplet motion would commence at the same time that the ignitor is retracted. A near real-time download of the color camera video was employed in order to verify successful droplet deployment, ignition, and overall progress of the experiment. Pressure and temperature data of the chamber environment was also recorded in near real time. The overall investigation approach can be summarized as: 1. Test parameters are determined, including pressure, temperature, fuel mixture, and humidity. 2. Fill the combustion chamber with the selected gas mixtures. 3. Deploy the droplet(s) carefully controlling the droplet diameter. 4. Allow the droplet to stabilize in the microgravity environment. 5. Ignite the droplet in a uniform and controlled fashion. 6. Monitor combustions and track flame evolution using high speed photography. 7. Monitor and adjust experimental conditions as needed. 8. Analyze data. The independently varied experimental parameters during FLEX-2 experiments were 1) Fuel type 2) Ambient gas composition 3) Ambient Pressure 4) Droplet initial diameter 5) Droplet translation velocity (and acceleration) 6) Droplet spacing and initial size in a binary linear array.
hypothesis: Fairly sophisticated numerical simulations of convective droplet combustion have been developed in the last decade where the key contribution is the inclusion of full Navier-Stokes equations for the gas-phase flow field. However, due to the inherent complexity of the problem, varying degrees of approximations have been made in treating the chemistry, radiation, and the coupling between the gas and liquid phases. The validity of the assumptions or the hypothesis used in these simulation have not been confirmed by using benchmark data. By conducting these experiments in a microgravity environment, the effects of buoyancy are minimized, and the droplet can be characterized only as a function of thermocapillary or solutalcapillary stresses allowing for a clear observation of the fundamental combustion processes, The present FLEX-2 experiments using bi-component mixtures. In addition, the microgravity environment allows study of such phenomena as the transitions between radiative and diffusive extension of the flame. The primary goal of the flight experiments is to provide benchmark experimental data on bi-component droplet combustion over a wide range of initial conditions that could be used to validate numerical simulations and to develop new theoretical models.
research_impacts: The combustion of liquid fuels is the overwhelming energy source in the transportation sector. Insights gained from these studies can lead to more efficient and cleaner combustion technologies which are crucial for reducing pollution and greenhouse gas emissions. By improving fuel efficiency and developing better fuels, these experiments can contribute to: 1) More sustainable energy production. 2) Future combustor designs with minimal carbon footprint, maximum fuel efficiency and less pollutant emissions. 3) Allow quantitative evaluation of the performance of future fuels in combustors through the development of surrogates (mixtures of pure fuels that simulate the behavior of real fuels). 4) Validation of jet engine models by engine manufacturers with support from prior droplet results.
hardware: Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR) Multi-user Droplet Combustion Appartatus (MDCA)

title: PSI-69 Version 5 Flame Extinguishment Experiment(FLEX) Investigation
objective: The FLEX (Flame Extinguishment Experiment) investigation aims to map the flammability limits of liquid fuels in microgravity environments, measure the effectiveness of various gaseous fire suppressants such as CO2, He, and SF6, and develop reliable predictive models for combustion limits under reduced gravity conditions. The mission seeks to validate and improve simplified models by incorporating detailed chemical reactions, heat transfer, and material movement, using both space-based data and extensive ground-based tests. Key flight experiment goals include obtaining high-resolution measurements of droplet burning rates, flame extinction behavior, heat radiation, soot levels, and temperature profiles, while systematically analyzing the effects of different ambient conditions and suppressant concentrations. These investigations are essential for advancing the fundamental understanding of combustion processes in microgravity and enhancing fire safety protocols for future space missions.
approach: The FLEX experiments involve igniting and observing the burning behavior of relatively large droplets. A primary objective of the experiments is to determine the Limiting Oxygen Index (LOI) as a function of ambient pressure and determine how the presence of a suppressant influences the LOI . The basic outline of the procedure to construct this diagram is as follows: 1. Select the test pressure (0.5 − 1.5 atm) for the LOI tests. 2. Select a smaller droplet size (≈ 3 mm) 3. Select an ambient oxygen mole fraction that, based on ground-based testing, will support droplets burning to completion (as opposed to extinguishing at a finite droplet size). 4. Perform a droplet combustion test. 5. Increase the droplet size or repeat the test (if finite extinction diameter at flame extinction observed). 6. Continue steps 4 and 5 until flame exists for only a short time after ignition (radiative extinction). 7. Continue steps 4 thru 6 at a decreased ambient oxygen mole fraction. 8. Continue step 7 to an ambient oxygen mole fraction where the droplet does not ignite. There were ambient conditions where the extinction droplet sizes at all ambient oxygen mole fractions were too small to either be observed or measured with the available diagnostics. In this case, the determination of the LOI is similar, but more iterative. Instead of observing flame extinction, however, the procedure involved an iterative sequence of tests (burn to completion followed by a no ignition test) with progressively smaller increments in ambient oxygen mole fraction to determine the LOI . For the slow flow tests (in the flight experiment), the configuration of the flight hardware did not allow for adequate diagnostics over the entire test for a droplet in a uniform, steady convective flow. In these tests, the procedure will be to duplicate tests above which yield finite-sized extinction droplet diameters. Near the end of the tests, prior to flame extinction, the droplet will be subjected to a small, sub-buoyant, convective flow (imparted by translating the droplet at a slow, uniform speed). The goal of the experiment is then to see how the presence of this flow influences the extinction process. Note, a large number of the tests involve free droplets (as opposed to fiber-supported droplets) and a number of these tests will have droplets with a slow drift velocity. Data gathered from these tests to examine the influences of a small, sub-buoyant flow on both the burning and extinction process.
hypothesis: The primary hypothesis of the FLEX mission is that microgravity conditions fundamentally alter the combustion and extinction characteristics of liquid fuel droplets due to changes in species and energy transport dynamics, radiative heat loss, and chemical kinetics. Specifically, the hypothesis posits that the lack of buoyant convection in microgravity will lead to significant differences in the flammability limits and suppression efficacy of various fire suppressant agents compared to normal gravity conditions. This hypothesis underpins the design of the FLEX experiments, which aim to map flammability boundaries, quantify suppressant efficacy, and develop predictive models to improve fire safety in space environments.
research_impacts: The research impacts and Earth benefits of the FLEX mission are significant and multifaceted. By enhancing our understanding of microgravity combustion, the mission directly contributes to improved fire safety protocols for future space missions, ensuring the safety of crew members in environments where traditional fire suppression methods may be ineffective. On Earth, the insights gained from these experiments have the potential to advance fire safety in confined and reduced-gravity environments, such as submarines or high-altitude aircraft. The mission's findings on the effectiveness of various fire suppressants, including CO2, He, and SF6, in microgravity can lead to the development of more efficient and less harmful fire suppression systems, reducing the risk of toxic byproducts during fire events. Additionally, the study of ''cool flames'' and low-temperature combustion processes observed in microgravity can inform the design of advanced combustion engines, leading to improved fuel efficiency and reduced emissions in automotive and industrial applications. Overall, the FLEX mission's contributions to combustion science have the potential to enhance both space exploration safety and terrestrial fire safety technologies.
hardware: Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR)-Fluids and Combustion Facility (FCF) Multi-user Droplet Combustion Appartatus (MDCA)

title: PSI-7 Version 3 Particle Stabilized Emulsions and Foams(PASTA) Investigation
objective: The work proposed in the PASTA project follows the line from characterizing the surface properties of particles via a complex analysis of the properties of layers at liquid/gas and liquid/liquid interfaces to studying the behaviour of liquid films and finally to model real foams and emulsions. The work comprises the application of available knowledge to the preparation and characterization of particle stabilized emulsions, produced by adapting to the Soft Matter Dynamics instrument. The role of gravity on quiescent wet foams can be captured in 2 key questions: Is the growth law for average bubble size R~√ time, such that R dR/dt is a constant? If so, what is the liquid-fraction dependence of this rate? How do the rate and the nature of the bubble rearrangement dynamics change as the liquid fraction is increased to the point of un-jamming (transition solid-like to liquid-like)? PASTA will address the SPECIFIC OBJECTIVES: Evaluate the characteristic time for the droplet coalescence as a function of the formulation Identify and investigate specific dynamic regimes for droplets dynamics (for example Brownian vs. Capillarydriven) during emulsion destabilization. Test and develop models for emulsion stability/destabilization prognosis.
approach: The PArticle STAbilised emulsions experiment (PASTA) is placed inside the Fluid Science Rack (FSL) in the European Columbus module of the ISS. Each PASTA sample cell is fitted with a piston that allows to agitate the mixture within the cell at various frequencies and durations to emulsify the mixture. The sample cells are grouped 4-by-4 in sample cell units that can be fitted on a carousel inside SMD. This carousel allows for placing each individual sample cell in the diagnostics position of SMD, where it can be observed with the SMD sensors and several diagnostic tools, like the overview camera that takes microscope image sequences in black and white of the sample cell.
research_impacts: Emulsions have large relevance for applications in a wide spectrum of technologies, processes, and products in different fields including oil and gas, specialty materials, pharmaceuticals, cosmetics, and foods. Both stable and unstable emulsions are needs that are shared across a variety of applications. For example, efficient de-emulsifiers are needed to facilitate the process of phase separation (breaking) in the crude oil emulsions extracted from the wells, while high stability oil-in-water emulsions are required in the final stage of production of the same well or to facilitate pumping high-viscosity oils through pipelines. In the food industry, many products based on emulsified fats or oils (condiments, sauces, frozen confections, and others) require long term stability. However, destabilizing emulsions are key to processing raw food materials such as milk and vegetable oils.

title: PSI-70 Version 3 Gradient Driven Fluctuation Experiment(GRADFLEX) Investigation
objective: The primary objectives of the GRADFLEX investigation can be summarized as follows: To investigate non-equilibrium fluctuations in microgravity by studying the behavior of gradient-driven fluctuations in a microgravity environment, where the stabilizing influence of gravity is significantly reduced. To measure the divergence of large-size fluctuations by observing and quantifying this divergence up to the limits imposed by the sample size. To quantify the amplitude and spatial extent of fluctuations by precisely measuring the mean-squared amplitude of the fluctuations as a function of both wave vector (spatial extent) and frequency (temporal dynamics). The investigation aims to rigorously test existing theoretical models of non-equilibrium fluctuations including comparing the measured amplitude and q-dependence of S(q) with predictions, both on Earth and in microgravity. Beyond the static properties (amplitude and spatial extent), the investigation also seeks to characterize the temporal dynamics of the fluctuations.
approach: The GRADFLEX experiment investigated gradient-driven fluctuations in fluids using a dual approach: a 12-day microgravity flight experiment aboard the Foton-M3 satellite and complementary ground-based tests with the same apparatus. Two fluid systems (CS₂ and polystyrene/toluene) were subjected to precisely controlled temperature gradients. Quantitative shadowgraphy, a sensitive optical technique, measured both static (S(q)) and dynamic (S(q,ω)) properties of the fluctuations, with images acquired at specific rates for each. Data analysis involved Fourier transforms and spectral techniques to extract fluctuation amplitudes and dynamics and to address unexpected noise. The core of the study was a rigorous, parameter-free comparison of experimental results with theoretical predictions for both terrestrial and microgravity environments. The approach combined and refined a sophisticated design, enabling robust testing.
hypothesis: In the absence of gravity, thermally-driven fluctuations in a fluid subjected to a temperature gradient will exhibit significantly enhanced amplitude and spatial extent, with their mean-squared amplitude diverging with the size of the fluctuation and exhibiting altered dynamics up to the limits imposed by the sample dimensions.
research_impacts: Throughout the course of this work it has been necessary to constantly improve the experimental method of choice, namely the quantitative shadowgraph. This development has now reached the stage where it is clear that this method, if handled properly, represents a viable method of carrying out both dynamic and static light scattering at scattering angles so small as to defy the imagination of of anyone who has worked in the field. Although it is likely to take some time for the knowledge we have gained to be disseminated, there is no reason this method cannot be added to the scattering arsenal. Furthermore, it can also be applied to X-rays, enabling one to extend the lower limit of X-ray scattering as well. The consequences of putting a new technique into the hands of researchers is difficult to asses in advance. Basically, however, this method will enable quantitative measurements of various systems having size ranges that are too large for existing techniques. Obvious examples are the crystallization process in colloidal systems, gelation processes, and aggregation and flocculation. Because scattering provides excellent statistical averages, the method should prove quite complementary to visualization techniques such as microscopy.

title: PSI-71 Version 5 Isothermal Dendritic Growth Experiment - Second United States Microgravity Payload - 2(IDGE USMP-2) Investigation
objective: The primary objective of the microgravity dendritic growth experiment was to measure definitively the kinetics and morphology of dendritic growth, and to account for the effects of natural convection. The experimental objective was to use a single,clearly defined experimental parameter, namely, the supercooling, to fully determine the resulting steady-state dendritic growth velocity, V, and tip radius R. Designated the IDGE, the first flight, manifested on the second United States Microgravity Payload (USMP-2) mission, was launched and operated on the STS-62 on March 4-18, 1994. This IDGE investigation met the objective of acquiring accurate dendritic growth speed and morphology data under diffusion-controlled conditions, while greatly reducing buoyancy-induced convective heat transport through the reduction of gravity. The microgravity environment broadened this range of supercooling and permitted for the first time a critical assessment of both the heat transport theory and the interfacial kinetics behavior.
approach: The approach was to observe and image dendritic growth as a function of undercooling such that dendritic tip velocities and radii could both be accurately measured and used as a critical test of theory. Succinonitrile (SCN), transparent when molten, was used as a model metal analog system for studying dendritic growth since it solidifies like the body centered cubic (BCC) ferrous metal alloys, i.e., with an atomically ''rough'' solid-liquid interface. In addition, SCN displays convenient properties for solidification experiments, such as a low melting temperature (58.08 °C), optical transparency, and the potential for accurate characterization of its thermophysical properties. Dendritic growth is initiated inside the experimental chamber by energizing thermoelectric coolers attached to one end a thin capillary injector tube called the stinger. The other end of the stinger, where the dendrite emerges in the center of the chamber, is notched, much like the tip of a fountain pen. This helps isolate the leading dendrite and reduces the time needed until the leading dendrite is isothermal and has achieved steady state. The IDGE flight experiment was divided into 60 operational cycles. The first cycle, the warm-up cycle, consists of bringing the system up to the operational temperature where all system components are checked and initialized. The second cycle measured the liquidus temperature of the SCN as a calibration point from which all subsequent supercoolings are measured. The remaining cycles were dendritic growth cycles where dendrites are grown and photographed at varying supercoolings. For each dendritic growth cycle, the experiment obtained a time series of stereo-pairs of 35-mm photographic images, low-resolution, binary, digitized electronic images and various data streams characterizing the dendrite's growth conditions during the cycle. For each image pair, either 35-mm film negative or digitized image, we measured the position of the dendrite tip, and the associated time that the image was recorded. The dendritic velocity was determined by calculating the slope of the displacement-time curve from the steady-state regime of the growth cycle. The velocity is then adjusted by appropriate stereographic and magnification factors. This procedure yields a set of dendrite velocity measurements accurate to about ± 2 percent.
hypothesis: The hypothesis of this investigation is that as a function of the supercooling there exists an explicit dendritic dynamic operating state defined by dendritic tip velocity, V and the dendrite tip paraboloidal radius of curvature, R. The Peclet number obtained from the Ivantsov solution for each specified supercooling yielded an infinite number of solutions for V and R. Therefore it is hypothesized that a second independent equation or length scale exists, which, when combined with the Ivantsov diffusion solution, will mathematically select the observed unique dynamic operating state. Two of the candidates for the additional crystal growth physics that could provide the second crucial equation are the effects from the solid-melt interfacial energy, the influence of temperature fluctuations in the melt, or both.
research_impacts: The size, shape, spacing, and orientation of the dendrites in cast metal alloys have a major effect on the strength, ductility and toughness. Nearly all cast-metal alloys used in everyday products, such as automobiles and airplanes, are composed of dendritic microstructures. Metallurgists have long sought to predict and control alloy microstructures. The development of automated, cost effective manufacturing techniques ultimately depends on the precision with which the problem in non-equilibrium pattern formation can be solved. In principle, the intent is to incorporate fundamental understanding of microstructures into computer codes that simultaneously help design materials with made to order properties and optimize their manufacturability and performance. Dendritic growth experiments conducted in the microgravity environment can provide benchmark data to validate such predictive models.

title: PSI-72 Version 4 Isothermal Dendritic Growth Experiment United States Microgravity Payload-3(IDGE USMP-3) Investigation
objective: Following the first IDGE flight on USMP-2, the second fight of lDGE took place on USMP-3 in February and March of 1996. The scientific objectives of the second flight of the IDGE was to: characterize the three-dimensional shape of a dendrite tip; accumulate a dense data set on dendritic velocities and radii in the diffusion-limited infinite boundary regime; and to form dendritic velocity data sets to clarify issues in the literature about whether convection or near-field boundary conditions affect the dendritic growth measurements in microgravity in the lower supercooling range.
approach: The sample material and temperature controls were identical to the USMP-2 investigation. In addition to the high-resolution film data collected after the shuttle landed, growth velocities were measured in near-real time by downlinked, binary CCD images. Many growths were measured from CCD images alone and these steady-state velocity measurements were accurate to 2%.
hypothesis: The hypothesis of this investigation is that as a function of the supercooling there exists an explicit dendritic dynamic operating state defined by dendritic tip velocity, V and the dendrite tip paraboloidal radius of curvature, R. The Peclet number obtained from the Ivantsov solution for each specified supercooling yielded an infinite number of solutions for V and R. Therefore it is hypothesized that a second independent equation or length scale exists, which, when combined with the Ivantsov diffusion solution, will mathematically select the observed unique dynamic operating state. Two of the candidates for the additional crystal growth physics that could provide the second crucial equation are the effects from the solid-melt interfacial energy, the influence of temperature fluctuations in the melt, or both. Aside from the original hypothesis for USMP-2, the USMP-3 also tested the hypothesis that both the magnitude of the microgravity level and the growth angle with respect to the quasi-static microgravity vector would affect the growth velocity. With additional and sufficient data from USMP-3 it was anticipated to construct a three-dimensional reconstruction of the non-parabolic, non-body-of-revolution dendritic tip shape.
research_impacts: The size, shape, spacing, and orientation of the dendrites in cast metal alloys have a major effect on the strength, ductility and toughness. Nearly all cast-metal alloys used in everyday products, such as automobiles and airplanes, are composed of dendritic microstructures. Metallurgists have long sought to predict and control alloy microstructures. The development of automated, cost effective manufacturing techniques ultimately depends on the precision with which the problem in non-equilibrium pattern formation can be solved. In principle, the intent is to incorporate fundamental understanding of microstructures into computer codes that simultaneously help design materials with made to order properties and optimize their manufacturability and performance. Dendritic growth experiments conducted in the microgravity environment can provide benchmark data to validate such predictive models.

title: PSI-73 Version 4 Isothermal Dendritic Growth Experiment United States Microgravity Payload - 4(IDGE-4) Investigation
objective: Following the first and second IDGE flight on USMP-2 and USMP-3, the third and final IDGE flight (USMP-4) was launched on STS-87, in November of 1997. The last flight employed pivalic acid (PVA)—a face centered cubic (FCC) organic plastic crystal that solidifies analogous to many non–ferrous metals unlike SCN that solidifies similar to BCC ferrous metal alloys. In comparison to SCN, PVA exhibits a large anisotropy of its solid–melt interfacial energy. The primary objective was to investigate if the anisotropy of solid-melt interfacial energy is indeed a key physical parameter in the subtle selection process of dendritic operating states.
approach: The experimental approach was similar to USMP-3 and USMP-4 with the exception that PVA was utilized as the sample material to quantify growth velocity as a function of undercooling. In addition, the spacing between nearest neighbors were also quantified during this USMP-4 investigation.
hypothesis: The hypothesis of the IDGE investigations is that as a function of the supercooling there exists an explicit dendritic dynamic operating state defined by dendritic tip velocity, V and the dendrite tip paraboloidal radius of curvature, R. The Peclet number obtained from the Ivantsov solution for each specified supercooling yielded an infinite number of solutions for V and R. Therefore it is hypothesized that a second independent equation or length scale exists, which, when combined with the Ivantsov diffusion solution, will mathematically select the observed unique dynamic operating state. Two of the candidates for the additional crystal growth physics that could provide the second crucial equation are the effects from the solid-melt interfacial energy, the influence of temperature fluctuations in the melt, or both. Aside from the original hypothesis for USMP-2, the USMP-3 also tested the hypothesis that both the magnitude of the microgravity level and the growth angle with respect to the quasi-static microgravity vector would affect the growth velocity. With additional and sufficient data from USMP-3 it was anticipated to construct a three-dimensional reconstruction of the non-parabolic, non-body-of-revolution dendritic tip shape. For the final USMP-4 investigation the use PVA was to test the hypothesis if interfacial anisotropy has any significant effect on growth velocity and if there exist a minimum nearest neighbor distance below which the growth velocity begins to decrease due to overlapping of thermal fields.

The development of automated, cost effective manufacturing techniques ultimately depends on the precision with which the problem in non-equilibrium pattern formation can be solved. In principle, the intent is to incorporate fundamental understanding of microstructures into computer codes that simultaneously help design materials with made to order properties and optimize their manufacturability and performance.
