title: PSI-74 Version 4 Investigating the Structures of Paramagnetic Aggregates from Colloidal Emulsions-2(InSPACE-2) Investigation
objective: InSPACE-2 studied the kinetics of chain formation in DC fields for suspensions of monodisperse, super-paramagnetic colloidal microspheres. Objectives included: 1) To understand the percolation transition of MR suspensions in microgravity and the behavior of structures around this point (incipient structure). The fluctuations of these chains can also be used to estimate the microrheological response of the MR fluid. Additionally, measurements of the chain fluctuations in the final gelled material provide an estimate of the storage modulus of the suspension. 2) To determine the lowest energy configuration of 3D particle structures formed in a magnetorheological (MR) fluid in a pulsed magnetic field. Visual observations of microscopic structures will yield a better understanding of the interplay of the forces and interactions (magnetizing/demagnetizing, surface energy, and repulsion between structures) in MR suspensions. The most important dipolar interactions are the demagnetizing field, surface energy, and repulsion between structures.
approach: InSPACE-2 employed a microscopic video technique to study the internal microstructure in MR fluid suspensions. The investigation studied the assembly of magnetic particles in the presence of a toggled magnetic field. The microstructure of the suspension as the particles assemble was characterized by light microscopy. Samples for InSPACE-2 consisted of 1.05 μm diameter colloidal particles suspended in an aqueous phase. The particles were Dynabeads MyOne Carboxylic Acid from Invitrogen at four different concentrations, 0.40, 0.48, 0.56, 0.65%. When exposed to a continuous magnetic field each particle in the fluid acquires a magnetic dipole moment. Such dipoles mutually interact and align to form a particle chain structures. At sufficient concentrations and field strengths these chains form columns that cross-link to form an interconnected network. The effects of sedimentation, which prohibits maintaining the particle concentration uniformity throughout the fluid, affect the study of MR fluids. Mechanical properties of the particle assemblies, especially buckling instabilities, will be characterized.
hypothesis: The primary hypothesis is that energy barriers preventing colloidal phase transition can be overcome by changing the magnetic driving frequency and forces. In these gel systems, gravity plays a dominant role and would slowly compress and deform the gel structures when similar experiments are performed on Earth, whereas in space these structures can be maintained as long as the magnetic forces are applied.
research_impacts: The MR fluids studied in InSPACE-2 are a unique model system for studying the fundamental mechanisms of phase transitions and self-assembly. Suspension phase behavior affects the processing, stability and final properties of foods, personal care products, agrochemicals, paints, inks, pharmaceuticals and numerous other products and materials in which fine particles are suspended in fluids. Additionally, InSPACE-2 research emphasizes how to harness external fields in order to direct the assembly of novel micro- and nano-structured materials and devices. Such field-directed self-assembly represents a bottom-up approach to material and device fabrication, with the potential to dramatically reduce the cost of advanced technologies in photonics, heat transfer and photovoltaics. The MR response provides the basis for technologies ranging from actively controlled dampers and actuators to magnetically sealed bearings and sensitive stress transducers. MR fluids are currently used in wide range of applications, including active automotive shock absorbers, and engineers have explored their use in seismic dampers to protect large-scale structures during violent earthquakes. Applications for space exploration include their potential use in robots, rovers, and for mobility augmentation crew suits. Understanding the microstructural evolution of MR suspensions under time-varying conditions provides critical information for engineering and for tailoring their mechanical behavior.
hardware: InSPACE with sample Vial Assemblies (VA) Microgravity Science Glovebox (MSG)

title: PSI-75 Version 5 Investigating the Structures of Paramagnetic Aggregates from Colloidal Emulsions-3(InSPACE-3) Investigation
objective: InSPACE-3 investigated the assembly of paramagnetic colloidal ellipsoids in pulsed magnetic fields. An objective was to study the effect of particle shape on the kinetics of aggregation and structures formed by DC and pulsed magnetic fields in suspensions of superparamagnetic particles. Specifically, the investigation studied the suspensions of paramagnetic ellipsoid-shaped particles and quantify the effect of particle shape on the interactions of dipolar chains and the resulting suspension microstructure.
approach: InSPACE-3 employed video microscopy to obtain suspension structural information. Two particle shapes were tested for four frequency conditions and four field strengths, for a total of 24 experimental runs. Each run took approximately one hour. Each sample had a particle volume fraction of 0.52%. This concentration represents an optimum value based on previous microgravity experiments, designed to balance the ability to capture aggregation kinetics at short times in DC fields the structural evolution in pulsed fields such that the final coalescence stage is observed. For detailed experimental approach please refer Science Requirements Document (SRD).
hypothesis: Based on the science results of InSPACE-2, InSPACE-3 hypothesizes that particle shape will alter the aggregation kinetics, microstructures and microscopic mechanics, such as buckling instabilities that are observed for suspensions of polarizable spheres. This research will potentially lead to the ability to engineer enhanced properties of these suspensions, including the ability to suppress lateral aggregation in magnetorheological fluid-based electromechanical devices or the ability to create new functional materials that control the flow of electromagnetic and thermal energy.
research_impacts: The quick phase-shifting property of magnetic colloidal fluids studied in InSPACE-3 makes them potentially useful for devices such as optical interfaces, active noise, and vibration dampers inside spacecrafts. Future uses could include robotics, energy-transfer devices such as clutches, and other control systems and on Earth directed self-assembly of crystalline structures from particles that may eventually allow creation of new nano-materials fabricated from nanoparticle building blocks, with potential applications in medicine, energy storage, chemical separations, and catalysis. Magnetic colloidal fluid technology is currently used for shock absorbers in race cars and sport cars. This technology is expanding to include making large-scale building foundation stabilizers for areas prone to earthquakes.
hardware: InSPACE with sample Vial Assemblies (VA) Microgravity Science Glovebox (MSG)

title: PSI-76 Version 4 Investigating the Structures of Paramagnetic Aggregates from Colloidal Emulsions-1(InSPACE-1) Investigation
objective: InSPACE-1 studied the response of MR fluids under continuous and pulsed magnetic fields in a microgravity environment. An objective was to determine the true three-dimensional low-energy (equilibrium) structure of an magneto-rheological (MR) emulsion in a pulsed magnetic field. InSPACE-1 aimed to conduct a microscopic video study of the MR fluid in a pulsed magnetic field to determine the effect of varying magnetic field, pulse frequency, and particle size on the equilibrium microstructures. A pulsed magnetic field is used to mimic the forces applied to these fluids in real applications, such as vibration damping systems. A pulsed field also tends to produce intricate, thick structures with different properties than structures produced by a constant magnetic field.
approach: The MR samples for InSPACE-1 were ferrofluid emulsions consisting of iron oxide nanoparticles suspended in a solution of sodium dodecyl sulfate (SDS, an anionic surfactant), and ultrapure water. These samples were comprised of uniform particles sizes of 0.31, 0.40, and 0.66 μm and volume fraction 2 percent. The parameters varied during the series of tests were the field strength, the particle size, and the pulse frequency. During experimental runs the Lightbox Assembly provided the backlighting source to illuminate the samples. The InSPACE Avionics Assembly was used to output an electrical current and frequency that could be adjusted to produce a pulsed-magnetic field inside the Helmholtz coil. This magnetic field caused the particles in the fluid to group together, or aggregate, and form microstructures inside the fluid. A camera was used to record the display on the avionic assembly. The Optics Assembly was composed of two cameras with optic lens for a right angle view and a straight view of the sample. A Helmholtz coil was mounted on the optic assembly and housed the InSPACE-1 sample. For InSPACE-1, the Helmholtz Coil Assembly (CA) and the sample Vial Assemblies were integrated as a single unit.
hypothesis: The primary hypothesis is that energy barriers preventing colloidal phase transition can be overcome by changing the magnetic driving frequency and forces. In these gel systems, gravity plays a dominant role and would slowly compress and deform the gel structures when similar experiments are performed on Earth, whereas in space these structures can be maintained as long as the magnetic forces are applied.
research_impacts: MR fluids can quickly transition into a nearly solid-like state when exposed to a magnetic field and return to their original liquid state when the magnetic field is removed. Their relative stiffness can be controlled by adjusting the strength of the magnetic field. Due to the rapid-response interface that they provide between mechanical components and electronic controls, for terrestrial applications MR fluids can be used to improve or develop new brake systems, seat suspensions, robotics, clutches, airplane landing gear, and active damping systems for bridges (to counter act wind gusts) and buildings. For space exploration the results will lead to MR applications for limb and dextrous motion in robotic components and human-robotic interfaces for EVA suits.
hardware: InSPACE with sample Vial Assemblies (VA) Microgravity Science Glovebox (MSG)

title: PSI-77 Version 4 In Space Soldering Investigation(ISSI) Investigation
objective: The primary objective is to better understand the quality of solders in a microgravity environment. In microgravity, gas bubbles, or void spaces are found in the solder joint and at contact surfaces. These voids reduce the thermal and electrical conductivity and also provide sites for crack initiation. Bubbles have less chance to escape in the reduced gravity environment of space. Hence, by designing a systematic series of simple experiments, the objective was to investigate and better understand porosity development, surface wetting, and equilibrium shape formation while soldering in a reduced gravity environment.
approach: The proposed experiments basically consisted of taking pieces of silver-coated copper wire and bending/twisting them into simple configurations for test coupons. Selected lengths of Kester “44”® 60-40 rosin core solder (5 and 10 cm) were then cut and wrapped around a selected portion of the coupon, to be later melted by heat conduction through the wire using the kit’s soldering iron. A second set of experiments involved feeding 5 and 10 cm lengths of solder onto similar shaped coupons that were being heated by the iron. In principle, the soldering iron was never meant to come in contact with the molten solder. All in all, five soldering sessions were conducted on the ISS that culminated in 86 samples comprising seven different wire configurations, two different solder lengths (5 and 10 cm), and two different melt procedures (conduction melting of wrapped solder and conduction melting of solder being fed onto the wire). The melting experiments took place in the flame retardant Maintenance Work Area, a portable facility in the ISS used to make repairs and conduct other operations in the ISS. A digital camera is placed behind the samples to record the melting and subsequent solidification experiments. Video footage and still pictures were down linked after each experimental session.
hypothesis: Due to minimized buoyancy in the microgravity environment, it is hypothesized that one would expect additional porosity and enhanced surface tension contributions to porosity shape and mobility. Brazing, soldering, and welding operations in microgravity can be influenced greatly by both wetting and surface tension-driven flows, primary factors in achieving or not achieving a sound joint. For example, processes that rely on gravity-driven separations in the terrestrial environment, such as the removal of gas bubbles from a liquid, may rely on completely different interfacial phenomenon in microgravity.
research_impacts: An investigation of soldering practices and behavior in a microgravity environment is relevant to our technological needs, particularly with regard to in-space fabrication and repair. The ISSI payload provides unique insight into microgravity soldering methods, which could play a fundamental role in maintaining the International Space Station as well as provide understanding of repair capabilities on future missions to the Moon and to Mars. The study of soldering in space could lead to better soldering techniques here on Earth.

title: PSI-78 Version 4 IntraVenous Fluid GENeration for Exploration Missions(IVGEN) Investigation
objective: The main goal of this experiment is to demonstrate in a space environment, a prototype system that produces USP grade SWI, and mixes the SWI with sterile USP sodium chloride to produce a homogeneous Normal Saline IV fluid. The experiment shall also demonstrate at least one bubble removal apparatus, as this is a critical step to prevent delivering harmful gas emboli to patients when the deployed system is used. The system will utilize a single flow rate, determined by the maximum volume/hour required for a worst-case-scenario medical event.
approach: The IVGEN investigation employs a comprehensive and well-structured approach to demonstrate and validate the feasibility of producing IV fluids in space. The approach encompasses a combination of on-orbit experimentation, ground-based testing, and meticulous data analysis, as summarized below: On-Orbit Experimentation: The core of the investigation involves a flight experiment onboard the International Space Station (ISS), utilizing a prototype IV fluid generation system. This experiment simulates the conditions and constraints of a space mission, allowing for direct testing of the system's performance in a microgravity environment. Ground-Based Testing: Prior to the flight experiment, a rigorous ground-based test program is conducted to: -Concept Verification: Validate the design and performance of key system components, such as the bubble separators and mixers, in both normal and reduced gravity environments. -Input Water Analysis: Characterize the quality of potential water sources, including ISS potable water and various CEV water sources, to ensure the system's compatibility and effectiveness. -Temperature Effects: Assess the impact of varying temperatures on the system's performance, particularly on the DI cartridge and the conductivity sensors. Data Acquisition and Analysis: During the on-orbit experiment, a comprehensive dataset is collected, including: -Environmental Data: Temperature, pressure, and acceleration measurements to understand the system's operating environment and potential impact on performance. -System Performance Data: Conductivity, flow rate, and image data to assess the purification, mixing, and bubble removal processes. Post-Flight Sample Analysis: The two 1.5-liter bags of NS produced on orbit are returned to Earth for rigorous testing by a certified laboratory, ensuring the produced IV fluid meets USP standards. Data Interpretation and Scaling: The collected data is meticulously analyzed to: -Validate System Performance: Confirm the successful production of USP-compliant NS solution in microgravity. -Identify Challenges and Limitations: Assess potential issues and areas for improvement based on observed system behavior. -Enable System Scaling: Utilize the data to inform the design and development of a larger, operational system capable of meeting the needs of future exploration missions.
hypothesis: It is hypothesized that a prototype system, utilizing deionization, magnetic stirring, and bubble separation techniques, can effectively produce USP-compliant normal saline solution from readily available spacecraft potable water sources in a microgravity environment.
research_impacts: Due to mass and volume limitations, space vehicles cannot carry sufficient IV fluid for medical contingencies. A filtering and mixing system that can make IV fluid in situ would provide the treatment capability without the mass and volume constraints. IVGEN was designed and will be tested to meet that need. IVGEN technology could be used on Earth to generate IV fluid in Third World countries where medical resources are limited.

title: PSI-79 Version 4 Light Microscopy Module Biophysics-1(LMMBIO-1) Investigation
objective: Specific objectives of this investigation were 1. On the ISS and concurrently in earth control experiments, compare incorporation of protein aggregates (monomers versus dimers, trimers, etc.) into growing protein crystals. Detection of aggregates in the crystal will be qualitatively assessed via LMM’s and laboratory fluorescence confocal microscopes and quantitatively measured using mass spectrometry (ion spray and/or MALDI). Based on the percentage incorporation of larger aggregates within the crystal, the effect of molecular filtering based on differences in diffusion rates will be assessed. 2. Measure crystal growth rates in 1g versus μg for different size aggregates of proteins with molecular weights ranging from less than 20kDa to more than 1,200kDa. 3. Compare the defect density and crystal quality via mass spectroscopy and x-ray diffraction quality of crystals grown at different rates in a 1g environment.
approach: A total of four cassettes were sent to the ISS, containing eight samples each. Each sample could contain either; (1) Lysozyme, (2) pfGST, (3) BSA, or (4) XptA1. For each protein investigated, preparative size exclusion chromatography (SEC) was used to fractionate protein monomers from the naturally occurring protein aggregates. The aggregates were then segmented into small, medium, and large categories. Fluorophores (excitation wavelengths: 594 and 488) were chosen and attached to the macromolecules, producing a bright fluorescent signal (red and green) and each exhibited a slow photo-bleach so that fluorescence was maintained for the duration of the proposed crystallization experiments. The samples were upmassed frozen at -80C and thawed to ambient temperature (~20C). After thawing nucleation of the proteins were observable within 24 – 96 hours. Observations were conducted with a confocal fluorescent microscope where the total fluorescence observed for each crystal (after normalizing for the different crystal volumes) provides an estimation of the relative amount(s) of aggregated (containing the fluorophore) versus monomeric (no fluorophore) protein incorporated within the growing crystal.
hypothesis: This investigation addresses the hypothesis that improved quality of microgravity-grown protein crystals is the result of two macromolecular characteristics that exist in a buoyancy-free, diffusion-dominated solution: • Slower crystal growth rates, due to slower protein transport to the growing crystal surface • Predilection of growing crystals to incorporate protein monomers versus higher protein aggregates due to differences in transport rates
research_impacts: Using three-dimensional protein structure information, researchers can determine how proteins function and in cases where these proteins are involved in disease processes, the structure is often used to design new drugs that specifically interact with the protein. Many leading drugs today are the product of structure-based drug design. While enormous strides have been made in the last decade, there remain a large number of important proteins where the difficulty of obtaining crystals of sufficient quality is the chief barrier to their structural analysis. The impact of this investigation is for one important class of proteins, membrane proteins, comprises a number of targets identified by the pharmaceutical industry as high-value commercial opportunities (membrane proteins were the targets for approximately 67% of all past marketed drugs and it is estimated that they will comprise targets for an equal percentage of all future drugs). Membrane protein crystallization represents one area where the onset of space commercialization can maximize the impact of the microgravity environment in space-based research applications for the academic, government and pharmaceutical industries. Other areas include high-value aqueous proteins and protein complexes (based on their functional importance in biological systems) many of which yield crystals of poor quality under 1g laboratory conditions. Access to unique data optimized in microgravity could have great relevance for understanding protein structures and advancing new drugs into the pharmaceutical market.

title: PSI-8 Version 2 Characterization of Biofilm Formation, Growth and Gene Expression on Different Materials and Environmental Conditions in Microgravity(Space Biofilms) Investigation
objective: 1. To use microbial strains that are relevant to human spaceflight, and nosocomial infections that have also occurred in spaceflight, and substrata materials that are relevant to (i) spacecraft structures and surfaces, (ii) life support systems, (iii) space biology research hardware, and (iv) medical instrumentation. We are meeting this objective by the use of the same fungal strain that was isolated from a bio-damaged Mir window (Penicillium rubens), and an uropathogenic bacterial strain (Pseudomonas aeruginosa). 2. To culture the selected microbial strains in a way that enables biofilm formation, during an up- to-6-month experiment. To achieve this goal, we used BioServe’s already spaceflight- proven hardware and conducted preliminary testing during the first year of the experiment. 3. To quantify potential changes on biofilm mass, thickness, and overall morphology (including the formation of the “column-and-canopy structures) on the spaceflight cultures with respect to matched ground controls. This was achieved by acquiring post-flight (samples fixed in paraformaldehyde) morphological data through confocal laser scanning microscopy. 4. To elucidate the molecular mechanisms behind the observed morphological changes. This was done with the bacterial samples by acquiring post-flight transcriptomic data (samples fixed with RNA Later II) and conducting differential gene expression analyses between spaceflight cultures and matched ground controls. 5. To assess differential expression of genes associated with conferring microbes with oxidative, acidity, and antimicrobial resistance. This was done through RNA Sequencing and comparative gene analysis. 6. To determine physical mechanisms of material/microorganisms interaction in biofilms and their associated molecular basis. The morphological and transcriptomic data was utilized to identify potential correlation in between the differential gene expression and altered material/microorganism interaction in space, with respect to matched ground controls. Different topographic structures were assessed to provide further insight into this aspect (topographical patters with periodicities, same size, as the microbial size).
approach: The Space Biofilms project, performed at the International Space Station, contributes to the understanding of microbial communities in space by characterizing the morphology and gene expression of bacterial and fungal biofilms formed in microgravity with respect to ground controls. The project has two big branches, the bacterial and the fungal side. Pseudomonas aeruginosa was used as model organism for the bacterial side and both morphology and transcriptomic (selected samples) studies were performed with bacterial samples, while Penicillium rubens was used as model organism for the fungal side and a morphology study was performed for fungal samples. Bacterial biofilm formation was characterized at one, two, and three days of incubation (37°C) over six different materials: stainless steel 316, passivated stainless steel 316, a lubricant impregnated surface (LIS), catheter grade silicone with and without a linear microtopography, and cellulose membrane. Fungal biofilm formation (mold) was characterized at 10, 15, and 20 days of incubation (25°C) over seven different materials: stainless steel 316, aluminum alloy (Al6061), titanium alloy (Ti-6Al-4V), quartz, catheter grade silicone, carbon fiber, and a superhydrophobic surface “nanograss”. Bacterial samples: 144 flight and 144 ground samples were prepared for the Space Biofilms bacterial experiment. The experiment independent variables were two gravitational regimes (Earth gravity and microgravity), three incubation times (1, 2, and 3 days), six material-media combinations (LBK media was used for samples grown over SS316, pSS316, and LIS; while mAUMg-hi Pi media was used for samples grown over cellulose, silicone, and silicone DLIP), two types of fixative/preservative (PFA and RNAlater), and replicates (four). To provide the necessary levels of containment, each sample was prepared in a Fluid Processing Apparatus (FPA) and eight FPAs were integrated into a Group Activation Pack (GAP). Once in microgravity, samples were activated by introducing the bacterial inoculum into the sterile medium and placing the samples at 37°C for the corresponding incubation time. After the incubation time the samples were terminated by introducing the fixative (for morphology samples) or the preservative (for transcriptomic samples). The morphology samples were stained (one dye for lipids and one dye for nucleic acids) and imaged with a confocal microscope. The resulting 3D images of the biofilms (.nd2 files) were processed and analyzed using the COMSTAT2 software to quantify biofilm mass, biofilm thickness, and biofilm surface area coverage. The transcriptomic samples had their RNA extracted and sequenced. The resulting transcriptomic data files (fastq files) were processed and used for gene expression analysis using DeSeq2. For more information on the bacterial sample preparation see section 4, and for information about the experiment performance in space see section 5 of the following paper: https://doi.org/10.1016/j.actaastro.2022.07.015 For more information on the bacterial morphology and transcriptomic analyses see the Methods section of the following paper: https://doi.org/10.1038/s41526-023-00316-w Fungal samples: 288 flight and 288 ground samples were prepared for the Space Biofilms fungal experiment. The experiment independent variables were two gravitational regimes (Earth gravity and microgravity), three incubation times (10, 15, and 20 days), seven material substratum (stainless steel 316, aluminum alloy Al6061, titanium alloy Ti-6Al-4V, quartz, catheter grade silicone, carbon fiber, and a superhydrophobic surface “nanograss”), two types of fixative/preservative (PFA and RNAlater), and replicates (6-12 depending on the specific set). To provide the necessary levels of containment, each sample was prepared in a well of a 24-well plate and sealed with a gas permeable membrane. Additionally, four 24-well plates were integrated into a Plate Habitat (PHAB). Once in microgravity, samples were activated by wetting pads inside the PHAB to increase the environment humidity and by placing the samples at 25°C for the corresponding incubation time. After the incubation time the samples were terminated by introducing the fixative (for morphology samples) or the preservative (for transcriptomic samples)*. *The transcriptomic samples were not analyzed as part of this project. The morphology samples were stained (one dye for chitin and one dye for extracellular matrix proteins) and imaged with a confocal microscope. The resulting 3D images of the biofilms (.nd2 files) were processed and analyzed using the COMSTAT2 software to quantify biofilm mass, biofilm thickness, and biofilm surface area coverage. For more information on the bacterial sample preparation, the experiment performance in space, and the fungal morphology analyses see section 2 of the following paper:- https://doi.org/10.3390/life13041001
hypothesis: It is hypothesized that, in comparison to matched ground controls: a) Biofilm mass and thickness in microgravity will be increased for all bacterial and fungal species, growth medium, and substratum material; b) Gene expression will vary as a function of growth medium, substratum material, and gravitational regime; c) A systematic increase in expression of the genes that confer microorganisms with oxidative, acidity, and antimicrobial resistance will be observed in space (becoming more pronounced with time in space); and d) The formation of the “column-and- canopy” bacterial biofilm architecture and the material/microorganism interaction mechanisms in space will vary from one microbial species and material to the other, and will be associated with the differential expression of specific genes.
research_impacts: This project is relevant to the space program and the “Biophysics – Biomaterials” emphasis of this NRA as it investigates biofilm formation (which can increase the risk of astronaut infection and equipment failure) on spacecraft-relevant materials. This work is relevant to the Space Biology Program and the Human Research Roadmap as it utilizes human pathology-associated bacterial species (uropathogenic Pseudomonas aeruginosa), growth media (e.g. modified artificial urine media), and materials (e.g. silicone from catheters).The knowledge produced may help address Gaps Micro-01, -02, -03, and -04 by characterizing bacterial and fungal responses to spaceflight, by interrogating the expression of genes associated with drug resistance, and by elucidating the governing mechanisms behind the observed phenomena. Furthermore, due to our proposed approach, the knowledge derived from this project may be translatable to biofilm-associated illnesses on Earth.
hardware: Bacterial Side: BioServe’s Fluid Processing Apparatus (FPA) housed in the Group Activation Pack (GAP) Fungal Side: BioServe’s Plate Habitat (PHAB).

title: PSI-80 Version 4 Light Microscopy Module Biophysics-3(LMMBIO-3) Investigation
objective: The primary objectives of this investigation are: 1. Use molecular biology to produce closely related protein constructs that display differences in growth rate dispersion during crystallization. Measure the intermolecular ‘attractiveness’ of each construct, then model the inter-particle forces, diffusion and convection. 2. Measure and compare the growth rate dispersion of ground and microgravity grown crystals. Growth rate dispersion will be measured for ground control crystals using routine crystallization apparatus. In addition, growth rate dispersion will be measure for ground and microgravity grown crystals using the flight apparatus. 3. Characterize the quality of both ground and microgravity grown crystals. Sophisticated X-ray analysis along with X-ray structural data collection will be used to quantify and characterize crystal quality. 4. Link the knowledge about inter-particle forces, measured acceleration levels, calculated flow rates and the resultant X-ray analysis to develop a model and predictive ground-based tests to identify those samples producing crystals on the ground that would be improved in microgravity.
approach: Approach: Several cassettes were configured with cassettes identically configured containing three samples, one set in capillaries 1-6, another sample in capillaries 7-12, and the third in capillaries 13-18. Six constructs and the T4 wild type (WT) were loaded into the capillaries at various concentrations and frozen to -80C. The samples were thawed and observed in the LMM facility on board the ISS. Several cassettes were identically configured containing three samples, one set in capillaries 1-6, another sample in capillaries 7-12, and the third in capillaries 13-18. The capillaries were loaded so that capillaries 1-6 contained theWT* construct, capillaries 7-12 the S44E WT* construct and finally, capillaries 13-18 the S44F WT* construct. The cassettes were kept at -80°C until moving to the space station microscope facility. The capillaries were filled as follows: • Capillaries 1-6 with 50 mg/ml WT* in 0.1 M Zn(C 2 H3 O2 )2 , 0.1 M Tris, pH 8, 35% PEG 8K, and 0.1 M NaCl • Capillaries 7-12 with 64 mg/ml S44E WT* in 0.05 M NaC 2 H3 O2 0.1 M Tris, pH 8 30% PEG 8K and 15% glycerol • Capillaries 13-18 with 53 mg/ml S44F WT* in 0.2 M Zn(C 2 H3 O2 )2 , 0.1 M NaC2H3O2, pH 5 and 20% PEG 20K. On return to earth X-ray analysis of samples took place using the IMCA (Industrial Macromolecular Crystallography Association) beamline of the Advanced Photon Source.
hypothesis: Removing or greatly reducing the effects of buoyancy-driven convection and sedimentation in microgravity will result in slower, diffusion-controlled molecular transport that can yield larger crystals with fewer defects. It is postulated that growth rate dispersion is reduced in microgravity due to the diffusive rather than convective flow regime that delivers macromolecules to the crystal. Based on previous experimental observations it is hypothesized that the presence of growth rate dispersion in macromolecular crystals grown on the ground is an indicator of crystals that can be improved when grown in microgravity.
research_impacts: Research Impacts/Earth Benefits: X-ray crystallography is the main method scientists use to study the molecular structures of biology, but it is difficult to crystallize proteins, with only a poor success rate even in the best laboratories. This investigation uses ground and microgravity-based observations to predict which proteins would benefit from crystallization in microgravity, improving the information that may be obtained from them. Long-duration protein crystal growth experiments on the ISS with photo documentation, and subsequent analysis of the comparisons between 1g and μg crystals, will enable a more complete understanding of why proteins and other macromolecules often form more perfect crystals in microgravity than they do on earth. If it could be predicted which macromolecular samples could be improved by crystal growth in microgravity, then the true potential of this medium could be exploited in an efficient manner. Structural biology of protein-protein complexes and integral membrane proteins are currently a high NIH priority due to their importance for systems biology, disease mechanisms and structure-guided drug development. Hauptman Woodward Medical Research Institute has a data archive of millions of time-resolved crystallization images (from over 14,000 different biological macromolecules) that could be used to identify candidates likely to benefit from crystallization in microgravity.

title: PSI-81 Version 4 Microheater Array Boiling Experiment(MABE) Investigation
objective: 1. To characterize the boiling curve in a very low g-jitter environment: The experiment aims to determine the boiling curve in a microgravity environment with minimal gravitational disturbances (g-jitter). This objective is driven by the understanding that g-jitter can significantly influence bubble dynamics and, consequently, the heat transfer process. By minimizing g-jitter, the researchers hope to obtain a clearer picture of boiling behavior in a true microgravity environment. 2. To understand the parameters governing the size of the primary bubble and develop a predictive model for it: A key objective is to identify the factors that determine the size of the primary bubble in microgravity. These parameters could include heater size, nucleation site density, subcooling, gravity level, fluid properties, superheated layer thickness, wall superheat, and surface tension. By understanding these parameters, the researchers aim to develop a model that can accurately predict the primary bubble size under different conditions. 3. To investigate the mechanism of critical heat flux (CHF) in microgravity and its relationship to the primary bubble: The research aims to elucidate how CHF occurs in microgravity and to determine its relationship to the size and behavior of the primary bubble. CHF is a critical parameter in boiling, representing the maximum heat flux that can be transferred from a surface before a transition to film boiling occurs. Understanding the factors influencing CHF in microgravity is essential for the safe and efficient operation of space-based thermal systems. 4. To determine the effect of heater size on the formation of the primary bubble and its impact on the boiling curve: MABE investigates the influence of heater size on boiling behavior. Two different heater array sizes are used, allowing the researchers to compare how heater size affects the formation of the primary bubble, the occurrence of dryout, and the shape of the boiling curve in microgravity.
approach: MABE utilizes a multi-pronged approach to achieve its research objectives. The experiment combines a carefully designed experimental setup with a comprehensive data analysis strategy. Here's a breakdown of the key elements of the investigation approach: Experimental Setup: Microscale heater array: The experiment utilizes an array of 96 individually controlled platinum resistance heaters deposited on a quartz substrate. Constant temperature control: Each heater is maintained at a constant temperature, allowing for accurate quantification of substrate heat conduction and reducing the risk of heater burnout. Variable experimental conditions: The experiment manipulates key parameters such as bulk liquid subcooling, pressure, and heater size to study their influence on boiling. Multiple gravity levels: The experiment is designed to allow data acquisition in Earth gravity, lunar gravity, Martian gravity, and microgravity, enabling a comprehensive comparison of boiling behavior across different gravitational environments. High-speed video imaging: A high-speed digital camera captures images of the boiling process beneath the heater array, providing valuable insights into bubble dynamics. Interferometry: The experiment employs interferometry to measure temperature profiles around the vapor bubble, providing additional data for analysis. Data Acquisition and Analysis: Data Acquisition: Data is collected at a high frequency, capturing the instantaneous power dissipated by each heater, bulk fluid temperature, pressure, and acceleration. Data Processing: Raw data is converted into engineering units, synchronized, and analyzed to generate boiling curves, heat transfer maps, and other relevant data visualizations. Correlation with video and interferometry data: The heat transfer data is correlated with visual observations from the high-speed video and interferometry data to gain a deeper understanding of bubble behavior and heat transfer mechanisms. Analytical and Numerical Modeling: The experiment employs analytical and numerical models to simulate the boiling process and validate the experimental findings. Ground-Based Testing and Validation: Preliminary Engineering Model: A preliminary engineering model of the experiment is developed and tested on the KC-135 aircraft, providing essential validation of the design and data acquisition procedures. Calibration and Validation: The heater array is calibrated on the ground and recalibrated in flight to ensure accurate measurements. This investigation approach combines a sophisticated experimental setup with rigorous data analysis and modeling to provide a comprehensive understanding of boiling in microgravity.
hypothesis: This study will test three central hypotheses: (1) Bubble coalescence dominates heat transfer in microgravity, creating a large primary bubble that induces local dryout; (2) A transition between buoyancy-dominated and surface-tension-dominated boiling regimes occurs depending on the interplay between the heater size and the gravitational acceleration; (3) Heat transfer in the surface-tension-dominated regime shows minimal dependence on gravitational acceleration.
research_impacts: In microgravity, a bubble can cover an entire heater array instead of just a small area, resulting in burnout of components if local hot spots are present. The increased spatial resolution of these measurements will enable the extent of the dry spot to be measured along with the heat transfer from the liquid surrounding the dry spot. This technique can be applied to other areas including spray cooling, turbulence measurements and flow boiling. The proposed research has shown that transient conduction is the dominant heat transfer mechanism in boiling of refrigerants-like fluids. This research will provide insight into creating more efficient cooling systems on Earth.

title: PSI-82 Version 4 Microstructure Formation in Casting of Technical Alloys under Diffusive and Magnetically Controlled Convective Conditions/Comparison of Structure and Segregation in Alloys Directionally Solidified in Terrestrial and Microgravity Environments(MICAST/CSS) Investigation
objective: The objective of the proposed investigation is to better understand how the intensity of convection and the direction of the flow influences the evolution of the mushy zone, macro- and micro-segregation, morphology of dendrites, the growth mode and spatial arrangement of intermetallic precipitates.
approach: 3 different Al-Si alloys were directionally solidified under different thermal gradient and furnace translation velocities. Along with micro and macro-segregation, dendritic characteristics including primary arm spacing and trunk diameters were quantified. Microgravity results were compared to those obtained under terrestrial conditions. A finite volume modeling approach was undertaken in the absence of convection and predictions were compared to data obtained from microgravity and terrestrial samples.
hypothesis: Dendritic metrics of the directionally solidified (DS) samples are expected to have dendritic characteristics that compare very well to model predictions for growth in the absence of convection. Earth-grown samples are not anticipated to compare well, indicating that the convection in Earth grown alloys does indeed play a role in microstructural development during the solidification process. Further, Earth-grown samples exhibit a type of macrosegregation called ''steepling” in which the periphery of a DS-ed sample is of eutectic composition and is seen in alloys with solutes that increase the density of the liquid during solidification. Samples grown aboard the ISS are not expected to have steepling.
research_impacts: The research is relevant to a process known as directional solidification, which is used for producing critical castings that are used in gas turbine engines. Gas turbine engines power aircraft (i.e., often called ''jet engines'') and are also used to generate electric power. These castings are made of vacuum melted alloys that are capable of withstanding the demanding conditions at high temperatures and consequently the metallurgical structure of the alloys must be of the highest quality. The research is leading to an improved understanding of how microstructures and segregation form in directionally solidified castings; hence the science of producing such castings will be enhanced as a result of the research. In addition, the research findings relate to many other types of castings, including billets and ingots, of alloys (i.e., steel, aluminum alloys, etc.) that are critical for metal fabrication. In addition, the benchmark microgravity data allows validation of models predicting dendritic metrics such as primary and secondary arm spacing and trunk diameter. Such validated simulation models can enable optimization of casting parameters.
hardware: Low Gradient Furnace (LGF); Solidification and Quenching Furnace (SQF)

title: PSI-83 Version 6 Microgravity Investigation of Cement Solidification - Multi-use Variable Gravity Platform(MICS-MVP) Investigation
objective: The purpose of the MICS-MVP is to investigate and understand the complex process of cement solidification as a function of variable gravity and to advance the use of concrete materials for extraterrestrial infrastructure. MICS-MVP will identify the differences between the hydration reaction and microstructural formation at the different gravity levels.
approach: Two different mixture combinations of with water and gypsum and tricalcium silicate (C3S) with water were hydrated under 5 different gravity levels, namely, Earth's gravity, microgravity, and simulated gravity levels of the Moon, Mars, and a statistical point at 0.7g. The different components were each placed in opposing compartments of a plastic pouch and separated by a middle burstable seal. To burst the seal, the water filled compartment was rolled up from the outside edge towards the middle until enough forward pressure was achieved to burst the seal. The water is then completely moved into the compartment containing the tricalcium aluminate (C3A) or tricalcium silicate (C3S) and the paste is mixed by a rubber spatula and/or kneaded by hand to reach a homogeneous state. A plastic clip is then attached to help consolidate the paste at one end of the pouch. This mixing procedure generally took a few minutes per sample. The ISS itself provides a microgravity environment, whereas the gravity levels of extraterrestrial bodies that are less than Earths were simulated with centrifugal forces within the Multi-use Variable-gravity Platform (MVP). Samples at different gravity levels were hydrated for different lengths of time, following which the centrifuge was shut off and the samples continued to hydrate till they were returned to earth. The samples were characterized for pore size, pore distribution, portlandite size distribution, crystal morphology, and phase content.
hypothesis: It is hypothesized that under variable reduced gravity conditions different transport phenomena such as buoyancy, sedimentation, and convection are minimized and a more diffusion dominant transport will lead to varying degree of uniformity in distribution ofphases, porosity, and crystal morphology. A different microstructure is expected to form in at different gravity levels which possibly leads to different physical properties of the reduced gravity hardened cement paste with respect to that hardened in terrestrial gravity (1g).
research_impacts: The MICS investigation directly addresses the high priority need for lightweight space structures for habitats that protect crew. Results from this investigation enable the characterization of microstructural development in the hardening of cement paste and improve understanding of crystal growth and hydration kinetics, phase formations, pore distribution, and material properties. Also, MICS can increase understanding and control of the crystal growth kinetics, and morphology, to improve concrete properties. Improved cement properties can lead to improved concrete properties, durability, and lower CO2 emission.

title: PSI-84 Version 8 Microgravity Investigation of Cement Solidification(MICS) Investigation
objective: The objective of the proposed investigation is to better understand the complex process of cement solidification by conducting experiments in the microgravity environment aboard the International Space Station (ISS) and further the development of an in-situ lunar concrete material.
approach: Several different mixture combinations of tricalcium aluminate (C3A), tricalcium silicate (C3S), ordinary portland cement (OPC), superplasticizer (SP) and ratios of cement to water were packed in commercially available plastic bags (Burst Pouches®) with separate compartments divided by an internal, burstable seal which allowed mixing of materials under sealed conditions in microgravity and terrestrial conditions. Space and ground samples were mixed simultaneously and at the same conditions of 20 ºC ± 2 ºC, 1 ATM and 35% RH. As such, gravity is considered the only variable between the space and ground experiments. After a specific period of hydration samples were subjected to a wide variety of characterization techniques such as image analysis and mercury intrusion porosimetry (MIP) to assess porosity and pore size distribution, thermogravimetric analysis (TGA) to estimate degree of hydration, x-ray diffraction (XRD) for crystalline phase identification, energy dispersive spectroscopy (EDS) and electron microprobe analysis (EMPA) for compositional analysis. Phase distribution, pore structures, and crystal morphology as a function of composition and gravity level was documented.
hypothesis: The research hypothesis for the ISS experiments is that minimizing gravity-driven transport phenomena, such as buoyancy, sedimentation, and convection results in a purely diffusion-controlled hydration process. Without the physical effects induced by gravity, diffusion will lead to a more uniform distribution of phases. As such, the dissolving cement particles will disperse in the aqueous solution, resulting in greater uniformity of features such as pore structures and crystal morphology in the hardened cement matrix. A different microstructure is expected to form in microgravity (µg), which possibly leads to different physical properties of µg-hardened cement paste with respect to that hardened in terrestrial gravity (1g).
research_impacts: The MICS investigation directly addresses the high priority need for lightweight space structures for habitats that protect crew. Results from this investigation enable the characterization of microstructural development in the hardening of cement paste and improve understanding of crystal growth and hydration kinetics, phase formations, pore distribution, and material properties. Also, MICS can increase understanding and control of the crystal growth kinetics, and morphology, to improve concrete properties. Improved cement properties can lead to improved concrete properties, durability, and lower CO2 emissions.
hardware: Commercially available plastic bags (Burst Pouches®) with two separate compartments divided by an internal and burstable seal allowing material mixing under sealed conditions.

title: PSI-85 Version 5 Nucleate Pool Boiling eXperiment(NPBX) Investigation
objective: The primary objective of the proposed study is to develop a mechanistic model for nucleate boiling under microgravity conditions. Specific objectives included: - Single bubble dynamics (nucleation, growth, and departure) under microgravity conditions under constant wall temperature. - Effect of liquid subcooling, wall superheat, and system pressure on single bubble dynamics. - Heat flux variation on the heated surface during single bubble evolution. - Lateral merger of bubbles formed at neighboring sites and mechanism of vapor removal from the surface.
approach: The research utilized a systematic and comprehensive approach to understand the complexities of nucleate pool boiling in a microgravity environment. The approach was characterized by a strategic ''building block'' strategy, progressing from simpler to more complex scenarios, enabling a gradual and insightful understanding of the underlying physics. Here's a detailed breakdown of the investigation approach: 1. Single Bubble Dynamics: The research commenced by focusing on the behavior of a single bubble nucleating from a pre-fabricated cavity on the aluminum wafer. This fundamental building block allowed for a detailed examination of bubble growth, departure (if any), and the associated heat transfer processes in microgravity conditions. 2. Multiple Bubble Mergers: Building upon the knowledge gained from single bubble studies, the investigation then explored the interactions of multiple bubbles. Experiments were conducted to study the merger of bubbles nucleating from different cavities. This stage investigated how bubbles merge in the lateral direction, the mechanisms of vapor removal from the heated surface after merger, and the impact of these interactions on the overall heat transfer rates. 3. Integral Nucleate Boiling: The investigation then broadened its scope by conducting experiments with boiling occurring over the entire heater surface. This aimed to obtain the boiling curve, which depicts the relationship between heat flux and wall superheat, under microgravity conditions. This provided a macroscopic view of nucleate pool boiling, considering the collective behavior of numerous bubbles. 4. Numerical Simulations: The experimental work was tightly coupled with complete numerical simulations of the boiling process. These simulations employed advanced computational fluid dynamics (CFD) techniques to capture the intricate details of bubble dynamics and heat transfer. The simulations accounted for a range of factors including time-varying system pressure and temperatures, the presence of dissolved gas in the liquid, surface tension effects, and the influence of microlayer evaporation. The numerical model was rigorously validated against the experimental data obtained in the NPBX experiments. 5. Model Development: The ultimate goal of the research was to develop a mechanistic model for nucleate pool boiling heat transfer under microgravity conditions. This model, based on the physical understanding derived from experimental observations and validated numerical simulations, aimed to provide a reliable tool for predicting boiling behavior across a wide range of parameters and conditions relevant to space applications.
hypothesis: In microgravity conditions, where buoyancy forces become negligible, it is expected that forces arising from the inertia of the liquid, evaporation, and condensation at the vapor-liquid interface, disjoining pressure, capillary pressure gradient, and the resulting flow field will become more dominant. The study aimed to understand and quantify the effect of these forces and identify the conditions under which quasi-static or steady-state boiling is possible under prolonged microgravity duration.
research_impacts: While the primary motivation for this investigation was to advance our understanding of boiling heat transfer in the context of space applications, the knowledge gained has significant implications for Earth-based technologies and scientific understanding as well. Here are some key potential impacts and benefits: 1. Improved Understanding of Boiling at Earth Gravity: By studying boiling in a microgravity environment where buoyancy forces are negligible, researchers can gain a clearer understanding of the interplay of other forces and phenomena that influence boiling behavior. This knowledge can, in turn, enhance our comprehension of boiling processes under Earth's gravity, where buoyancy often masks the effects of these more subtle factors. 2. Development of More Efficient Heat Transfer Systems: The insights gained from this research can contribute to the development of more efficient boiling heat transfer systems for a wide range of applications on Earth. Enhanced efficiency translates to reduced energy consumption, lower operational costs, and a reduced environmental footprint. 3. Advancements in Miniaturization of Electronics: As electronic devices continue to shrink in size, effective thermal management becomes increasingly critical. Understanding boiling in microgravity is crucial for developing innovative cooling solutions for miniaturized electronics, as these devices often operate at high heat fluxes and face challenges in dissipating heat effectively. 4. New Insights into Fluid Physics: This research offers valuable insights into fundamental fluid physics phenomena, including the behavior of bubbles, interfacial phenomena, and the dynamics of multiphase flows. This knowledge can lead to advancements in diverse fields, such as materials science, biomedical engineering, and environmental science.

title: PSI-86 Version 4 Observation and Analysis of Smectic Islands in Space(OASIS) Investigation
objective: OASIS studies the unique behavior of liquid crystals in microgravity, including their overall motion and the merging of crystal layers known as smectic islands. Liquid crystals are used for display screens in televisions and clocks, and they also occur in soaps and in cell membranes. The experiment allows detailed studies of the behavior of these structures, and how microgravity affects their unique ability to act like both a liquid and a solid crystal. The specific research objectives are: -To exploit the unique characteristics of freely suspended liquid crystals in a microgravity environment to advance the understanding of fluid state physics. -Study basic 2D hydrodynamics/fluid physics, probe droplet/island diffusion, hydrodynamic interactions, and droplet/island coalescence
approach: The OASIS experiment’s goal is to better understand the unique behavior of liquid crystals in microgravity. OASIS observes the various aspects of liquid crystals behavior in microgravity such as overall fluid motion, diffusion (the movement of particles from an area of high concentration to low concentration) and the merging of liquid crystal film layers called islands, Fundamental studies of complex fluid physics behavior will be accomplished in two dimensional fluids using freely suspended liquid crystals. The impact of the research is to advance the understanding of two-dimensional system physics of complex fluids. Space helmets could use ferroelectric liquid crystal micro-displays. It could advance the understanding of well aligned very high speed electro-optic devices.
hypothesis: In a microgravity environment, freely suspended smectic liquid crystal (FSLC) films will exhibit unique hydrodynamic and interfacial behaviors, such as reduced coarsening rates of island emulsions, enhanced 2D thermocapillarity effects, and distinct equilibrium spatial organization of islands, due to the absence of gravitational forces, convection, and sedimentation, enabling precise tests of theoretical models of 2D hydrodynamics and phase behavior.
research_impacts: Future space helmets may use certain types of liquid crystals in small display screens directly applied to the face shield where astronauts can easily view them. Understanding how liquid crystals behave in microgravity helps researchers to design liquid crystal displays (LCDs) that can perform better in space. Liquid crystals can flow like a liquid, but contain molecules that are arranged in a specific pattern, just like a crystal. Greater understanding of the physics behind these structures could lead to improved liquid crystal display devices, including devices with improved color contrast and response times. It could also advance research in high-speed electro-optic devices used to control a light beam.

title: PSI-87 Version 4 Pool Boiling Experiment(PBE) Investigation
objective: The program described here seeks to improve the understanding of the fundamental mechanisms that constitute nucleate pool boiling. The vehicle for accomplishing this is an investigation, including experiments to be conducted in microgravity and coupled with appropriate analyses, of the heat transfer and vapor bubble dynamics associated with nucleation, bubble growth or collapse, and subsequent motion. Certain effects that can be neglected at normal Earth gravity, such as surface tension and vapor momentum, can become quite significant in microgravity. Momentum imparted to the liquid by the vapor bubble during growth tends to draw the vapor bubble away from the surface, depending on the rate of growth, which in turn is governed by the temperature distribution in the liquid. Thermophoretic forces, arising from the variation of the liquid-vapor surface tension with temperature, on the other hand, tend to move the vapor bubble toward the region of higher temperature. The bubble motion will be governed by which of these two effects prevail. The elements of nucleate boiling, for which research conducted under microgravity would advance the basic understanding, are: 1. Nucleation or onset of boiling. Indications are that both heater surface temperature and temperature distribution in the liquid are necessary to describe nucleation. 2. The dynamic growth of a vapor bubble in the vicinity of the heater surface. This includes the shape as well as motion of the liquid-vapor interface as growth is taking place. These are influenced by the liquid temperature distribution at the initiation of growth. 3. The subsequent behavior of the vapor bubble. This includes the motion, whether departure takes place or not, and the associated heat transfer.
approach: The approach encompasses a comprehensive experimental methodology designed to dissect the nuances of the boiling process in an environment where gravity's influence is minimal. This approach aims to isolate and analyze the core mechanisms that drive nucleate pool boiling, offering insights that are obscured under normal Earth gravity conditions. Here is an outline of the investigation's methodological approach: 1. Experimental Setup in Microgravity: a. The investigation utilizes a specially designed experimental apparatus capable of accurately controlling and measuring heat flux, liquid subcooling levels, and temperature distribution within the liquid and at the heater surface. This apparatus is deployed in a microgravity environment provided by space-based platforms to ensure the minimization of gravity's influence on the boiling process. 2. Controlled Heat Flux Application: a. A key component of the approach involves applying a controlled heat flux to a pool of liquid, initiating the boiling process. The heat flux is carefully modulated to explore a range of boiling conditions, from gentle nucleation to vigorous boiling, under varying levels of liquid subcooling. 3. High-Resolution Data Acquisition: a. To capture the dynamics of bubble formation, growth, and departure, the investigation employs high-resolution, high-speed imaging techniques, along with precise temperature and heat flux measurement tools. This data acquisition setup allows for the detailed observation and analysis of bubble behavior and heat transfer phenomena during the boiling process. 4. Parameter Variation: a. The investigation systematically varies key parameters, including the heat flux magnitude, the degree of liquid subcooling, and the pressure within the system, to study their effects on the nucleation process, bubble dynamics, and heat transfer rates. This parameter variation helps in identifying the critical factors that influence nucleate pool boiling under microgravity. 5. Data Analysis and Model Development: a. The collected data undergoes rigorous analysis to elucidate the fundamental mechanisms of nucleate pool boiling, focusing on nucleation criteria, bubble growth rates, and heat transfer characteristics. Insights gained from the analysis are used to develop and refine predictive models that can accurately describe boiling behavior under a variety of conditions. 6. Cross-Comparison with Earth Gravity Data: a. Findings from the microgravity experiments are compared with data obtained from similar experiments conducted under Earth gravity conditions. This cross-comparison aids in isolating the effects of gravity on the boiling process and contributes to the development of generalized models that can predict boiling behavior across different gravitational environments.

title: PSI-88 Version 5 Packed Bed Reactor Experiment - 2(PBRE-2) Investigation
objective: The objective of the flight experiment is to study the hydrodynamics of packed beds in microgravity and under different conditions that lead to different flow regimes. The hydrodynamics consists of the pressure drop inside the packed bed and the liquid hold-up. The different regimes are the results of different liquid and gas flow rates, and different initial conditions embodied by gas and liquid pre-flows or flushes prior to beginning of the runs. Another objective of the experiment was to understand transient flow rates and the hysteresis in the pressure drop as a function of the flow rates.
approach: The PBRE-2 investigations employed a systematic and comprehensive approach to study the hydrodynamics of two-phase flow in packed bed reactors under microgravity conditions. The approach can be summarized in the following key steps: 1. Ground-Based Research and Model Development: Prior to the spaceflight experiments, extensive ground-based research was conducted to develop theoretical models and establish a foundation for understanding two-phase flow in packed beds. This included: Literature review: A thorough review of existing literature on single-phase and two-phase flow through porous media, focusing on pressure drop, flow regimes, and the influence of various parameters. Development of hydrodynamic models: Formulation of mathematical models, such as the modified Ergun equation, to predict pressure drop and flow regime transitions in microgravity. Ground-based experiments: Conducting experiments in reduced gravity environments, such as parabolic flights and drop towers, to gather preliminary data and validate initial model predictions. 2. Design and Development of Spaceflight Experiment: A dedicated experimental facility was designed and developed for operation on the ISS. This involved: Test facility design: Engineering a flow control system, test section, and data acquisition system capable of operating reliably in microgravity and meeting the specific requirements of the investigation. Definition of test matrix: Developing a comprehensive test matrix encompassing a wide range of gas and liquid flow rates, pre-flow conditions, and transient flow scenarios. 3. Execution of Spaceflight Experiments: The PBRE-2 experiments were conducted on the ISS, following the defined test matrix and procedures. This involved: Preflow procedures: Implementing the chosen pre-flow treatment (liquid flush or gas flush) before each test run. Flow control: Precisely controlling and varying the gas and liquid flow rates according to the test matrix. Data acquisition: Collecting data from pressure sensors, temperature sensors, and high-speed cameras throughout each test run. Downlinking data: Transmitting the acquired data to the ground for analysis. 4. Data Analysis and Interpretation: The downlinked data was meticulously analyzed to: Characterize flow regimes: Identify and classify the different flow regimes observed in the experiments based on pressure traces and video recordings. Evaluate pressure drop: Analyze the pressure drop data and compare it with model predictions to assess the validity and accuracy of the models. Investigate flow regime transitions: Determine the conditions and mechanisms leading to transitions between different flow regimes. Assess the influence of packing properties and pre-flow conditions: Analyze the impact of packing material wettability, size, and pre-flow treatments on the flow behavior and pressure drop. 5. Dissemination of Results: The findings of the PBRE-2 investigations were disseminated through: Peer-reviewed publications: Publishing research papers in scientific journals to share the results with the broader scientific community. Presentations at conferences: Presenting the research findings at relevant scientific conferences and workshops.
hypothesis: It is hypothesized that in microgravity two-phase packed bed flows, pressure drop will be a function of surface tension (captured by a modified Ergun equation), packing wettability and size, and pre-flow conditions. Furthermore, bubble removal will depend on bubble volume and liquid flow rate, and distinct flow regimes will emerge, with transitions governed by specific gas and liquid flow rate combinations.
research_impacts: Fundamental understanding the impact of reduced or zero gravity on the hydrodynamics (pressure drop, as well as distribution and holdup of each phase) is relevant to systems that involve two-phase flow such as life support systems, fuel cells, in-situ resource utilization, heat pipes, materials processing, production of pharmaceutical-grade water, and transport of nutrients in soils. Design and operation of many chemical and biological processing systems require this fundamental understanding of two-phase gas-liquid flows through porous media because many of these space-based systems or unit operations involve gas-liquid flows through porous media. Some examples of current space systems involving two-phase flow through fixed porous media include the Volatile Removal Assembly (VRA), the Integrated Advanced Water Recovery System (AWRS), and IntraVenous Water GENeration system (IVGEN). The ability to predict flow regimes and corresponding pressure drop in a particular system involving two-phase flow is crucial to the design of the fluid system and the pumping requirements.
