title: PSI-9 Version 1 Electrically Driven Liquid Film Flow Boiling in the Absence of Gravity(EHD) Investigation
objective: a-Provide fundamental understanding of the combined electrically driven (based on EHD conduction phenomenon) liquid film flow and dielectroporetic vapor extraction mechanism in the presence of phase change (liquid to vapor) in the absence of gravity. b-Provide a phenomenological foundation for the future development of electric field based two phase thermal management systems, leveraging EHD engineering advantages to develop systems of arbitrary mass flow requirements and geometries.
approach: As vapor bubbles cover the surface and grow or coalesce, the modes of heat transfer will be limited to conduction and possibly radiation. To avoid this and to enable boiling to take place, EHD-driven liquid film will be fed from the condenser section towards the heater. The inertia of liquid film flow along with DEP extraction force will repel vapor bubbles that have formed on the heater surface. In order to study the competing effects of flow inertia/DEP extraction force vs. bubble behavior in zero gravity, one needs to understand EHD generated liquid film flow and the DEP mechanism. The flow inertia is a function of applied EHD potential, electrode design, liquid film thickness and working fluid properties. The DEP extraction force is also a function of its corresponding electrode design, the spacing between its electrode and heated surface, and the applied potential for a given working fluid. Thus, the controlling parameters for this study are applied EHD conduction pumping potential, applied DEP potential, heat flux, and liquid film height for the selected working fluid and electrode designs. The electrode designs for EHD conduction pumping and DEP mechanism are based on our previous numerical and experimental work. Therefore, the electrode dimensions, design or distance from the heater surface will not need to be varied during this study.
hypothesis: Boiling is not acceptable in the absence of gravity unless the generated vapor bubbles can be expelled from the boiling surface and fresh liquid can be pumped onto the hot surface through some mechanism. EHD conduction pumping has the capability of pumping thin liquid films toward the heat source where the boiling takes place, with sufficient inertia to begin expelling bubbles from the heated surface at low heat fluxes. Furthermore, applying an EHD Dielectrophoretic (DEP) extraction force near the boiling surface guarantees the repulsion of vapor bubbles away from the heated surface even at high heat fluxes. Finally, the combined EHD driven liquid film flow boiling and DEP extraction force are expected to sustain and enhance the critical heat flux in the absence of gravity. Combining EHD conduction and DEP effects is therefore critical to the success of the ISS experiment.
research_impacts: This multi-physics proposal will provide basic scientific understanding about competing physical phenomena of flow inertia and bubble dynamics in electrically driven liquid film flow boiling in the presence of electric bubble extraction force (i.e., dielectrophoretic force) in microgravity. The electrically driven liquid film flow boiling data aboard ISS will determine the critical heat flux, onset of boiling, absence of hysteresis, and bubble characteristics in the absence of gravity.There are a number of potential terrestrial and space applications for this electrohydrodynamic (EHD) driven two-phase heat transport device in all scales (from macro-scale to truly micro-scales). For example, this device can be used to effectively remove heat from electronics in micro- and zero-gravity environment for NASA's future space stations and long term missions. It can also be used in satellites (e.g., embedded system into satellite's multi-functional structure).Terrestrially, it can be used in high intensity electronics cooling as well as in various phase change devices. To achieve these applications, the basic scientific understanding about competing physical phenomena of flow inertia and bubble dynamics in electrically driven liquid film flow boiling in the presence of electric bubble extraction force (i.e.,dielectrophoretic force) in microgravity is needed.

title: PSI-90 Version 3 Packed Bed Reactor Experiment(PBRE) Investigation
objective: The PBRE studies the behavior of gases and liquids when they flow simultaneously through a column filled with fixed porous media. The porous media or “packing” can be made of different shapes and materials and are used widely in chemical engineering as a means to enhance the contact between two immiscible fluid phases (e.g., liquid-gas, water-oil, etc.). Packed columns can serve as reactors, scrubbers, strippers, etc. in systems where efficient interphase contact is desired, both on Earth and in space.
approach: The PBRE investigation employs an approach that combines theoretical modeling with rigorous experimental testing to achieve its objectives. Here's a breakdown of the key aspects: 1. Theoretical Modeling: Existing Models: PBRE builds upon existing models for pressure drop and flow regime transitions in packed bed reactors, particularly those developed by Motil et al. (2003) and Guo et al. (2004). Model Validation: The experiment focuses on validating these models, extending them to lower flow rates relevant to water recovery systems, and bridging them with other models. New Models: The data collected through PBRE is used to develop new models and scaling laws that accurately predict flow characteristics in 0-g and partial-g environments. 2. Experimental Setup and Procedures: Test Sections: PBRE utilizes two identical test sections, each a 60 cm long, 5 cm diameter cylindrical column. One section is packed with glass beads (wetting), the other with Teflon beads (non-wetting) to isolate surface tension effects. Fluid Flow: The experiment uses nitrogen and water as the gas and liquid phases, with a wide range of flow rates, from very low to high, to cover operational regimes. Instrumentation: A comprehensive suite of sensors is used to measure flow rates, temperatures, and pressures. The experiment also includes two high-speed video cameras to visualize flow patterns. Test Matrix: The investigation is organized into several test series (''Ops''), each focused on specific flow conditions and packing materials. Data Acquisition: The experiment meticulously collects data, with careful time-correlation of measurements to ensure accurate analysis. 3. Addressing Anomalies: Flow Rate Control: The team encountered anomalies with the GN2 flow rate and pressure fluctuations, leading to troubleshooting and adjustments in the experiment's setup and procedures. High-Speed Video: The cameras experienced limitations with operating at the desired frame rates, requiring modifications to data acquisition strategies. 4. Data Analysis: Model Validation: Data is analyzed to compare experimental results with model predictions, identifying any discrepancies and refining the models. New Model Development: The collected data is used to develop new models and scaling laws, aiming for greater accuracy and applicability in microgravity environments. 5. Data Organization: Physical Sciences Informatics (PSI): The PBRE team meticulously organizes the experimental data in PSI, a database for physical sciences data, to ensure accessibility and analysis. The PBRE investigation relies on a combination of theoretical modeling, rigorous experimental testing, and comprehensive data analysis to achieve its objectives. This approach is designed to contribute to a deeper understanding of the behavior of packed bed reactors in microgravity, leading to improved design tools and operational strategies for future space applications. 6. Dissemination of Results: The findings of the PBRE-2 investigations were disseminated through: Peer-reviewed publications: Publishing research papers in scientific journals to share the results with the broader scientific community. Presentations at conferences: Presenting the research findings at relevant scientific conferences and workshops. Reports and documentation: Preparing detailed reports and documentation of the experimental procedures, data analysis, and conclusions.
hypothesis: It is hypothesized that the gravity plays a significant role in determining the flow characteristics (pressure drop, flow regime transitions, liquid holdup, and mass transfer) of gas-liquid flows through porous media.
research_impacts: Water-recovery systems, fuel cells and other equipment on the International Space Station use packed bed reactors, but currently none are designed to handle both liquid and gas at the same time. With improved understanding of how packed bed two-phase flow works in microgravity, scientists are be able to design more efficient, lightweight thermal management and life support systems that use less energy, benefiting the Space Station and future lunar and Mars missions. Design rules for gas-liquid flows through packed columns are well developed on Earth (i.e., for normal gravity) but lacking for reduced or zero gravity. The Packed Bed Reactor Experiment seeks to fill this knowledge gap by studying the hydrodynamics of gas-liquid flows in zero gravity through packed columns. By understanding how gravity affects gas-liquid flows through packed columns (or packed beds, as they are known in the industry) better, more predictive correlations for pressure drops and flow regime maps can be developed with the proper gravity-dependent terms included.

title: PSI-91 Version 4 Physics of Colloids in Space(PCS) Investigation
objective: The primary objectives of the PCS investigation were to successfully grow binary colloidal crystal alloy structures to monitor their nucleation and growth kinetics with static and dynamic light scattering, determine their structures using laser light crystallography and the properties of the superlattices using dynamic light scattering. In addition, the structure and dynamics of gel-like structures formed by colloid-polymer mixtures will be measured using static and dynamic light scattering and the ultimate equilibrium structures behavior of the mixture will be determined. Finally, large scale fractal colloid aggregates and gels will be grown to measure their mechanical properties using dynamic light scattering, and potentially the cell oscillation techniques.
approach: For binary colloidal crystal alloy the samples will consist of polymethylmethacrylate (PMMA) particles, stabilized by a thin coating of poly-12-hydroxystearic acid, and suspended in a mixture of decalin and tetralin adjusted to exactly match the index of refraction of the PMMA. Once in orbit, the samples will be homogenized by rapidly spinning each sample cell and suddenly stopping it. Subsequent to homogenization, the nucleation and growth of the binary colloidal alloy crystallites will be monitored by static light scatter in the forward direction. The small angle light scattering will be complemented by larger angle scattering examining the Bragg reflections of the crystals. For the colloidal-polymer mixture part of the investigation the colloidal particles will again be PMMA spheres suspended in an index matched fluid. The volume fractions of these samples will range from about 1% to 30%. The polymer will be polystyrene, with a molecular weight ranging from about 100,000 to 1,000,000. The colloid-polymer mixtures will be homogenized using the same procedure used for the binary colloid mixtures. Immediately after they are homogenized, the small angle scattering will be monitored to measure the formation of the gel-like structure. Dynamic light scattering will be performed concurrently as the gel forms to obtain a sensitive indication of the final formation of the gel. Once equilibrium is achieved, if colloidal crystals are formed in one of the phases the growth and structure of the crystals will be studied using both powder average Bragg scattering and dynamic light scattering. For the fractal colloidal aggregate and gels the aggregation of the colloidal particles will be initiated by mixing the colloidal suspension with another chemical that causes aggregation. Upon initiation of the aggregation, the growth of the colloidal aggregates will be monitored by both dynamic and static light scattering. In addition to the light scattering measurements, small amplitude oscillations of the gel structure will be performed to measure the shear modulus of the gel directly and compare with the light scattering measurements.
hypothesis: The availability of microgravity will allow binary colloidal superlattices to be formed from different materials providing new insights into the nucleation and growth kinetics of binary colloidal crystal alloy and thereby establish the new field of “colloid engineering.” This work will unambiguously determine the equilibrium phase diagram for attractive colloidal particles where the attraction is induced by depletion effects through the addition of polymer. It will also provide important new insight into the transition between equilibrium and kinetically limited behavior, in the absence of sedimentation. Further, this investigation will also lead to the fabrication of fractal colloidal structures that extend over the largest range of length scales ever produced, providing a critical test of our understanding of the formation of these structures. With such extended structures, it will be possible to study their physical properties and determine the consequences of the scale invariance on the properties. It will determine the fundamental limits of the range over which fractal structures can exist.
research_impacts: The long term goal of this research is to establish a new method of fabricating materials, “Colloid Engineering,” where novel materials are fabricated using colloidal particles as precursors. With appropriate choices of the sizes of the particles, it should be possible to form colloidal alloy crystals of higher volume fraction than can be made with monodisperse particles. These colloidal alloys may form the precursors for very high quality ceramics. Alternatively, the particles could be made from different materials, forming colloidal superlattices with novel properties. Then, for example, one set of particles could be plastic and the other set of particles could be a metal or a semiconductor. Alternatively, these structures may be useful in forming materials with reduced phase space available for radiation, allowing a much simpler way of fabricating structures which possess photonic band gaps. Colloid engineering may offer a simple method for making these materials that completely bypasses the difficulties faced by traditional lithography techniques. The superlattices could also be used as novel optical switches or displays.
hardware: EXpedite the PRocess of Experiments to Space Station (EXPRESS) Rack

title: PSI-93 Version 7 Pore Formation and Mobility Investigation(PFMI) Investigation
objective: The scientific objective of the investigation was to observe porosity formation and its movement. Methods to minimize porosity and its influence will also be examined. Experimental variables that was investigated include, but are not limited to, bubble size, bubble number, imposed temperature gradient, material properties, and the effect of applying vibration to the system. The role of ''spring and piston'' assemblages and in-situ thermocouples was also investigated and assessed.
approach: The experimental approach consisted of employing a 10mm inside diameter quartz tubes on the order of 30 cm in length that was filled with pure succinonitrile (SCN) and SCN to which a small amount of water has been added to simulate alloy solidification. To investigate pore formation the sample tubes was filled by, at least, the three following methods. (1) Pieces of SCN was put in the tube. (2) SCN was cast into the tube. (3) SCN was cast into the tube and then be directionally solidified. Case 1 ensured porosity in the sample, case 2 allowed porosity to develop, and case 3 was prepared with the intent of minimizing porosity. Each sample tube was outfitted with an effective “spring and piston” assemblage and in-situ thermocouples. While thermocouples were required to accurately characterize the temperatures and temperature gradients they could also act as sites for pore nucleation and holding. The sample tubes were then inserted in a directional solidification furnace, which establishes a temperature gradient in the liquid and permits observation of the molten region. The furnace mounts on g-limit, a MSFC developed vibration isolation platform; this assemblage fits and was designed to operate within the ISS microgravity Glovebox. Porosity, which forms in the samples, was tracked and recorded with two video cameras set at 90 degrees from each other and orthogonal to the sample tube.
hypothesis: Direct observation of pore/bubble formation and their mobility during processing in a microgravity environment will provide insight regarding the minimization of this detrimental feature during solidification processing of important metal alloys and semiconductors.
research_impacts: PFMI provides insight on how materials solidify in the space environment. Once this process is understood and improvements are made, future manufacturing processes can take place in the microgravity environment providing robust products. On Earth, materials that contain pores created and trapped during solidification degrade properties and cause a distinct weakening in the overall structure of the cast product. Examples of these materials include semiconductors and aircraft turbine blades.

title: PSI-94 Version 3 Physics of Hard Spheres Experiment(PHaSE) Investigation
objective: By significantly reducing gravitational sedimentation the primary objective of this microgravity investigation was to quantify the volume fractions at which dispersions of hard spheres freeze, melt, and become glasses; the equilibrium structure associated with each phase; the dynamics of Brownian fluctuations in each phase; the kinetics of the nucleation and growth of the crystalline phase; the static elastic modulus of the crystalline and glassy phases; the low shear viscosity from the freezing point to close packing, and the yield stress and plasticity of the crystalline phase.
approach: The experiment involved making a series of measurements on approximately 8 different samples of different concentrations (i.e. volume fractions of PMMA in an index matching fluid). The samples were made from a mixture of decalin, tetralin, and PMMA spheres with a stabilizing polymer grafted onto them. The decalin (index - 1.48) and the tetralin (index - 1.54) was mixed in a combination which index matches the PMMA (index - 1.51), allowing the use of single photon counting techniques to probe the particle dynamics at different concentrations. Once in orbit, the experiment was initialized and each of the samples melted to start the nucleation and growth phase. After melting, each sample was examined to ensure that complete melting has occurred, and immediate static scattering measurements will begin and progress for 24 hours on the nucleating sample. After each melting phase, a concentration dependent nucleation and growth phase occurred and was monitored by static light scattering measurements. These measurements proceeded while the experiment entered into an equilibration phase during which longer range order formed. The static light scattering measurements proceeded until the Bragg peaks were well developed and sufficient data for ensemble averages were taken for a sound statistical basis for the conclusions intended to experimentally ascertain. Periodic measurements, both static and dynamic, were made to gage the progress and determine if alternate procedures are required. During this period, dynamic light scattering measurements were performed on the nucleating sample. Other measurements such as rheology measurements were performed on the other seven samples after this 24 hours period.
hypothesis: Some colloids (a system of fine particles suspended in a fluid) have the ability to act like a gas, liquid, solid, or even glass, depending on the relative concentration between the suspended material and the solution they are suspended in, and/or the presence or absence of gravity. The behavior of a densely packed colloid here on earth mimics glass in the distribution of its particles, while in space, the same density colloid acts more closely like a solid. This results in a highly organized, lattice-like arrangement of particles in the colloid. It is hypothesized that the complete set of data from the microgravity experiments to test scalings proposed in the literature, e.g. the shear rate dependence of the viscosity and the rate of crystal growth with either the short- or the long-term self diffusion coefficient; the relationships among the osmotic pressure, the static shear modulus, and the yield stress for solid phases.
research_impacts: The colloidal engineering process will play a fundamental role in the creation of new materials and products in space, such as optical switches and lasers for communications and displays, and 3D Bragg crystals for controlling light. Understanding the physics describing the Packing of Hard Spheres has everyday impacts and benefits here on earth including Grain packing; Structure of Liquids, Solids and Glasses; Freezing Transition; Flow and Plasticity of Sand; Optimization of data storage and transmission in the presence of Noise and Opto-electronic Materials, Light Localization and Photonic Bandgaps. The ultimate payoff will be a definitive set of data for the hard spheres useful for (a) testing fundamental correlations among physical properties, (b) serving as a reference for understanding the behavior of systems with more complex interaction potentials, and (c) guiding attempts to control or modify the structure of densely packed media.
hardware: PHaSE H/W with 8 Samples MSL-1 Glovebox

title: PSI-95 Version 5 Plasma Kristall-3 Plus(PK-3 Plus) Investigation
objective: Plasma crystals are a new kind of matter, rediscovered in 1994. They form under certain conditions in a complex (dusty) plasma. There, the electrically charged dust particles arrange in a regular macroscopic crystal lattice. This structure allows for an investigation of the properties of condensed matter on the kinetic level. This means that basic processes, such as melting, can be followed by observing the motion of individual particles. PK-3 will give investigators a better understanding of plasma in space and will determine the critical points for the plasma. Gravity plays an important role for the structure of plasma crystals. In microgravity large 3-dimensional plasma crystals can be grown and studied in detail on the most fundamental, the kinetic level. Complex plasmas can be seen as model systems for the investigation of fundamental phenomena in liquids and crystals and provide information on the motion of single particles (“atoms”). This provides new insights into the field of condensed matter.
approach: PK-3 Plus is a symmetrical driven radio-frequency plasma discharge with special features for the investigation of complex plasmas under microgravity conditions. As a second generation laboratory, PK-3 Plus provides major new possibilities for these investigations due to its design improvements relative to the first long-term experiment PKE-Nefedov. The PK-3 Plus apparatus allows investigations at neutral gas pressures between 0.05 - 2.5 millibar and radio frequency (rf) power of 0.01 - 1 W. The complex plasma can consist of monodisperse particles in a size range from 1 - 20 micrometers. Up to six particle sizes can be added to the experimental volume. It is possible to change the number of particles, the composition of particles, the plasma conditions and the neutral gas pressure during one experiment. The particle cloud can be excited by an electrical low frequency signal on the electrodes (0.1 - 100 Hz at a maximum amplitude of 50 V) or by a low frequency modulation of the rf-amplitude in different wave forms (sinusoidal, square, pulse, etc.). The PK-3 Plus investigation has two major pieces of equipment: the experimental block, and the telescience system (TS). The research will be performed on the ISS inside the plasma chamber situated inside of the experimental block. The experimental block is attached via a tube to the space environment to produce the prevacuum for turbomolecular pump, which can produce pressure in the plasma chamber less than 10-5 millibar. The TS is the computer in which the chamber conditions can be altered via actuators in the experimental block and the storage unit for the data collected. This PK3 Plus laboratory has state of the art hardware and software, and provides better diagnostics than previous hardware. The PK-3 Plus laboratory was operated on the Russian segment of ISS by Russian cosmonauts mostly. Typical experimental campaigns have 3 or 4 runs to meet the requirements of the investigator. There are two modes, automatic and manual, for this investigation. During the manual mode, crew time will be required to complete the investigation. Experimenters are following live video transmission from the experimental block in the control center in Korolev guiding the cosmonaut via audio contact for experiment parameters optimization. Full set Recorded videos and housekeeping data are to be returned on hard drives via Soyuz capsule. The experiments run on three or four consecutive days during single experimental campaign. Some days areon automatic, as mentioned above, and some days are manual operations, depending on the cosmonaut availability and investigators plans. On automatic days, the machine can be left alone to run, passively taking measurements of the complex plasma behaviors under microgravity. On the manual day, there will be a cosmonaut present, adjusting settings to achieve the required states of the plasma. The experiment is expected to take approximately 90 minutes each day.
research_impacts: 99% of the visible matter in the universe is in the plasma state and dust is ubiquitous, too. Thus so called dusty plasmas can be found in interstellar media, in planetary forming discs, in cometary atmospheres, in Saturn rings, etc. The results from the PK-3 Plus laboratory on the ISS on the charging of the microparticles/dust and their interaction with each other and the surrounding plasma, the so-called basic fundamental questions, are very helpful in the understanding of dusty plasmas in space. Additionally, complex plasmas are models for liquid and crystalline systems providing new insights into the formation and behavior of condensed matter.

title: PSI-96 Version 6 Pore-Mushy Zone Interaction during Directional Solidification of Alloys: Three Dimensional Simulation and Comparison with Experiments Investigation
objective: The primary objective of this research was to develop a numerical 3D model capable of simulating the pore-mushy zone interaction during directional solidification of Succinonitrile -Water alloys in microgravity and test the simulation results against the Pore Formation and Mobility Investigation (PFMI) microstructural observations, quantitatively and qualitatively.
approach: This investigation exploited forefront methods in microscale solidification and developed models based on phase filed (PF), cellular automaton (CA) and Lattice Boltzmann (LB) to simulate pore formation and its motion during directional solidification. The results from the Pore Formation and Mobility Investigation (PFMI) experiments were conducted in the microgravity environment aboard the Space Station with the intent of better understanding the role entrained porosity/bubbles play on microstructure during controlled directional solidification (DS). Several sets of time-temperature-interface-bubble interaction data were extracted and analyzed from the PFMI videos. The simulation results were tested against the PFMI microstructural observations.
hypothesis: Previous real time observations in transparent analogues of interactions between a bubble and an array of primary dendrites are essentially “two-dimensional” (2D) and are affected by the “wall” effects. Contrary to earlier belief, it is now recognized that the basic premise of such experiments, i.e. 2D dendrites represent morphology of a three-dimensional (3D) array, is false. This investigation hypothesizes that understanding pore-mushy zone interaction in real castings requires both the experimental observations and also the theoretical/numerical modeling with 3D array of dendrites.
research_impacts: This investigation helped to explain fundamental aspects of the mechanisms that regulate the formation of microporosities. The formation of these defects depends on microstructure features that cannot be properly captured by current meso- and macro-scale models based on averaging techniques. The direct numerical simulation of bubble dynamics in a dendritic network can provide a relation between macroscopically observable variables like cooling rate or temperature gradient and difficult to measure dynamic microscopic features like microporosity distribution, interdendritic permeability, solute redistribution, and dendrite arm spacing. This research not only provided valuable contribution to the understanding of pore-mushy zone interaction during solidification in the absence of gravity, which would be helpful for future in-space fabrication processes involving solidification, but it was a first step to quantitatively simulate such 3D interactions during terrestrial directional solidification in realistic size sample domains. Although much observation has been done in pictures of static microstructures at different stages of solidification, it has never been possible to capture the dynamic response of these features in an evolving mushy zone. This information is critical to assess, validate, and improve macroscale mushy zone models used in current casting and welding codes.
hardware: Microgravity experimental data for validation was obtained using PFMI furnace

title: PSI-97 Version 4 Ring-Sheared Drop - Amyloid Fibril Formation(RSD-AFF) Investigation
objective: This campaign centered on four main objectives: (i) engineering the RSD to flight proven hardware, (ii) testing measurement and instrumentation methods aboard the ISS, (iii) studying protein kinetics under interfacial shear, and (iv) measuring and modeling protein solution rheology. The primary obective of this investigation is to quantify the effects of flow on fibrillization in the bulk and at interfaces, specifically at the air/water interface. This includes studying protein kinetics under interfacial shear, and measuring and modeling protein solution rheology. The overall objective is project to advance the mechanistic description of fibrillization by determining how shearing flow affects each of the stages of amyloid formation process − protein unfolding and nuclei formation, growth into protofibrils, and elongation and intertwining into mature fibrils and fibril growth − without any influence from solid boundaries.
approach: The Ring Shear Drop (RSD) is used to facilitate amyloidogenesis and study flow dynamics without solid wall interactions. It uses surface tension to contain fluids in a microgravity environment. Techniques like Particle Tracking Velocimetry (PTV) are used to measure fluid dynamics and protein interactions. This information was used to create high-fidelity computational models. Formation and flow of protein aggregates on the surface of the drop will be imaged by the microscope as a function of time. The RSD imaged the surface of a 2.50 cm diameter drop of protein solution with shear imposed by the rotation of one of the two sharp-edged rings (essentially knife edges) that constrain the drop. A separate measure of the turbidity quantified by the extinction of a light beam through the center of the drop provided an independent signal for fibril formation. A variable degree of shear was imposed on the drop with a negligible contact with solid boundaries. Velocity of the fluid on the surface of the drop will be determined by standard cross-correlation techniques from images obtained by the microscope. Details regarding sample composition and experimental parameters can be found in RSD Experimental Table.
hypothesis: The absence of gravity in a microgravity environment will significantly alter the amyloid fibril formation process in proteins.The hypothesis tested was that if protein solutions in microgravity are seeded with fibrils and subject to steady interfacial shear, then amyloidogenesis will occur with the extent of gelation depending on total protein concentration.
research_impacts: Amyloid fibril formation in proteins is of great interest because of its role in diseases such as Alzheimer’s and Parkinson’s. For example, the waxy plaque choking off neurons in Alzheimer’s patients consists of the A-beta protein that has formed into amyloid fibrils. The microgravity environment aboard the ISS was utilized to study the biophysics of protein amyloidogenesis. The absence of gravity allows surface tension to provide fluid containment so that wall nucleation and other complications associated with solid containers can be avoided. Flow effects on protein fibrillization was studied at fluid interfaces similar to physiological processes, as all brain tissue consists of interfaces with fluidity, being comprised of cell membranes. The goal is to advance mechanistic descriptions of amyloid fibril formation.

title: PSI-98 Version 4 Spacecraft Fire Safety Experiment-I(SAFFIRE-I) Investigation
objective: The objectives of this investigation were to: (1) determine how rapidly a large scale fire grows in low-gravity and (2) investigate the low-g flammability limits compared to those obtained in NASA’s normal gravity material flammability screening test.
approach: The Saffire-1 experiments was performed on the Orbital Science’s Cygnus resupply vehicle after it deberthed from the ISS. The sample material for Saffire-I is a composite fabric called Sibal consisting of cotton on a fiberglass substrate (75% cotton, 25% fiberglass by weight). It has been used in many space experiments because it burns like cotton but maintains structural integrity after the cotton is consumed. The sample was approximately 0.94 meters long and 0.4 meters wide, simulating a large piece of flammable fabric. The Saffire-1 flight unit had a sample card installed in the middle of a large flow duct. Air is drawn through the flow duct by fans located at the top of the duct with flow straighteners at the bottom of the experiment module. Saffire-I was conducted at an air flow velocity of 20 cm/s. Once the sample was ignited flame images were captured using two cameras. In addition, thermocouples provided flow, flame, and plume temperatures, two radiometers recorded flame radiation, solid state sensors were used to measure pressure, CO2 and O2 mole faction, and two anemometer tracked flow velocity. All data was compressed, and subsequently downlinked.
hypothesis: This investigation hypothesizes that due to large differences between fire behavior in normal and reduced gravity, the use of terrestrial fires and fire standards to design spacecraft fire safety systems presents an inherent risk to the vehicle because of the significant level of uncertainty. While this approach has been successful thus far, the uncertainty and risk will increase as exploration missions venture further from earth with considerably longer transit times for a safe return. There is a significant lack of microgravity data available for spacecraft designers on which to base their fire safety designs and procedures. To address this knowledge gap, this investigation proposed to conduct large-scale fire safety experiments in an expendable spacecraft without risk to a crew.
research_impacts: The Saffire-I experiment provides a new way to study a realistic fire on an exploration vehicle, which has not been possible in the past because the risks are too high. Instruments on an unmanned cargo vessel measure oxygen, carbon dioxide, heat, pressure and flame growth, and two video cameras provide views of the flame. Results determine microgravity flammability limits for several spacecraft materials, help to validate NASA’s material selection criteria, and how microgravity and limited oxygen affect flame size. The investigation is crucial for the safety of current and future space missions. Studying fire in small, sealed environments such as the Cygnus cargo supply vehicle benefits fire safety and prevention efforts on Earth, including inside mines, airplanes, or submarines.
